stem_md:
Let  $A$  be a  $n\times n$  complex matrix whose eigenvalues have absolute value at most  $1$ . Prove that   $$  \|A^n\|\le \dfrac{n}{\ln 2} \|A\|^{n-1}.  $$   (Here  $\|B\|=\sup\limits_{\|x\|\leq 1} \|Bx\|$  for every  $n\times n$  matrix  $B$  and  $\|x\|=\sqrt{\sum\limits_{i=1}^n |x_i|^2}$  for every complex vector  $x\in\mathbb{C}^n$ .)

(Proposed by Ian Morris and Fedor Petrov, St. Petersburg State University)
solution_md:
Official solution:
<details><summary>Hint</summary>Apply the Cayley-Hamilton theorem.</details>
<details><summary>Solution 1.</summary>Let  $r=\|A\|$ . We have to prove  $\|A^n\| \leq \frac{n}{\ln2} r^{n-1}$ .

As is well-known, the matrix norm satisfies  $\|XY\|\leq \|X\|\cdot \|Y\|$  for any matrices  $X,Y$ , and as a simple consequence,  $\|A^k\|\leq \|A\|^k = r^k$  for every positive integer  $k$ .

Let  $\chi(t)=(t-\lambda_1)(t-\lambda_2)\dots (t-\lambda_n)=t^n+c_1t^{n-1}+\dots+c_n$  be the characteristic polynomial of  $A$ . From Vieta's formulas we get   $$  |c_k| = \left| \sum_{1\le i_1 < \ldots < i_k\le n} \lambda_{i_1}\cdots\lambda_{i_k} \right| \le \sum_{1\le i_1 < \ldots < i_k\le n} \big|\lambda_{i_1}\cdots\lambda_{i_k} \big| \le \binom{n}{k} \quad (k=1,2,\ldots,n)  $$   By the Cayley-Hamilton theorem we have  $\chi(A)=0$ , so   $$  \|A^n\| = \|c_1A^{n-1}+\dots+c_n\| \leq \sum_{k=1}^n \binom{n}k \|A^k\| \leq \sum_{k=1}^n \binom{n}k r^k = (1+r)^n-r^n.  $$   Combining this with the trivial estimate  $\|A^n\|\le r^n$ , we have   $$  \|A^n\| \leq \min\big( r^n, (1+r)^n-r^n) \big).  $$   Let  $r_0=\frac1{\sqrt[n]2-1}$ ; it is easy to check that the two bounds are equal if  $r=r_0$ , moreover   $$  r_0 = \frac1{e^{\ln2/n}-1}  <  \frac{n}{\ln2}.  $$   For  $r\leq r_0$  apply the trivial bound:   $$  \|A^n\| \leq r^n \leq r_0\cdot r^{n-1}  <  \frac{n}{\ln2} r^{n-1}.  $$   For  $r >  r_0$  we have   $$  \|A^n\| \leq (1+r)^n-r^n = r^{n-1} \cdot \frac{(1+r)^n-r^n}{r^{n-1}}.  $$   Notice that the function  $f(r)=\frac{(1+r)^n-r^n}{r^{n-1}}$  is decreasing because the numerator has degree  $n-1$  and all coefficients are positive, so   $$  \frac{(1+r)^n-r^n}{r^{n-1}}  <  \frac{(1+r_0)^n-r_0^n}{r_0^{n-1}} = r_0 \big((1+1/r_0)^n-1) = r_0  <  \frac{n}{\ln2},  $$   so  $\|A^n\|  <  \frac{n}{\ln2} r^{n-1}$ .</details>
<details><summary>Solution 2.</summary>We will use the following facts which are easy to prove:

1. For any square matrix  $A$  there exists a unitary matrix  $U$  such that  $U A U^{-1}$  is upper-triangular.
2. For any matrices  $A$ ,  $B$  we have  $\|A\|\leq\|(A|B)\|$  and  $\|B\|\leq\|(A|B)\|$  where  $(A|B)$  is the matrix whose columns are the columns of  $A$  and the columns of  $B$ .
3. For any matrices  $A$ ,  $B$  we have  $\|A\|\leq\|\left(\frac{A}{B}\right)\|$  and  $\|B\|\leq\|\left(\frac{A}{B}\right)\|$  where  $\left(\frac{A}{B}\right)$  is the matrix whose rows are the rows of  $A$  and the rows of  $B$ . \item Adding a zero row or a zero column to a matrix does not change its norm.

We will prove a stronger inequality \[ \|A^n\| \leq n \|A\|^{n-1} \] for any  $n\times n$  matrix  $A$  whose eigenvalues have absolute value at most  $1$ . We proceed by induction on  $n$ . The case  $n=1$  is trivial. Without loss of generality we can assume that the matrix  $A$  is upper-triangular. So we have \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & \cdots & a_{1n} 0 & a_{22} & \cdots & a_{2n} \cdots &\cdots & & \cdots 0 & 0 & \cdots & a_{nn} \end{pmatrix}. \] Note that the eigenvalues of  $A$  are precisely the diagonal entries. We split  $A$  as the sum of  $3$  matrices,  $A=X+Y+Z$  as follows: \[ X = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & 0 & \cdots & 0 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \cdots &\cdots & & \cdots 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \end{pmatrix},\quad Y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & a_{12} & \cdots & a_{1n} 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \cdots &\cdots & & \cdots 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \end{pmatrix},\quad Z = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 0 & a_{22} & \cdots & a_{2n} \cdots &\cdots & & \cdots 0 & 0 & \cdots & a_{nn} \end{pmatrix}. \] Denote by  $A'$  the matrix obtained from  $A$  by removing the first row and the first column: \[ A' = \begin{pmatrix} a_{22} & \cdots & a_{2n} \cdots & & \cdots 0 & \cdots & a_{nn} \end{pmatrix}. \] We have  $\|X\|\leq 1$  because  $|a_{11}|\leq 1$ . We also have \[ \|A'\|=\|Z\|\leq \|Y+Z\| \leq \|A\|. \] Now we decompose  $A^n$  as follows: \[ A^n = X A^{n-1} + (Y+Z) A^{n-1}. \] We substitute  $A=X+Y+Z$  in the second term and expand the parentheses. Because of the following identities: \[ Y^2=0,\quad YX=0,\quad ZY=0,\quad ZX=0 \] only the terms  $Y Z^{n-1}$  and  $Z^n$  survive. So we have \[ A^n = X A^{n-1} + (Y+Z) Z^{n-1}. \] By the induction hypothesis we have  $\|A'^{n-1}\|\leq (n-1)\|A'\|^{n-2}$ , hence  $\|Z^{n-1}\|\leq (n-1)\|Z\|^{n-2}\leq (n-1)\|A\|^{n-2}$ . Therefore \[ \|A^n\| \leq \|X A^{n-1}\| + \|(Y+Z) Z^{n-1}\| \leq \|A\|^{n-1} + (n-1) \|Y+Z\| \|A\|^{n-2}\leq n \|A\|^{n-1}. \]</details>

Triangle $BCF$ has a right angle at $B$ . Let $A$ be the point on line $CF$ such that $FA=FB$ and $F$ lies between $A$ and $C$ . Point $D$ is chosen so that $DA=DC$ and $AC$ is the bisector of $\angle{DAB}$ . Point $E$ is chosen so that $EA=ED$ and $AD$ is the bisector of $\angle{EAC}$ . Let $M$ be the midpoint of $CF$ . Let $X$ be the point such that $AMXE$ is a parallelogram. Prove that $BD,FX$ and $ME$ are concurrent.
I claim that they are concurrent at circumcenter of $\triangle BXE$ $\boxed{\textbf{Claim 1:}\; D \; \text{lies on}\; \omega \; \text{(circumcircle of}\; \triangle BCF)}$
ProofLet $L$ be intersection of $BA$ with $\omega$ - which is circumcircle of $\triangle BCF$ . Since $L \in \omega$ , we have $\angle LCA = \angle LCF = \angle LBF = \angle BAF = \angle LAC$ since $FA = FB$ . Hence $LC = LA$ or $L$ lies on perpendicular bisector of segment $AC$ . On other hand, line $AD$ is reflection of line $AB$ over line $AC$ , combine with $D$ lies on perpendicular of $AC$ , we have $D$ is reflection of $L$ over $CF$ - which is diameter of $\omega$ , implies that $D$ lies on $\omega$ .
$\boxed{\textbf{Claim 2:}\; X, D, E \; \text{are collinear and}\; X \;\text{lies on}\; \omega}$
ProofSince $ED = EA$ and $AD$ is internal bisector of $\angle CAE$ , we have $\angle ADE = \angle DAE = \angle CAD$ or $DE \parallel AC$ . On other hand, the assumption gives us $EX \parallel AC$ , which implies $X, D, E$ are collinear. Note that $\angle MCD = \angle MED$ or $MCDE$ is parallelogram, which implies $ME = CD = AL$ , since $ME \parallel AB$ , we conclude that $ALME$ is also parallelogram, thus $ML = AE = MX$ and $ML \parallel AE \parallel MX$ , or $X$ is reflection of $L$ over $M$ (this also means $X$ lies on $\omega$ )
$\boxed{\textbf{Claim 3:}\; DA = DB \; \text{and}\; F\; \text{is incenter of}\;\triangle DAB}$
ProofSince **Claim 1**, $LCDA$ is a parallelogram or $\angle FAD = \angle CAD = \angle ACD = \angle FBD$ . Note that $FA = FB$ , hence $D$ also lies on perpendicular bisector of segment $AB$ and $BF$ is internal bisector of $\angle DBA$ since $FA$ is internal bisector of $\angle DAB$ .
$\boxed{\text{Claim 4:}\; B, F, E \; \text{are collinear}}$
ProofSince $MCDE$ is parallelogram and $M$ is midpoint of $CF$ , we have $MFED$ is parallelogram. Hence $\angle FED = \angle FMD = \angle LCD = \angle FBA + \angle FAB = \angle BFC$ . We knew that $DE \parallel FC$ , then $BF\parallel FE$ or $B, F, E$ are collinear.
Since **Claim 3**, we have $DB = DA$ and $DA = XF$ since $XFAD$ is parallelogram. On other hand, $BXDF$ is cyclic quadlaterial. Thus, $BXDF$ is isocesles trapezoid, and $FD \parallel BX$ . Since $BXDF$ is isocesles trapezoid, we have $\angle EBX = \angle EXB$ or $\triangle BEX$ is isocesles triangle. Easily we get $EM$ is internal bisector of $\angle BEX$ or $EM$ is perpendicular bisector of $BX$ . Now suppose $BD$ cuts $XF$ at $J$ . Since $BFDX$ is isoceles trapezoid we conclude $JB = JX$ or $J$ lies on perpendicular of $BX$ . Thus, $J \in EM$ . We're done.

Now we are done,just look at circles  $\odot(BMDEA),\odot(BCXDF)$  and  $\odot(FMXE)$ ,their radical axis are concurrent.

My solution:
Let  $\angle BAC=x$ .
Since  $DA=DC$  and  $\angle ADC=180-2x=2(180-\angle ABC)$  it implies that  $D$  is center of circumcircle of  $\triangle ABC$ .
Since  $\angle MAE=2x$  and  $\angle AED=180-2x$  it implies that  $E,D,X$  are collinear.
Since  $\angle BAC=\angle CAD=\angle DAE=x$  and  $ \angle DAB=\angle DBA=2x$  it implies  $\angle FBD=\angle FCD=x$  it implies  $BCFD$  is cyclic.
Now since  $\angle XDC=x$  and  $\angle XMC=2x$ , it implies  $XBCFD$  is cyclic(  $M$  is center of circle  $BCFD$ ).
Let  $BD\cap FC=Y$ . It implies  $\angle YDF=\angle YFD=90-2x$  so  $YF=YD$ .
Now since  $\angle AFD=90+x$  it implies  $E$  is center of circumcircle of  $\triangle AFD$ .
Now we have  $EF=ED$ , $MF=MD$  and  $FY=YD$ , which implies  $E,M,Y$  are collinear which implies  $BD,FX,ME$  are concurrent.

Let  $\angle BAC = \angle CAD = \angle DAE$  be denoted as  $\alpha$ . Now  $\angle AEX = \pi - 2\alpha$ , while from  $\triangle ADE$  we have that  $\angle AED = \pi - 2\alpha$ , hence  $\angle AEX = \angle AED$ , implying that  $X-D-E$  are collinear. Also as  $\angle DCA = \angle DAC = \angle BAC$  we have that  $BA \parallel DC$ .

Let the bisector of  $AC$  cuts  $AB$  at  $Z$ , then  $Z$  is the reflection of  $D$  wrt  $AC$ . Now we have that  $\angle CDZ + \angle CBZ = \frac{\pi}{2} - \angle CDX + \frac{\pi}{2} + \angle FBA = \pi$ . Hence  $BCDZ$  is cyclic. Now as  $\angle DCA = \angle DAC = \angle ZAC = \angle ZCA$  we have that  $\angle DBA = \angle ZCD = 2\alpha$ . This implies that  $BF$  is angle bisector of  $\angle DBA$ . This implies that  $F$  lies on the circumcircle of  $BCDZ$ . 

Similarly now reflect  $E$  wrt  $AD$  and name the new point  $Y$ . Now  $\angle DEY + \angle DFY = \frac{\pi}{2} - \angle DAY + \angle XDC + \angle CDF = \frac{\pi}{2} - \alpha + \alpha + \frac{\pi}{2} = \pi$ . Hence  $FDYE$  is cyclic. Now  $\angle EFA = \angle EDY = 2\alpha = \angle BFC$ , which implies that  $B-F-E$  are collinear. Additionally this implies that  $\angle XFC = \alpha$ , as  $\angle MED = \alpha$ , hence  $ME \parallel CD$  and  $\triangle MFX \sim \triangle EAD$ . Therefore  $\angle XDC = \angle XFC$  implying that  $X$  lies on the circumcircle of  $BCDFZ$ .

Now it's easy to notice that  $BXDF$  is trapezium and hence by Ceva's Theorem  $E$  and the midpoints of  $BX$  and  $DF$  are collinear and that line passes through the intersection of  $BD$  and  $FX$ . But as  $M$  is the circumcentre it also lies on this line and hence the proof.

Plugging the second into the first yields   $$ x^2+\frac{b^2x^2}{a^2}=b^2. $$   Solving yields  $x=\frac{-ab}{c}$ . We take the negative square root because A must lie to the left of the y-axis. Plugging this into the equation for line  $FC$ , we have  $A=(\frac{-ab}{c},\frac{b^2+bc}{c})$ .

Now we seek to find the equation for line  $AD$ . We reflect  $B$  over  $AC$  to get a point  $B'$  on line  $AD$ . We have that  $BB'$  has equation  $y=\frac{a}{b}x$ . We then compute the intersection of  $BB'$  and  $AC$ .
The point at which they intersect has an x-coordinate satisfying the equation  $\frac{a}{b}x=\frac{-b}{a}x+b$ . solving gives  $x=\frac{ab^2}{c^2}$ , and plugging this in gives the intersection as  $(\frac{ab^2}{c^2},\frac{a^2b}{c^2})$ . This is the midpoint of  $BB'$ , so  $B'=(\frac{2ab^2}{c^2},\frac{2a^b}{c^2})$ .

Then we can compute that the line  $AB'$  has equation   $$ y=\frac{2a^2b-b^2c-bc^2}{2b^2a+abc}x+\frac{2b^4a+2a^3b^2+2ab^3c}{2ab^2c+abc^2}, $$   which simplifies to   $$ y=\frac{2a^2-bc-c^2}{2ab+ac}x+\frac{2b(b+c)}{2b+c}. $$  Next we compute the equation for the perpendicular bisector of  $AC$ , which also goes through  $D$ . This has slope  $\frac{a}{b}$  and goes through the midpoint of  $AC$   $(\frac{ac-ab}{2c}, \frac{b^2+bc}{2c}).$  This has equation   $$ y=\frac{a}{b}x+\frac{a^2b-a^2c+b^3+b^2c}{2bc}=\frac{a}{b}x+\frac{b^2-a^2+bc}{2b}. $$  We can then compute the intersection that is  $D$ . \[

\]
This is homogenous so let  $z=1$ . Note that  $Y:=2\left(\frac{S_C}{b^2},\,0,\,\frac{S_A}{b^2}\right)-(0,\,1,\,0)=\left(\frac{2S_C}{b^2},\,-1,\,\frac{2S_A}{b^2}\right)$  is the reflection of  $B$  over line  $AC$ .  $X$  lies on line  $AY$  so  $y=-\frac{b^2}{2S_A}$ . Solving for  $x$  gives

\frac{(a^2-c^2)b^2}{2S_A}+b^2(1-x)&=0

\end{align*}

\[
-a^2y+b^2\left(z-x+\frac{c}{b}\right)+c^2y=0.
\]

\[

\]

1 & 0 & 1
b+2c & -b & 0

\end{vmatrix}
=-bc(b+2c)-b^2(b+2c)+b(b+c)(b+2c)=0

stem_md: Let  $P=A_1A_2\cdots A_k$  be a convex polygon in the plane. The vertices  $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_k$  have integral coordinates and lie on a circle. Let  $S$  be the area of  $P$ . An odd positive integer  $n$  is given such that the squares of the side lengths of  $P$  are integers divisible by  $n$ . Prove that  $2S$  is an integer divisible by  $n$ .
solution_md:
Sketch:
 <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Lemma 1: If an integer n divides the square of the length of every side of a convex cyclic polygon with integer coordinates, n also divides the square of the length of every diagonal.
Proof: Induction with law of cosines on the number of vertices diagonals "skip".
Lemma 2: If an odd positive integer n divides  the square of the length of every side of a triangle with integer coordinates and area  $S$ ,  $n|2S$ .
Proof:WLOG  $(0,0)$ ,  $(x_1,y_1)$ , and  $(x_2,y_2)$  are the vertices in clockwise order. 
By the Shoelace Theorem,  $\underline{2S=\frac{|x_1y_2-y_1x_2|}{2}}$ .
Since  $n|x_1^2+y_1^2$ ,  $n|x_2^2+y_2^2$ , and  $n|x_1^2+y_1^2+x_2^2+y_2^2 - 2(x_1x_2+y_1y_2)$ ,  $\underline{n|x_1x_2+y_1y_2}$ .  $n^2|(x_1^2+y_1^2)(x_2^2+y_2^2) \to n|x_1^2x_2^2+x_1^2y_2^2+y_1^2x_2^2+y_1^2y_2^2 \to n^2|(x_1x_2+y_1y_2)^2-2x_1x_2y_1y_2+x_1^2y_2^2+y_1^2x_2^2 \to  n^2|(x_1x_2+y_1y_2)^2+(x_1y_2-y_1x_2)^2.$ Since  $n|x_1x_2+y_1y_2$ ,  $n^2|(x_1x_2+y_1y_2)^2$ , so  $n^2|(x_1y_2-y_1x_2)^2$  and  $\underline{n|x_1y_2-y_1x_2}$ , so  $\boxed{n|2S}$ .

Divide up P into triangles  $A_1A_2A_3, A_1A_3A_4,...,A_1A_{k-1}A_k$ . n divides all of the edges, so Lemma 1 tells us it divides all of the sides of every triangle, so by Lemma 2, n divides twice the sum of the areas of the triangles, or twice the area of P.</details>

Let us work in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ . Let the coordinates of the points $A_i$ be $z_i$ for $1 \le i \le k$ . We note that it suffices to prove for odd prime power $n = p^e$ with $p \ge 3$ . If $p = 4t+3$ , then $p^e \mid \lvert z_i - z_{i+1} \rvert^2$ implies $p^f \mid z_i - z_{i+1}$ in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ where $f = \lceil e/2 \rceil$ . Then all the points $A_1, \dots, A_k$ are contained in a coset of $p^f \mathbb{Z}[i]$ and hence $2S$ is divisible by $p^{2f}$ , which is again divisible by $p^e$ . If $p = 4t+1$ , let the factorization of $p$ in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ be $p = q \bar{q}$ . Denote by $\nu_q(x)$ and $\nu_{\bar{q}}(x)$ the exponent of $q$ and $\bar{q}$ in the prime factorization of $x$ respectively. Since $p^e \mid \lvert z_i - z_{i+1} \rvert^2$ , we have $\nu_q( z_i - z_{i+1}) + \nu_{\bar{q}}(z_i - z_{i+1}) \ge e$ for all $1 \le i \le k$ . We now claim the following: “There is a triangulation of the polygon such that for each triangle, there is some $0 \le s \le e$ for which $q^s \bar{q}^{e-s}$ divides all the side vectors.” To prove this, we use induction on $e$ . Let us first look at the case where $e = 1$ . Then every side is either a multiple of $q$ or a multiple of $\bar{q}$ . If there exist two consecutive sides that are both multiples of $q$ , then the triangle formed by those two sides will have sides that are all multiples of $q$ . Hence we can cut out that triangle and obtain a smaller polygon whose sides are either multiples of $q$ or $\bar{q}$ . This smaller polygon will be triangulated, because it is small. (We are implicitly using induction again on the number of sides.) Likewise, if two consecutive sides are both multiples of $\bar{q}$ , then we are also done. Now suppose that there exist no pairs of consecutive sides that are both multiples of $q$ or both multiples of $\bar{q}$ . Then multiples of $q$ and multiples of $\bar{q}$ will alternate, and hence the number of sides must be even. Let $k = 2l$ , and suppose without loss of generality that $q \mid z_1 - z_2$ . Because $z_1, \dots, z_{k} = z_{2l}$ lie on a circle, we see that \[ \frac{(z_1 - z_2) (z_3 - z_4) \cdots (z_{2l-1} - z_{2l})}{(z_2 - z_3) \cdots (z_{2l} - z_1)} \] must be a real number, and hence \[ (z_1 - z_2) (z_3 - z_4) \cdots (z_{2l-1} - z_{2l}) (\bar{z}_2 - \bar{z}_3) \cdots (\bar{z}_{2l} - \bar{z}_1) = (\bar{z}_1 - \bar{z}_2) (\bar{z}_3 - \bar{z}_4) \cdots (\bar{z}_{2l-1} - \bar{z}_{2l}) (z_2 - z_3) … (z_{2l} - z_1) .\] The left hand side is a multiple of $q^{2l}$ , while there right hand side is not a multiple of $q$ . A contradiction. Let us now get to $e \ge 2$ , assuming that the statement is true for $e-1$ . Using the inductive hypothesis directly for $e - 1$ , we see that there exists a triangulation such that all sides are multiples of some $q^s \bar{q}^{e-1-s}$ . Suppose that the $s$ ’s are different for two triangles. We may assume that these two triangles share a side, because there is a path of triangles from one to the other. Let one triangle be a multiple of $q^{s_1} \bar{q}^{e-1-s_1}$ and the other triangle be a multiple of $q^{s_1} \bar{q}^{e-1-s_2}$ , and let $s_1 < s_2$ . The shared side must then be a multiple of $q^{s_2} \bar{q}^{e - 1 - s_1}$ , and hence the square of its length must be a multiple of $p^{e - 1 - s_1 + s_2}$ , which is divisible by $p^e$ . This side must be a diagonal, and thus we can divide the whole polygon by this diagonal and obtain two smaller polygons. The “inductive hypothesis” for smaller polygons will then take care of these. On the other hand, what if all triangles have the same $s$ ? Then the whole polygon is a multiple of $q^s \bar{q}^{e-1-s}$ and thus we can divide the polygon $P$ by $q^s \bar{q}^{e-1-s}$ and get a polygon $P^\prime$ whose squares of sides are multiples of $p$ . We can apply the statement for $e = 1$ and see that $P^\prime$ can be triangulated. After that, we can multiple the whole thing back to get a triangulation of $P$ such that each triangle is either a multiple of $q^s \bar{q}^{e-s}$ or a multiple of $q^{s+1} \bar{q}^{e-1-s}$ . Hence this case is also covered. This finishes the proof of our claim. Going back to the problem, we see that the polygon is partitioned into triangles that are multiples of $q^s \bar{q}^{e-s}$ for some $s$ . The area of each of these triangles must be a multiple of $\lvert q^s \bar{q}^{e-s} \rvert^2 / 2 = p^e / 2$ . Therefore $2S$ is a multiple of $p^e = n$ .

For any polygon  $Q$  with vertices on lattice points, Pick's theorem tells us that  $\text{a}(Q)=I+\tfrac{B}{2}-1$ , where  $I$  and  $B$  are the number of lattice points in and on the boundary of  $Q$ , respectively. Case  $k\geq 4$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Note that it suffices to prove the statement when  $n = p^e$ , an odd prime power. We proceed by strong induction on  $k$ .

Suppose  $k = 3$ , and without loss of generality, let the vertices of  $P$  be  $(0, 0)$ ,  $(a, b)$ , and  $(c, d)$ . Then, we have
\[a^2 + b^2, \quad c^2 + d^2, \quad \text{and} \quad (a - c)^2 + (b - d)^2\]
are all divisible by  $p^e$ . Now, the right hand side of the identity
\[(ad - bc)^2 = (a^2 + b^2)(c^2 + d^2) - (ac + bd)^2\]
is divisible by  $p^{2e}$ , so the left hand side is as well. This means that  $|ad - bc|$  is divisible by  $p^e$ . However, this is equal to  $2S$  by the shoelace formula, so  $2S$  is divisible by  $n$ .

For every  $a \in \mathbb{N}$ , define  $v_p(\pm\sqrt{a}) = \frac{1}{2}v_p(a)$ . We define  $v_p(0) = \infty$ .

*Lemma.* If  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$  satisfy  $a^2, b^2, c^2 \in \mathbb{N}_0$  and  $a + b + c = 0$ , then the smallest two of  $v_p(a)$ ,  $v_p(b)$ , and  $v_p(c)$  are equal.

*Proof.* Suppose not; without loss of generality, suppose  $v_p(a) < v_p(b)$  and  $v_p(a) < v_p(c)$ . Then, from  $a + b + c = 0$ , we get
\[(a + b + c)(-a + b + c)(a - b + c)(a + b - c) = 0,\]
or
\[a^4 + b^4 + c^4 = 2a^2b^2 + 2b^2c^2 + 2c^2a^2 \implies (b^2 + c^2 - a^2)^2 = 4b^2c^2.\]
Observe that the above equation does not have square roots of integers. However, the  $v_p$  of the left hand side is equal to  $2v_p(a)$  and the  $v_p$  of the right hand side is equal to  $v_p(b) + v_p(c) > 2v_p(a)$  (since  $p$  is odd), a contradiction.

Note that the lemma is still true if the hypothesis is  $a + b = c$  instead of  $a + b + c = 0$ , by the transformation  $c \to -c$ .
------
Now, suppose  $k = 4$ . Let  $P$ 's sides be  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$ , and  $d$  in order, and let  $x$  and  $y$  be its diagonals. From Ptolemy's theorem, we get  $ac + bd = xy$ . We have  $v_p(ac) \ge e$  and  $v_p(bd) \ge e$ , so  $v_p(xy) \ge e$ , or  $v_p(x^2y^2) \ge 2e$ . This implies that one of  $x^2$  and  $y^2$  is divisible by  $p^e$ ; splitting  $P$  along this diagonal leads to two triangles, both of whose areas are divisible by  $p^e$  by the inductive hypothesis.

Now, consider a general  $k$ -gon  $A_1A_2 \cdots A_k$ , with  $k \ge 5$ . If the square of any of its diagonals is divisible by  $p^e$ , then we can split  $P$  along this diagonal, giving two polygons with less sides whose areas are divisible by  $p^e$ . Thus, we may assume that any diagonal squared has  $v_p$  less than  $e$ . We claim that this is impossible.

Consider a quadrilateral of the form  $Q = A_iA_{i + 1}A_jA_{j + 1}$ , where  $i$  and  $j$  are chosen such that the four vertices of  $Q$  are distinct. Let  $a = A_iA_{i + 1}$ ,  $b = A_{i + 1}A_j$ ,  $c = A_jA_{j + 1}$ ,  $d = A_{j + 1}A_i$ ,  $x = A_iA_j$ , and  $y = A_{i + 1}A_{j + 1}$ .
By Ptolemy, we have  $ac + bd = xy$ . However, we have  $v_p(ac) \ge e$  and  $v_p(xy) < e$  (by assumption, as we assumed  $v_p(x^2) < e$  and  $v_p(y^2) < e$ ), so the lemma implies  $v_p(bd) = v_p(xy)$ , or
\[v_p(A_{i + 1}A_j) + v_p(A_{j + 1}A_i) = v_p(A_iA_j) + v_p(A_{i + 1}A_{j + 1}).\]
Now, sum this equation over all such quadrilaterals  $Q$ . Without loss of generality, suppose  $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_k$  are in counterclockwise order around the circle, and consider all indices modulo  $k$ . We consider what happens to each term. Note that the quadrilateral  $Q$  is valid (no two vertices are equal) if and only if  $j - i \not\equiv -1, 0, 1 \pmod{k}$ .



- Term  $v_p(A_{i + 1}A_j)$ : As  $j - i \not\equiv -1, 0, 1\pmod{k}$ , the terms excluded are  $v_p(A_{i + 1}A_{i - 1})$  and  $v_p(A_{i + 1}A_i)$ . In other words, this counts every diagonal twice except for "short" diagonals (such as  $A_{i - 1}A_{i + 1}$  which split one vertex off from the rest) once, and counts each side once.
- Term  $v_p(A_{j + 1}A_i)$ : By symmetry between  $i$  and  $j$ , this counts everything the same number of times  $v_p(A_{i + 1}A_j)$  does.
- Term  $v_p(A_iA_j)$ : Since  $j - i \not\equiv -1, 0, 1\pmod{k}$ , the terms excluded are  $v_p(A_iA_{i - 1})$  and  $v_p(A_iA_{i + 1})$ . Thus, this term counts every diagonal twice and doesn't count any side at all.
- Term  $v_p(A_{i + 1}A_{j + 1})$ : By the transformation  $i \to i - 1$  and  $j \to j - 1$ , this counts everything the same number of times  $v_p(A_iA_j)$  does (note that  $j - i \not\equiv -1, 0, 1 \pmod{k}$  is still preserved).
[/list]

Thus, our sum equation has (after dividing by  $2$  to account for the symmetry present)
[list]
- on the left hand side, each side once, each short diagonal once, and each other diagonal twice, and
- on the right hand side, each diagonal twice.

This means that, after simplifying, our sum equation reduces to
\[\sum_{i = 1}^{k} v_p(A_iA_{i + 1}) = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} v_p(A_iA_{i + 2}).\]
However, note that every term on the left hand side is at least  $\frac{1}{2}e$ . Since both sides have  $k$  terms, some term  $v_p(A_rA_{r + 2})$  on the right hand side must be at least  $\frac{1}{2}e$ . Then,  $(A_rA_{r + 2})^2$  is divisible by  $n = p^e$ , a contradiction, and we are done.</details>

Note that  $2S$  is always an integer for any lattice polygon, so it remains to show that it is divisible by  $n$ . It clearly suffices to prove the problem for when  $n=p^m$  is a prime power. We proceed using induction on  $k$ , with the base case of  $k=3$  settled by Heron's formula: If  $a,b,c$  are the side lengths of the triangle, then the square of the area is  $S^2=\frac{2a^2b^2+2b^2c^2+2c^2a^2-a^4-b^4-c^4}{16}$ . As  $n\mid a^2,b^2,c^2$ , we have that  $n^2\mid S^2\implies n\mid S$ , as desired.

For the inductive step, we claim that there exists a diagonal whose length squared is also divisible by  $n$ . Then, we may split  $P$  into two polygons with less vertices and areas divisible by  $n$  by assumption. Let  $3\le i\le k-1$  be such that  $v_p(A_1A_i^2)=q$  is minimized. By Ptolemy's Theorem on cyclic quadrilateral  $A_1A_{i-1}A_iA_{i+1}$ , we have that  $\sqrt{A_1A_{i-1}^2\cdot A_iA_{i+1}^2}+\sqrt{A_1A_{i+1}^2\cdot A_iA_{i-1}^2}=\sqrt{A_1A_i^2\cdot A_{i-1}A_{i+1}^2}$ , or  $\sqrt{\frac{A_1A_{i-1}^2\cdot A_iA_{i+1}^2}{np^q}}+\sqrt{\frac{A_1A_{i+1}^2\cdot A_iA_{i-1}^2}{np^q}}=\sqrt{\frac{A_1A_i^2\cdot A_{i-1}A_{i+1}^2}{np^q}}$ . As we have  $p^q\mid AA_{i-1}^2,AA_{i+1}^2$  and  $n\mid A_iA_{i+1}^2,A_iA_{i-1}^2$ , the terms under the square roots on the LHS are integers, so the LHS is an algebraic integer. This implies that the term under the square root on the RHS is also an integer, so  $np^q\mid A_1A_i^2\cdot A_{i-1}A_{i+1}^2\implies n\mid A_{i-1}A_{i+1}^2$ , as desired.

Here's a different solution using  $\mathbb{Z}*$ . 

Note that it suffices to prove that odd prime powers work; especially integers of the form  $p^m$ , where  $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$  work.

We induct on  $k$ . For  $k=3$ , Heron's formula kills the problem.

Now let us move to the inductive step.
For a polygon  $P$ , let its [i]side vectors* be  $\{ \overrightarrow{A_1A_2}, \overrightarrow{A_2A_3}, \cdots, \overrightarrow{A_kA_1} \}=\{ v_1, v_2, \cdots, v_n\}$ . We consider vectors as complex numbers on  $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ .

Assume that  $p=\pi \bar{\pi}$  on  $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ . Let  $m_i$  be the maximal integer such that  $\pi^{m_i}$  divides  $v_i$ . Since  $p^m$  divides  $v_i \overline{v_i}$ , either  $m_i \ge m$ , or  $\pi^{m_i} \overline{\pi}^{m-m_i}$  divides  $v_i$ .

Consider  $\chi=\min_{i} m_i$ . Taking  $\pmod {\pi^\chi}$  on each sides of  $0=v_1+v_2+\cdots +v_n$ , we deduce that there are at least  $2$  indices  $t$  such that  $\chi=m_t$ . Call these indices  $a,b$ . Note that for any permutation  $\sigma$  of  $\{v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_n\}$ , every polygon  $Q$  having  $\sigma$  as its side vectors is inscribed in a circle, and has exactly same area with  $P$ . Hence, if we switch  $v_a$  and  $v_b$ , then the new polygon obtained has same area as  $P$ . So, WLOG assume that  $b=a+1$ . Then, since  $m_a=m_b$ ,   $$ \overline{A_aA_{a+2}}^2=(v_a+v_b)(\overline{v_a}+\overline{v_b}) $$   is a multiple of  $p^m$ . Hence, from the induction hypothesis on polygons  $A_1A_2\cdots A_aA_{a+2} \cdots A_k$  and  $A_aA_{a+1}A_{a+2}$ ,  $2S$  is a integer divisible by  $p^m$ .  $\square$

Select  $m$  so that  $3\le m\le k-1$  and  $\nu_p(A_1A_{m-1}^2)\ge\nu_p(A_1A_m^2)\le\nu_p(A_1A_{m+1}^2)$ . If this is not possible, then either  $2e\le\nu_p(A_1A_2^2)\le\nu_p(A_1A_3^2)$  or  $\nu_p(A_1A_3^2)>\nu_p(A_1A_4^2)>\cdots>\nu_p(A_1A_k^2)\ge2e$ . In either case,  $n\mid A_1A_3^2$ , and we are already done.

Let  $A$  denote the set of algebraic integers. Let  $E=e+\nu_p\left(A_1A_m^2\right)$ , so  $\nu_p\left(A_1A_{m-1}^2\cdot A_mA_{m+1}^2\right)\ge E$  and  $\nu_p\left(A_1A_{m+1}^2\cdot A_mA_{m-1}^2\right)\ge E$ . By Ptolemy's theorem on  $A_1A_{m-1}A_mA_{m+1}$ , we have \[\sqrt{\frac{A_1A_m^2\cdot A_{m-1}A_{m+1}^2}{p^E}}=\sqrt{\frac{A_1A_{m-1}^2\cdot A_mA_{m+1}^2}{p^E}}+\sqrt{\frac{A_1A_{m+1}^2\cdot A_mA_{m-1}^2}{p^E}}\in A,\]
so  $p^E\mid A_1A_m^2\cdot A_{m-1}A_{m+1}^2$ . It follows that  $p^e\mid A_{m-1}A_{m+1}^2$ , and the induction is complete.

<details><summary>Remark</summary>In fact, we find a diagonal that dissects  $P$  into a triangle and a polygon of  $k-1$  sides, so regular induction suffices.</details>
<details><summary>Remark</summary>Here is an algebraic proof for squarefree  $n$ . Let  $A_i=(x_i,y_i)$ . Shift the points so that the circumcenter is at the origin, and dilate appropriately (while also scaling  $n$ ).

    Take indices modulo  $n$ . Then if the circumradius is  $R$ , we have  $x_i^2+y_i^2=R^2$  and 
    \begin{align*}
        0&\equiv(x_{i+1}-x_i)^2+(y_{i+1}-y_i)^2
        &\equiv2R^2-2(x_ix_{i+1}+y_iy_{i+1})\pmod n,
        \implies R^2&\equiv x_ix_{i+1}+y_iy_{i+1}\pmod n.
    \end{align*}
    It follows that
    \begin{align*}
        R^2&=\left(x_i^2+y_i^2\right)\left(x_{i+1}^2+y_{i+1}^2\right)
        &=(x_ix_{i+1}+y_iy_{i+1})^2+(x_iy_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i)^2.
        \implies 0&\equiv(x_iy_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i)^2\pmod n.
    \end{align*}
    By the assumption  $n$  is squarefree,  $n\mid x_iy_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i$ , so  $n\mid2S$  by Shoelace formula.</details>

First, note that it suffices to prove the problem for  $n=p^e$ , where  $p$  is a prime and  $e\ge 1$ . Now, we will induct on  $k$  with base case  $3$ .

For  $k=3$ , note that by law of cosines we have  $A_2A_3^2=A_1A_2^2+A_1A_3^2-2A_1A_2\cdot A_1A_3\cos\angle A_2A_1A_3$ . Thus, we have that  $
u_p(A_1A_2\cdot A_1A_3\cos\angle A_2A_1A_3)\ge e$ . So,   $$ 
u_p[A_1A_2A_3]=
u_p\left( rac{1}{2}A_1A_2\cdot A_1A_3\sin\angle A_2A_1A_3ight)=
u_p\left( rac{1}{2}A_1A_2\cdot A_1A_3\cos\angle A_2A_1A_3ight)\ge e $$  as desired, since  $\sin$  and  $\cos$  have the same integer denominator.

Now, for the inductive step, note that as long as there exists a diagonal whose square is divisible by  $n$ , we are done, since this diagonal splits our  $k$ -gon into 2 smaller cases which can both be finished by inductive hypothesis. To show that there always exists such a diagonal, we assume the contrary, namely that if  $A_iA_j$  is not a side, then  $
u_p(A_iA_j^2)\le e$ .

Denote  $
u_p(A_iA_{i+1}^2)$  as  $v_i$ , and  $
u_p(R^2)$  as  $v_R$ , where  $R$  is the circumradius.We know from Law of Sines that   $$  rac{A_iA_{i+1}}{2\sin\angle A_iA_{i+2}A_{i+1}}=R\implies 
u_p(\cos^2\angle A_iA_{i+2}A_{i+1})=v_i-v_R $$   Now, consider Law of Cosines with  $\angle A_iA_{i+2}A_{i+1}$ . We have   $$ A_iA_{i+1}^2=A_iA_{i+2}^2+A_{i+1}A_{i+2}^2-2A_iA_{i+2}\cdot A_{i+1}A_{i+2}\cos\angle A_iA_{i+2}A_{i+1} $$  By assumption,  $
u_p(A_iA_{i+2})^2<
u_p(A_{i+1}A_{i+2}^2),
u_p(A_iA_{i+1})$ , so the only way for this equality to hold is if   $$ 
u_p(A_iA_{i+2}^2)=
u_p((A_{i+1}A_{i+2}\cos\angle A_iA_{i+2}A_{i+1})^2)=v_i+v_{i+1}-v_R $$  We now prove with induction that  $
u_p(A_iA_j^2)=v_i+v_{i+1}+\ldots+v_{j-1}-(j-i-1)v_R$ . We have just done the base case, so assume that this is true for  $j-i<d$ , and consider when  $j=i+d$ . In particular, consider the quadrilateral  $A_iA_{j-2}A_{j-1}A_j$ . By Ptolemy, we need that   $$ A_iA_{j-2}\cdot A_{j-1}A_{j-2}+A_{j-2}A_{j-1}\cdot A_jA_i=A_iA_{j-1}\cdot A_{j-2}A_j $$  By inductive hypothesis,   $$ 
u_p(RHS^2)=(v_i+\ldots +v_{j-2})+(v_{j-2}+v_{j-1})-(j-i-1)v_R $$   and  $
u_p$  of the square of the first term on the left is   $$ v^*=(v_i+\ldots +v_{j-3})+v_{j-1}-(j-i-3)v_R $$  If  $v^*\le 
u_p(RHS^2)$ , then  $v_{j-2}\ge v_R$ . However, this would mean  $
u_p(A_{j-2}A_j^2)\ge v_{j-1}\ge e$ , which is a contradiction. So,  $v^*>
u_p(RHS^2)$ Hence, in order to get the desired equality, we must have  $
u_p(A_{j-2}A_{j-1}\cdot A_jA_i)=
u_p(RHS)$ , which quickly implies the result. So, the induction is complete.

Note that, with this induction, we can go all the way to  $j=i+k-1$ . So,  $v_{i-1}=v_i+v_{i+1}+\ldots+v_{j-1}-(j-i-1)v_R$ . From similar relations, it is easy to get that the average of all the  $v_i$  is  $v_R$ . However, this means that we have  $i$  such that  $v_i\ge v_R$ , which, as we have shown above, leads to a contradiction. Hence, our assumption was wrong and we can always find a diagonal to split our  $k$  gon into smaller cases, as desired.

Great problem, not at all what you'd expect in a number theory problem. I think the idea of recursively generating diagonal lengths is is the easiest way to motivate the use of Ptolemy:
<details><summary>solution</summary>By Pick's theorem,  $2S$  is indeed an integer.

Now, WLOG let  $n = p^e$  for p prime. Proceed by strong induction on  $k$ , as in prior solutions. This clearly holds for  $k=3$  by Heron. Now, assume that this holds for all polygons with fewer than  $k$  sides. Then, for a polygon with  $k \ge 4$  sides, let  $t_i = |A_1A_{1+i}|, s_i = |A_iA_{i+2}|, a_i = |A_iA_{i+1}|$ , with all indices  $\pmod k$ . Now, assume that for all  $2 \le i \le k-1$ ,  $\nu_p{s_i^2} < e$ . Then, by Ptolemy on  $A_iA_{i+1}A_{i-1}A_1$ :  $$ t_ia_{i-1} + t_{i-2}a_i = t_{i-1}s_{i-1} \implies p^e | t_{i-1}^2s_{i-1}^2 \implies p |t_{i-1}^2 \implies p | t_j^2 \text { for } 1 \le j \le k-2 $$   Additionally, this holds for  $k - 1$  by assumption. Hence, for all  $i$ ,   $$ p | t_i^2 \implies p^{e+1} | t_{i}a_{i-1} + t_{i-2}a_i $$  . By repeating this logic on the recurrence relation, we find that if  $p^e$  does not divide  $s_i^2$  for all  $i$ , then  $ p^e | t_i^2$  for all  $i$ . Hence, there must be, in all cases, a diagonal  $A_iA_j$  of the polygon s.t.  $|A_iA_j|^2$  is a multiple of  $p^e$ . Assume that  $A_iA_j$  divides  $S$  into two sections of area  $S_1$ ,  $S_2$ . By the induction hypothesis,   $$ n|2S_1, n|2S_2 \implies n|2S = 2(S_1 + S_2), $$   as desired.</details>

We prove for  $n=p^{e}$  for a prime  $p$  with induction on  $k \ge 3.$  

If  $k=3,$  set  $A_1=(0,0),$   $A_2=(x_1,y_1),$  and  $A_3=(x_2,y_2)$  WLOG. So  $x_1^2+y_1^2 \equiv x_2^2+y_2^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$  and  $ 0 \equiv (x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2 \equiv -2x_1x_2-2y_1y_2 \pmod{n}.$  So  $x_1x_2+y_1y_2\equiv 0 \pmod{n}.$  So  $(x_1y_2-x_2y_1)^2 \equiv (x_1^2+y_1^2)(x_2^2+y_2^2)-(x_1x_2+y_1y_2)^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{n^2}$  which finishes by Shoelace.  $\square$ If  $k \ge 4,$  if we have a  $3 \le j \le k-1$  where  $p^e \mid A_1A_{j}^2$  we split the polygon in two and induct down. 

Otherwise we must have three consecutive vertices  $A_{m-1}, A_{m}, A_{m+1} \ne A_{1}$  where  $v_p( A_1A_{m-1}^2) \ge v_p( A_1A_{m}^2) \le v_p( A_1A_{m+1}^2).$  Ptolemy's on  $A_1A_{m-1}A_{m}A_{m+1}$  gives that  $p^e \mid A_{m-1}A_{m+1}^2$  so we split the polygon in two that way and induct down.  $\blacksquare$

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Clearly it is enough to prove when  $n$  is power of an odd prime. Let  $n=p^m$ .

We will prove the statement by strong induction on  $k$ .

For  $k=3$  it follows by Heron's formula.

For the inductive step, if we find a diagonal whose square is divisible by  $n$ , we are done, as we can apply the induction on the two polygons formed by that diagonal.

So assume that no diagonal has the square divisible by  $n$ .

For any  $i$ , as  $ A_1A_2A_iA_{i+1} $  is cyclic, by Ptolemy we have  $ A_1A_i\cdot A_2A_{i+1}=A_{1}A_{i+1}\cdot A_{2}A_i+A_1A_2\cdot A_iA_{i+1} $ . From our assumption it follows that  $ v_p(A_1A_i^2)+v_p(A_2A_{i+1}^2)=v_p(A_1A_{i+1}^2)+v_p(A_2A_i^2) $  or  $ v_p(A_1A_i^2)-v_p(A_2A_i^2)=v_p(A_1A_{i+1}^2)-v_p(A_2A_{i+1}^2) $ . When we apply this for  $ i=2,3,\dots,k-1 $  we get  $ v_p(A_1A_3^2)-v_p(A_2A_3^2)=v_p(A_1A_k^2)-v_p(A_2A_k^2) $ , which is impossible as the left member is negative and the right member is positive.

Therefore there is a diagonal whose square is divisible by  $n$  and we are done by induction.</details>

Define  $p_i=|A_iA_{i+1}|,$   $q_i=|A_1A_i|,$   $r_i=|A_{i-1}A_{i+1}|$  with cyclic numeration. By the Pick's theorem  $2S$  is an integer. Notice that it's enough to consider case  $n=p^{\alpha}$  for some odd prime  $p$  and nonnegative integer  $\alpha.$  Induct on  $k\geq 3.$ For base case  $k=3$  we use Heron's formula, which gives   $$ n^2\mid (-p_1^4-p_2^4-p_3^4+2p_1^2p_2^2+2p_2^2p_3^2+2p_3^2p_1^2)=16S^2\implies n\mid 2S\text{ } \Box $$  If  $p^{\alpha}$  divides the squared length of some diagonal of  $P,$  then we can divide  $P$  on two polygons by this diagonal and induct down. Thus we may assume the opposite. Since  $v_p(q_2^2),v_p(q_n^2)\geq \alpha,$  there exists such integer  $m,$  that   $$ v_p(q_{m-1}^2),v_p(q_{m+1}^2)\geq v_p(q_m^2)\quad \quad \quad v_p(q_m^2)<\alpha. $$   On the other hand, by Prolemy's theorem   $$ (q_mr_m)^2=(p_{m-1}q_{m+1})^2+(p_{m+1}q_{m-1})^2+2p_{m-1}p_{m+1}q_{m-1}q_{m+1}. $$   Clearly LHS is an integer, so we easily conclude that  $p^{\alpha +\min (v_p(q_{m-1}^2), v_p(q_{m+1}^2))}\mid (q_mr_m)^2\implies p^{\alpha} \mid r_m^2,$  contradiction.

We induct on  $k$ , and consider only the case  $n = p^r$  for some odd prime  $p$ . Note that for the case  $k=3$ , we have   $$ n^2 \mid 2(a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2)-(a^4+b^4+c^4) = 16S^2 $$   where  $a, b, c$  are the side lengths, which implies the result.

For the inductive step, write   $$ \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \frac{A_iA_{i+1}}{A_{k+1}A_i \cdot A_{k+1}A_{i+1}} = \frac{A_1A_k}{A_{k+1}A_1\cdot A_{k+1}A_k}, $$   which follows by inversion with arbitrary radius at  $A_{k+1}$ . Notice that every term on the LHS is the square root of a rational number, so it follows that there exist rational numbers  $r_i$  such that each term is of the form  $a_i = \sqrt q \cdot r_i$  for some rational number  $q$ . If any diagonal has square length divisible by  $p^r$ , we may induct down by splitting the polygon.

Assume otherwise. Then we can check that  $\nu_p(a_i) > \nu_p(a)$  where  $a$  is the last term. On the other hand this yields a contradiction when we look at the Ptolemy equation.

what is ptolemy By shoelace $2S$ is an integer. I will now show it is divisible by $n$ ; to do this, by CRT it clearly suffices to look at $n=p^e$ only for $p$ an odd prime. The circumcenter $O$ of $P$ can be found by intersecting any two perpendicular bisectors, which are rational lines (i.e. can be written with rational coefficients), hence $O$ is a rational point. Hence the circumradius $r$ of $P$ is the square root of a rational number. We take two cases.**Case 1:** $ u_p(r^2) \geq e$ . In this case, consider a triangle $OA_iA_{i+1}$ (with indices modulo $n$ ); let $a=A_iA_{i+1}$ with $a^2$ an integer divisible by $p^e$ . Then by Heron's, $$ p^{2e}\mid 16[OA_iA_{i+1}]^2=2(a^2r^2+a^2r^2+r^4)-r^4-r^4-a^4, $$ where $[ riangle]$ denotes *signed* area, hence $[OA_iA_{i+1}]$ is a rational number with $ u_p$ at least $e$ . Summing over all $i$ yields $ u_p([P]) \geq e$ , as desired.**Case 2:** $ u_p(r^2)Claim:** Let $ABC$ with a triangle with circumradius $r$ and side lengths $a,b,c$ as usual. Then $$ c=\left|a\sqrt{1- rac{b^2}{4r^2}}\pm b\sqrt{1- rac{a^2}{4r^2}} ight|. $$ Proof: By Law of Sines, $c=2r\sin\angle ACB$ . On the other hand, if WLOG $\angle ACO\geq \angle BCO$ , then $\angle ACB=\angle ACO \pm \angle BCO$ for some appropriate choice of sign. On the other hand, by dropping perpendiculars we have $\cos \angle ACO= frac{b/2}{r}$ , hence $\sin \angle ACO=\sqrt{1- frac{b^2}{4r^2}}$ . Symmetric equations hold for the sine and cosine of $\angle BCO$ , so we finish by the sine addition/subtraction formula, depending on sign choice. $ lacksquare$ Now consider the diagonal $A_1A_3$ . Since $A_1$ and $A_3$ are integer points, $A_1A_3^2 \in \mathbb{Z}$ . On the other hand, by the above formula (where $a=A_1A_2$ , $b=A_2A_3$ , $c=A_1A_3$ ), we have $$ c^2=a^2\left(1- rac{b^2}{4r^2} ight)+b^2\left(1- rac{a^2}{4r^2} ight)\pm 2ab\sqrt{\left(1- rac{a^2}{4r^2} ight)\left(1- rac{b^2}{4r^2} ight)}. $$ Since $ u_p(r^2)0 \implies u_p(1- frac{a^2}{4r^2}), u_p(1- frac{b^2}{4r^2})=0$ . Thus each individual term has $ u_p$ at least $e$ , since it can be expressed as the product of a number with $ u_p$ at least $e$ with a number with $ u_p$ at least $0$ . Thus $ u_p(c^2) \geq e$ as well. Therefore, we can dissect $P$ into $A_1A_2A_3$ and $A_1A_3A_4\ldots A_k$ and apply inductive hypothesis. These two cases finish the problem. $ lacksquare$ **Remark:** Originally I had a solution which used the same idea, but because I didn't realize that $c^2$ was an integer, I was working with some claim along the lines of $a^2/p^e,b^2/p^e$ in $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2^i}}$ implies $c^2/p^e$ in $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2^{i+1}}}$ . The finish is then that after we end up triangulating $P$ , we evaluate the area as a sum of Heron's statements to get that $16S^2/p^{2e}$ is in $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2^ ext{something}}}$ . But it's also rational, so it's in $\mathbb{F}_p$ and then $p^e \mid S$ follows. You can also replace these all with $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$ . Really, this solution is the same as the one above, but after someone pointed out that $c^2$ was an integer (oops) it turns out you can avoid this language and just work with $ u_p$ directly.

By Shoelace  $2S$  is an integer. It clearly suffices to show the problem where  $n$  is a prime power  $p^e$ .

Note that by Heron's formula, the area of a triangle with sidelengths  $\sqrt a$ ,  $\sqrt b$ , and  $\sqrt c$  is  $1/4\sqrt{-(a^2+b^2+c^2)+2ab+2bc+2ca}$ . We use this formula many times in our solution.

There are two cases:**Case 1:** The squares of the lengths of all diagonals are divisible by  $n$ . In this case, we may triangulate our polygon. By Shoelace, the area of each triangle is a half-integer, but by Heron's, the area is divisible by  $n$ , so we're done.**Case 2:** There exists a diagonal whose length squared is not divisible by  $n$ . By ``building up'' from side lengths there exists three vertices whose triangle consists of sidelengths  $\sqrt a$ ,  $\sqrt b$ , and  $\sqrt c$  where  $n\mid a,b$  but not  $c$ . Suppose  $\nu_p(c)=f<e$ .

The circumradius  $R$  satisfies
\[R^2=\frac{abc}{-(a^2+b^2+c^2)+2ab+2bc+2ca}\implies \nu_p(R^2)\ge (2e+f)-2f\ge e\implies n\mid R^2,\]
under the rational definition of divisibility.

Now, split the polygon into triangles like a pizza such that the circumcenter  $O$  is a vertex of all triangles. Since  $O$  is a rational point the squares of the sidelengths of all triangles are rational numbers divisible by  $n$ , so we're done as in Case 1!

It suffices to prove the result for prime powers  $p^n$ . To do this, strong induct on  $k$ . For triangles, the result follows by Heron's. For the inductive step, if any diagonal has squared length divisible by  $p^n$ , cut the polygon into two and use the inductive hypothesis.

Thus we may define  $a_{i,j}=\nu_p(|A_iA_j|^2)$ , and assume  $x_{i,j}<n$ . Further define  $X_i=\sum_{j=1}^ka_{j,i+j}$ . The main idea is that Ptolemy on  $A_sA_{s+1}A_tA_{t+1}$  implies that  $x_{s,t+1}+x_{s+1,t}=x_{s,t}+x_{s+1,t+1}$ , and summing this over all  $t-s=i$  gives \[X_{i-1}+X_{i+1}=2X_i.\] Hence  $X_i$  is an arithmetic progression, and  $X_1,X_{n-1}\ge nk$ , so  $X_i\ge nk$  for all  $i$ . By Pigeonhole, this implies that  $x_{j,j+i}\ge n$  for some  $j$ , contradiction. We are done.

stem_md:
Find all integers  $n$  for which each cell of  $n \times n$  table can be filled with one of the letters  $I,M$  and  $O$  in such a way that:


- in each row and each column, one third of the entries are  $I$ , one third are  $M$  and one third are  $O$ ; and [/*]
- in any diagonal, if the number of entries on the diagonal is a multiple of three, then one third of the entries are  $I$ , one third are  $M$  and one third are  $O$ .[/*]
**Note.** The rows and columns of an  $n \times n$  table are each labelled  $1$  to  $n$  in a natural order. Thus each cell corresponds to a pair of positive integer  $(i,j)$  with  $1 \le i,j \le n$ . For  $n>1$ , the table has  $4n-2$  diagonals of two types. A diagonal of first type consists all cells  $(i,j)$   for which  $i+j$  is a constant, and the diagonal of this second type consists all cells  $(i,j)$  for which  $i-j$  is constant.

It's obvious that  $3 \mid n$ . We consider all the squares indexed  $(3k+2,3l+2)$  and call it *good* square. Let  $a$  be number of *good* squares that are filled with  $I$ . We can see that every good square lies on both type of diagonals. So if we call  $D_1,D_2$  be the set of all squares in first type, second type of diagonal that are filled with  $I$ , respectively. We will have  $|D_1 \cap D_2|=a$  and  $|D_1|=|D_2|= \tfrac 19 n^2$ . Hence,   $$ |D_1 \cup D_2|=|D_1|+|D_2|+|D_1 \cap D_2|= \tfrac 29 n^2-a. $$  Hence, number of squares filled with  $I$  that either lie on first type of diagonal or second type but not in both is  $\tfrac 29 n^2-2a$ .

Now, these squares counted above doesn't fill the columns indexed  $3k+2$  and rows indexed  $3k+2$ . So we need to fill these squares with  $I$ . Let  $C$  be the set of squares in columns indexed  $3k+2$  that are filled with  $I$ , similar to set  $R$  of rows indexed  $3k+2$ . We have   $$ |C \cup R|=|C|+|R|-|C \cap R|= \tfrac 29 n^2-a. $$  From these, we find that the total number of squares filled with  $I$  is  $\tfrac 49 n^2-3a$ . Note that this is also equal to  $\tfrac 13 n^2$  so this means  $3a= \tfrac 19 n^2$  implies  $9 \mid n$ , which is the final answer.

The center cell of each box is the intersection of  $2$  good diagonals, the corner cells lie on only  $1$  good diagonal, while the squares adjacent to the center cell lie on no good diagonals. Clearly, no three good diagonals intersect at one cell. The table has  $2$  diagonals of length  $n$  and  $4$  diagonals of length  $d, 1 \le d < n$ . Since we need  $c$  entries in each column and each row, our task is to pair each element in the multiset   $$ L = \{\underbrace{1, 1, ..., 1, 1}_{c\text{ 1's}} \underbrace{2, 2, ..., 2, 2}_{c\text{ 2's}}, ..., \underbrace{3c, 3c, ..., 3c, 3c}_{c\text{ 3c's}}\} $$   with distinct elements of  $L$  such that no two pair  $(i, j)$  is the same. We claim that  $n$  satisfies the conditions if and only if  $9 \mid n$ .

For  $n=9$ , consider the following table \[
\begin{array}{|ccc|ccc|ccc|} \hline
I & I & I & M & M & M & O & O & O 
M & M & M & O & O & O & I & I & I 
O & O & O & I & I & I & M & M & M \hline
I & I & I & M & M & M & O & O & O 
M & M & M & O & O & O & I & I & I 
O & O & O & I & I & I & M & M & M \hline
I & I & I & M & M & M & O & O & O 
M & M & M & O & O & O & I & I & I 
O & O & O & I & I & I & M & M & M \hline
\end{array}
\]

and for other multiples of  $9$ , simply tile the board with copies of this  $9 \times 9$  grid.

We now establish that  $9 \mid n$ . Indeed, since each of  $I,M,O$  appears the same number of times,  $3 \mid n^2$  and so  $3 \mid n$ . Write  $n=3k$  and tile the board with  $3 \times 3$  sub-grids. For each  $3 \times 3$  grid call the central square its *representative* cell. To the letters  $I,M$  and  $O$ , assign the numbers  $1, \omega$  and  $\omega^2$  respectively. Add the numbers assigned to all rows and columns indexed  $2 \pmod {3}$  and all numbers assigned to the diagonals having number of entries a multiple of  $3$ . This total sum must be zero since each of the summands is zero for a row and a column and any diagonal having number of elements a multiple of  $3$ . However, the total sum is the sum of all entries of the  $n \times n$  board and the sum of all numbers assigned to the *representative* cells. As the sum of all entries is zero, it follows that the sum of all numbers assigned to the *representative* cells is zero. Let  $x$  of them be labelled  $I$ ,  $y$  of them be labelled  $M$ ,  $z$  of them be labelled  $O$ . We have  $x+y+z=k^2$  and  $x+y\omega+z\omega^2=0$ . 

There are two ways to conclude that  $x=y=z$  from here. 

Notice that multiplying the last equation with  $\omega$  and  $\omega^2$  we get  $z+x\omega+y\omega^2=0$  and  $y+z\omega+x\omega^2=0$ . Considering  $1,\omega,\omega^2$  as constants and  $x,y,z$  as parameters, we see that this system of equations has a solution if and only if the determinant   $$ \begin{vmatrix} x & y & z  z & x & y  y & z & x \end{vmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}(x+y+z)\left((x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\right)=0. $$   As  $x+y+z=k^2>0$ , we have  $x=y=z$ .

Alternatively,

Note that the polynomials  $1+X+X^2$  is irreducible and has no double roots. The polynomial  $x+yX+zX^2$  has a common root with  $1+X+X^2$  so if  $1+X+X^2 \nmid x+yX+zX^2$  then  $X-\omega$  is a polynomial with integer coefficients. This is clearly false, so the former must holds and we have  $x=y=z$ .

Thus,  $3 \mid x+y+z=k^2$  and  $3 \mid k$ . It follows that  $9 \mid n$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>I claim that for such condition to hold, we must have  $9|n$ . The construction for such  $n$  is simple (but I won't put it since I saw  the construction before working on the problem), and we will prove they're the only  $n$  which works. Clearly  $3|n$ , so write  $n = 3k$  for some  $k \in \mathbb{N}$ , and we need to prove that  $3|k$ . Through the solution, let  $\omega$  be a complex third root of unity, i.e a root of  $x^2+x+1$ . We begin by proving an auxiliary lemma**Lemma**: If  $a+b\omega+c\omega^2 = 0$  with  $a,b,c$  integers, then  $a = b = c$ . In particular,  $a+b+c \equiv 0 \mod 3$ . 
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Simple. Note that  $c+c\omega + c\omega^2 = 0$ , and hence substracting the original equation from this, we get  $(c-a) + (b-c) \omega = 0$ . Now define the polynomial  $P(x) := (c-a) + (b-c) x$ . As  $\omega$  is a root of  $P(x)$  with degree at max  $1$  while the minimal polynomial of  $\omega$  has degree two, we must have  $P(x) \equiv 0$ , hence  $c = a$  and  $b =c$ , or  $a = b= c$  as desired.</details>

Now in the  $3k \times 3k$  grid, replace  $I$  by  $1$ ,  $M$  by  $\omega$  and  $O$  by  $\omega^2$ . Also indexing from  $0$ , let  $a_{i,j}$  denote the number at the  $i$ -th row and  $j$ -th column.

Define these multisets (i.e sets with repetitions of elements are allowed)  $L_i := \{a_{i,0}, a_{i,1}, \cdots, a_{i,(n-1)}\}, R_i := \{a_{0,i}, a_{1, i}, \cdots, a_{n-1, i} \}$ ,  $D^{-}_{k} := \{a_{i,j} | i - j = k, 0 \leq i, j < n \},  D^{+}_{k} := \{a_{i,j} | i + j = k, 0 \leq i, j < n \}$ . Then define  $S$  to be the multiset   $$ S:= \{a_{i,j} | a_{i,j} \in R_k, k \equiv 1 \mod 3 \} \cup \{a_{i,j} \in D^{+}_{k} \text{such that} |D^{+}_k| \equiv 0 \mod 3 \} \cup \{a_{i,j} \in D^{-}_{k} \text{such that} |D^{-}_{k}| \equiv 0 \mod 3 \}  $$   and  $T$  to the multiset defined by  $T := \{a_{i,j} \in L_k | k \not \equiv 1 \mod 3 \}$ . 

It can be easily verified that 
- By the question's condition,  $\sum_{x \in S} x = 0 = \sum_{x \in T} x$  (because the condition in the problem is equivalent to the fact that sum of numbers in each row and column and each good diagonals (i.e diagonals as mentioned in the problem) are zero)
- $T \subset S$ ,  $S-T = \{a_{i,j}, a_{i,j} | i \equiv 1 \mod 3, j \equiv 1 \mod 3 \}$  (each element is repeated exactly twice) and  $|S-T| = 2k^2$
. 
Hence  $\sum_{x \in S-T} x = 0$ . On the other hand, since  $x$  are either  $1, \omega, \omega^2$ , by Lemma we have  $|S-T| = 2k^2 \equiv 0 \mod 3 \Rightarrow k \equiv 0 \mod 3$  as desired.</details>
What is motivation for counting all rows and columns mod 2 mod 3 and diagonals?

I think it's because the first thing you realize is that n is a multiple of 3. Now it is a shared property among all working n's that you can divide them into 3*3s. This process also allows you to think about the problem on a manageable scale because instead of n*n's now you are dealing with 3*3s. 

Now you want some novel way to count each square of a 3*3 square a certain number of times each, and the great way to do that is to count all rows and columns mod two plus the diagonals because you only overcount the center squares. This was my understanding.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>We claim that the answer is for any  $9 | n$ , since the construction has been posted many times already I won't spend time drawing the diagram for it.

Since the number of  $I, M$  and  $O$  in each row are equal,  $3$  must divide  $n$ . Let  $n = 3m$ .

In each entry, replace  $I$  with  $1$ ,  $M$  with  $-1$  and  $O$  with  $0$ .

Number the cells from  $(1, 1)$  in the bottom-left corner to  $(3m, 3m)$  in the top-right corner.
Let  $v(i, j)$  refer to the value in cell  $(i, j)$ .
Note that sum of the  $v(i, j)$  across any row, column, diagonal of length divisible by 3 or the entire board is  $0$ .

Consider the sum,
\[\sum_{i=1}^{3m} \sum_{j=1}^{3m} v(i, j) - \tfrac12\sum_{3 | i} \sum_{j=1}^{3m} v(i, j) - \tfrac12\sum_{i = 1}^{3m} \sum_{3 | j} v(i, j) - \tfrac12\sum_{k = 1}^m \sum_{3 | i - 1} v(i, j) - \tfrac12\sum_{i = 1}^{3m} \sum_{3 | j - 1} v(i, j) - \tfrac12\sum_{3 | i + j + 1} v(i, j) = 0\]
What this does is add all the values across the board, subtracts all the columns and rows which are  $0, 1 \mod 3$  and subtracts the diagonals of length divisible by 3 which are parallel to the diagonal from top-left to bottom right.
Leaving only the centres of smaller  $3 \times 3$  grids, which there are  $m^2$  of. This implies that the number of  $I$  and  $M$  in these  $m^2$  cells must be equal.

By symmetry, the number of  $I$ ,  $M$  and  $O$  in these  $m^2$  cells are equal which implies  $3 | m^2$ . Thus,  $3 | m$ .

Therefore,  $9 | 3m = n$ .  $\blacksquare$</details>

On the other hand, suppose  $n=3k$ ,  $3\nmid k$ . We will call squares which have two incident diagonals *leaks*. Note that there are  $k^2$  leaks, one in every 3x3, so WLOG there are at least  $\frac{k^2+2}{3}$   $I$ s among the leaks. Now, consider all rows which do not contain leaks. In these rows, all squares are intersected by at least one diagonal except those in the columns of leaks. There are at most  $k^2-\frac{k^2+2}{3}$  inside the columns of the leaks, and hence at least  $k^2+\frac{k^2+2}{3}$  in diagonal spots. So if we denote  $S$  as the sum of the number of  $I$ s across all diagonals, we get that   $$ S\ge 2\cdot\frac{k^2+2}{3}+\frac{k^2+2}{3}+k^2=2k^2+3 $$   However, we know that  $S=2\cdot (1+2+\ldots + (k-1)+k+(k-1)+\ldots+1)=2k^2<2k^2+3$ . Our construction is done. It remains to show that for $n$ satisfying $9 \nmid n$ , there is no such construction. First of all, we see that $3 \nmid n$ by the problem statement, which implies each row/column has a multiple of $3$ number of entries. Let $n = 3m$ . We count the number of $O$ 's in the $3m$ by $3m$ grid in two ways. Clearly there are a total of $\tfrac13 \cdot (3m)^2 = 3m^2$ entries $O$ in the grid. Next, consider all diagonals of multiple of $3$ length and all rows labeled $2 \pmod 3$ . We sum over all these and count the number of $O$ 's with repetition. Note that everything is counted once except for $(3i + 2, 3j + 2)$ for some $i, j$ , which are counted three times. Let $c$ denote the number of $O$ 's in $(3i + 2, 3j + 2)$ places. Thus, the total number of $O$ 's is also\[2m \cdot m + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{3} \cdot (3 + 6 + \ldots + 3m + 3(m-1) + \ldots + 3) - 3c\]so if we equate this to $3m^2$ and solve for $c$ we get $c = \tfrac{m^2}{3}$ which is only possible when $m = 3k$ for some positive integer $k$ . Thus $3 \mid m$ and thus $9 \mid n$ as desired. $\blacksquare$

Suppose some  $n\times n$  matrix works. Call its entries  $x_{ij} \in \{I,M,O\}$ . Consider an  $n\times n$  matrix with entries  $a_{ij}$ , which starts of as all 0's. We can add/subtract 1 to each element of any row, column, or diagonal, and performing any such operation preserves the fact that there are an equal number of  $I,M,O$  in the multiset  $S$  that has  $a_{ij}$  copies of  $x_{ij}$  for each  $i,j$ . Perform the following operations (rows/columns are 1-indexed):      
- add 1 to each  $2\pmod 3$  row,
- add 1 to each  $2\pmod 3$  column,
- add 1 to each of the  $4n-2$  diagonals,
- subtract 1 from each row.
 Splitting the  $n\times n$  matrix into  $3\times 3$  matrices, the above operations do \begin{align*}     \begin{bmatrix} 0&0&00&0&00&0&0\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix} 0&0&01&1&10&0&0\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix} 0&1&01&2&10&1&0\end{bmatrix} \to      \begin{bmatrix} 1&1&11&4&11&1&1\end{bmatrix} \to      \begin{bmatrix} 0&0&00&3&00&0&0\end{bmatrix}.  \end{align*} Now, there are an equal number of  $I,M,O$  in the multiset which has 3 of each middle element of the  $3\times 3$ 's. Hence, there is also an equal number of  $I,M,O$  in the set which has just 1 of each middle element. Hence,  $3\mid (n/3)^2$ , i.e.  $9\mid n$ , as claimed.

However, the idea is to notice that we can have 3 copies of a single element, and it is equivalent to just having 1 in order to satisfy the condition of an equal number of  $I,M,O$ .</details>

Now we prove that if  $n = 3k$  and  $3\not | k$ , then this is impossible. Define a otis-diagonal as a diagonal with a multiple of  $3$  number of entries. Observe that we can partition the  $n$  by  $n$  square into  $k^{2}$   $3$  by  $3$  squares. I claim that for each  $3$  by  $3$  square, the center will be on two otis-diagonals (call these type of squares kaguya), the squares adjacent to the center will be on none (call these type of squares chika if adjacent by a horizontal edge, and hayasaka if adjacent by a vertical edge), and the corner squares will be on one otis-diagonal (call these type of squares miyuki). This is true, because if we label the square with x and y axis (with 0-indexing), the otis-diagonals parallel to the major diagonal goes through squares with  $3 | x - y$ , and the diagonals parallel to the minor diagonal goes through squares with  $3 | x+y+1$ . 

Then, consider the number of I's, M's, and O's in all the otis-diagonals (with overlap). They are clearly equal. Each kaguya square is counted twice, and each miyuki square is counted once. Next, consider the number of I's, M's, and O's in each row that is not  $1\mod 3$ . These also must be equal. Then, we can subtract the first set of squares from the second, which will result in the sum of the hayasaka squares minus twice the kaguyas squares, and denote this triplet as  $T$ . Finally, consider the columns that are  $1\mod 3$ , and subtract  $T$  from this. This will result in  $3$  times the kaguya squares, and since every single triple was equal so far, this means the number of  $I$ s,  $M$ s, and  $O$ s in  $3$  times the kaguya squares must be equal. This also means the number of  $I$ s,  $M$ s, and  $O$ s in the kaguya squares must be equal, so the number of kaguya squares must be divisible by  $3$ . However, this is only valid when  $3 | k$  (since there is exactly  $1$  kaguya square in each of the  $k^{2}$   $3$  by  $3$  squares). Thus, our only solution is  $9 | n$ .

We claim that  $n$  works iff  $9\mid n$ .

Let a diagonal with slope  $1$  be a up-diagonal and a diagonal with slope  $-1$  be a down-diagonal. Remark that  $3\mid n$  by the first condition, so let  $n=3m$ . Observe that there are four types of cells; "lonely" cells in no up-diagonal or down-diagonal, "optimistic" cells in an up-diagonal but not in a down-diagonal, "pessimistic" cells in a down-diagonal but not an up-diagonal, and "experienced" cells in both types of diagonals. By working with  $(i,j)\pmod{3}$ , we find that we can separate the lonely cells into cells in the same column as experienced cells, or left cells, and cells in the same row as experienced cells, or right cells. By counting (alternately expected value), there are exactly  $m^2$  experienced cells,  $2m^2$  cells that are optimistic and  $2m^2$  cells that are pessimistic, and  $4m^2$  cells that are lonely ( $2m^2$  each of left and right cells). Let the letters be  $A,B,C$  instead for variable naming convenience. Let  $a_1,b_1,c_1$  be the numbers of instances of  $A,B,C$  among the experienced cells. Similarly define  $a_2,b_2,c_2$  for the optimistic cells,  $a_3,b_3,c_3$  for the pessimistic cells, and  $a_4,b_4,c_4$  for the lonely cells. By counting, we have
\begin{align*}

    a_2+b_2+c_2&=2m^2
    a_3+b_3+c_3&=2m^2
    a_4+b_4+c_4&=4m^2
    a_1+a_2+a_3+a_4&=3m^2
    b_1+b_2+b_3+b_4&=3m^2
    c_1+c_2+c_3+c_4&=3m^2
    a_1+a_3=a_1+a_2&=m^2
    b_1+b_3=b_1+b_2&=m^2
    c_1+c_3=c_1+c_2&=m^2.
\end{align*}
Then we immediately have  $a_2=a_3=m^2-a_1,\dots$ . Plugging this information in eliminates some of the equations to yield
\begin{align*}
	a_1+b_1+c_1&=m^2
    a_4+b_4+c_4&=4m^2
    2m^2-a_1+a_4=a_1+2m^2-2a_1+a_4&=3m^2

    2m^2-c_1+c_4=c_1+2m^2-2c_1+c_4&=3m^2.

This yields  $a_4=m^2+a_1,$  etc. Now split  $a_4$  into  $a_5$  and  $a_6$  where  $a_5$  is the number of left cells with  $A$  and  $a_6$  is the number of right cells with  $A$ . Similarly define  $b_5,b_6,c_5,c_6$ . It is clear that \[a_1+a_5=a_1+a_6=m^2.\]

solutionI claim $n$ works iff $9 \mid n$ . It is clear that $3 \mid n$ . Write $n = 3m$ , I'll prove that 3 must divide $m$ . Now, we divide the grid into $m^2$ $3\times 3$ blocks. Consider the set $S$ , consisting of only the tiles in the center of each $3 \times 3$ block. Say there's $a$ values of $I$ in this set, $b$ values of $M$ , and $c$ of $O$ . **Claim** a = b = c holds. *Proof.* Let $\omega$ be a primitive third root of unity. We will label each square of the grid with $\omega^1$ if it has an $M$ , with $\omega^2$ if it has an $I$ , and with $\omega^3 = 1$ if it has an $O$ . Observe by vieta that $$ \omega^2 + \omega^1 + 1 = 0. $$ Now, consider adding up all the squares in: - Rows congruent to $2 \pmod{3}$ . - Columns congruent to $2 \pmod{3}$ . - The diagonals that are divisible by 3. By the conditions given, this sum must be 0. Observe that we're adding every square in $S$ 4 times, and all the other squares once. stem_md: A set of positive integers is called *fragrant* if it contains at least two elements and each of its elements has a prime factor in common with at least one of the other elements.  Let  $P(n)=n^2+n+1$ .  What is the least possible positive integer value of  $b$  such that there exists a non-negative integer  $a$  for which the set   $$ \{P(a+1),P(a+2),\ldots,P(a+b)\} $$   is fragrant?
solution_md: SolutionThe answer is $b = \boxed{6}$ . First, a few preliminaries. **Claim 1:** For all nonnegative integers $n$ , $\gcd(P(n), P(n+1)) = 1$ .**Proof:** Note that for any nonnegative integer $n$ , \begin{align*} \gcd(P(n), P(n+1)) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, (n+1)^2+(n+1)+1) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, n^2+3n+3) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 2n+2). \end{align*} Note that $n^2+n+1$ is always odd for any nonnegative integer $n$ , so $\gcd(n^2+n+1, 2n+2) = \gcd(n^2+n+1, n+1)$ . Thus, \begin{align*} \gcd(P(n), P(n+1)) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 2n+2) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, n+1) &= \gcd(n(n+1) + 1, n+1) &= \gcd(1, n+1) &= 1, \end{align*} as desired.**Claim 2:**For all nonnegative integers $n$ , $\gcd(P(n), P(n+2)) \neq 1$ iff $n\equiv 2\pmod{7}$ . **Proof:** Note that for any nonnegative integer $n$ , \begin{align*} \gcd(P(n), P(n+2)) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, (n+2)^2+(n+2)+1) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, n^2 + 5n + 7) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 4n+6). \end{align*} Note that $n^2+n+1$ is always odd for any nonnegative integer $n$ , so $\gcd(n^2+n+1, 4n+6) = \gcd(n^2+n+1, 2n+3)$ . Since $2n+3$ is always odd for any nonnegative integer $n$ , $\gcd(n^2+n+1, 2n+3) = \gcd(2n^2+2n+2, 2n+3)$ . Thus, \begin{align*} \gcd(P(n), P(n+2)) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 4n+6) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 2n+3) &= \gcd(2n^2+2n+2, 2n+3) &= \gcd((2n^2+3n) - (2n^2+2n+2), 2n+3) &= \gcd(n-2, 2n+3) &= \gcd(n-2, 2n+3 - 2(n-2)) &= \gcd(n-2, 7). \end{align*} Note that $\gcd(n-2, 7) = 1$ if $n\neq 2\pmod{7}$ and $\gcd(n-2, 7) = 7 \neq 1$ if $n\equiv 2\pmod{7}$ . Thus, $\gcd(P(n), P(n+2)) \neq 1$ iff $n\equiv 2\pmod{7}$ , as desired.**Claim 3:** For all nonnegative integers $n$ , $\gcd(P(n), P(n+3)) \neq 1$ iff $n\equiv 1\pmod{3}$ .**Proof:** Note that for any nonnegative integer $n$ , \begin{align*} \gcd(P(n), P(n+3)) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, (n+3)^2 + (n+3)+1) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, n^2 + 7n + 13) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 6n+12). \end{align*} Note that $n^2+n+1$ is always odd for any nonnegative integer $n$ , so $\gcd(n^2+n+1, 6n+12) = \gcd(n^2+n+1, 3n+6)$ . Now, note that if $n\equiv 1\pmod{3}$ , then $3 \mid n^2+n+1$ and $3\mid 3n+6$ , so $3\mid \gcd(P(n), P(n+3)) = \gcd(n^2+n+1, 3n+6)$ , so $\gcd(P(n), P(n+3)) \neq 1$ when $n\equiv 1\pmod{3}$ . Now, assume that $n\not \equiv 1\pmod{3}$ . We will prove $\gcd(P(n), P(n+3)) = 1$ in this case. Note that if $n\not \equiv 1\pmod{3}$ , then $3\nmid n^2+n+1$ , so $\gcd(n^2+n+1, 3n+6) = \gcd(n^2+n+1, n+2)$ . Thus, if $n\not \equiv 1\pmod{3}$ , \begin{align*} \gcd(P(n), P(n+3)) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 6n+12) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 3n+6) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, n+2) &= \gcd((n+2)(n-1) + 3, n+2) &= \gcd(3, n+2) &= 1, \end{align*} as $n\not \equiv 1\pmod{3}$ , so we've proved both directions and so the claim is true.**Claim 4:** For all nonnegative integers $n$ , $\gcd(P(n), P(n+4)) \neq 1$ iff $n\equiv 7\pmod{19}$ .**Proof:** Note that for any nonnegative integer $n$ , \begin{align*} \gcd(P(n), P(n+4)) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, (n+4)^2+(n+4)+1) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, n^2+9n+21) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 8n+20). \end{align*} Note that $n^2+n+1$ is odd for every nonnegative integer $n$ , so $\gcd(n^2+n+1, 8n+20) = \gcd(n^2+n+1, 2n+5)$ . Note that $2n+5$ is odd for every nonnegative integer $n$ , so $\gcd(n^2+n+1, 2n+5) = \gcd(2n^2+2n+2, 2n+5)$ . Thus, \begin{align*} \gcd(P(n), P(n+4)) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 8n+20) &= \gcd(n^2+n+1, 2n+5) &= \gcd(2n^2+2n+2, 2n+5) &= \gcd((2n^2+5n) - (3n-2), 2n+5) &= \gcd(3n-2, 2n+5) &= \gcd(n-7, 2n+5) &= \gcd(n-7, 2n+5 - (2n-14)) &= \gcd(n-7, 19). \end{align*} Note that $\gcd(n-7, 19) = 1$ if $n\not \equiv 7\pmod{19}$ , and $\gcd(n-7, 19) = 19 \neq 1$ if $n\equiv 7\pmod{19}$ . Thus, $\gcd(P(n), P(n+4)) \neq 1$ iff $n\equiv 7\pmod{19}$ , as desired. Now, back to the problem. We will first show that all $1\leq b\leq 5$ fail. $b = 1$ fails by definition - a fragrant set must have at least one element. $b = 2$ fails, since in a fragrant set $\{P(a+1), P(a+2)\}$ for some nonnegative integer $a$ , we must have that $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+2)) \neq 1$ , but we know by our first claim that $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+2)) = 1$ for all nonnegative integers $a$ , a contradiction. $b = 3$ fails, since in a fragrant set $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3)\}$ for some nonnegative integer $a$ , we must either have that $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+2)) \neq 1$ or $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+3)) \neq 1$ . However, from our first claim, $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+2)) = \gcd(P(a+2), P(a+3)) = 1$ for all nonnegative integers $a$ , a contradiction. $b = 4$ fails. Consider a fragrant set $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4)\}$ for some nonnegative integer $a$ . By our first claim, $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+2)) = \gcd(P(a+2), P(a+3)) = 1$ , so we must have $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ (since $P(a+2)$ has to have some prime factor in common with another element in $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4)\}$ ). Similarly, we know that $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+3)) = \gcd(P(a+3), P(a+4)) = 1$ , so we must have $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+3)) \neq 1$ (since $P(a+3)$ has to have some prime factor in common with another element in $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4)\}$ ). However, by the second claim, we have that since $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ , $a+2 \equiv 2\pmod{7}$ . Similarly, since $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+3)) \neq 1$ , $a+1 \equiv 2\pmod{7}$ . Then, $1 \equiv (a+2) - (a+1) \equiv 2-2\equiv 0\pmod{7}$ , a contradiction. $b = 5$ fails. Consider a fragrant set $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4), P(a+5)\}$ for some nonnegative integer $a$ . By our first claim, $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+3)) = \gcd(P(a+3), P(a+4)) = 1$ . Thus, either $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+3)) \neq 1$ or $\gcd(P(a+3), P(a+5)) \neq 1$ , since $P(a+3)$ has to have some prime factor in common with another element in $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4), P(a+5)\}$ . If $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+3)) \neq 1$ , then note that $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+2)) = \gcd(P(a+2), P(a+3)) = 1$ by our first claim, so either $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ or $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+5)) \neq 1$ , since $P(a+2)$ has to have some prime factor in common with another element in $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4), P(a+5)\}$ . If $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ , then since $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+3)) \neq 1$ as well, it follows that $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4)\}$ is fragrant since $P(a+1)$ shares a prime factor with $P(a+3)$ and vice versa, and $P(a+2)$ shares a prime factor with $P(a+4)$ and vice versa, but we dispelled such a possibility above when we proved that $b = 4$ fails. Thus, we have that $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+5)) \neq 1$ . Note that $\gcd(P(a+3), P(a+4)) = \gcd(P(a+4), P(a+5)) = 1$ , by our first claim. Thus, since $P(a+4)$ needs to share another prime factor in common with another element in $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4), P(a+5)\}$ , we have that either $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ or $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ . We just explained that we cannot have $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ above, so we must have $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ . Also, note that from our above work, we have $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+5)) \neq 1$ . By our third claim, $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ means that $a+1\equiv 1\pmod{3}$ and $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+5)) \neq 1$ means that $a+2\equiv 1\pmod{3}$ . Thus, $1\equiv (a+2) - (a+1) \equiv 1 - 1 \equiv 0\pmod{3}$ , a contradiction. If $\gcd(P(a+3), P(a+5)) \neq 1$ instead, then use similar logic -- note that $\gcd(P(a+3), P(a+4)) = \gcd(P(a+4), P(a+5)) = 1$ by our first claim, so either $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ or $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ , since $P(a+4)$ needs to share a prime factor with another element in $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4), P(a+5)\}$ . We cannot have $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ as it would imply that $\{P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4), P(a+5)\}$ is fragrant, something we dispelled above by proving the $b = 4$ case. Thus, $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ . Now, note that $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+2)) = \gcd(P(a+2), P(a+3)) = 1$ by our first claim, so either $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ or $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+5)) \neq 1$ since $P(a+2)$ needs to share a prime factor with another element in $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4), P(a+5)\}$ . We cannot have $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ as discussed above, so we have that $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+5)) \neq 1$ . Then, $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+4)) \neq 1$ and $\gcd(P(a+2), P(a+5)) \neq 1$ , so by our third claim, $a+1 \equiv 1\pmod{3}$ and $a+2 \equiv 1\pmod{3}$ , which is a contradiction as explained in the $\gcd(P(a+1), P(a+3)) \neq 1$ case. Thus, $b = 5$ indeed fails. Now, we will show that $b = 6$ works. Take $a = 196$ , and consider the set $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4), P(a+5), P(a+6)\} = \{P(197), P(198), P(199), P(200), P(201), P(202)\}.$ Note that by our fourth claim, since $197 \equiv 7\pmod{19},$ $$ \gcd(P(197), P(201)) \neq 1. $$ By our second claim, since $198 \equiv 2\pmod{7}$ , $$ \gcd(P(198), P(200)) \neq 1. $$ By our third claim, since $199 \equiv 1\pmod{3}$ , $$ \gcd(P(199), P(202)) \neq 1. $$ Thus, $P(197)$ shares a prime factor with $P(201)$ and vice versa, $P(198)$ shares a prime factor with $P(200)$ and vice versa, and $P(199)$ shares a prime factor with $P(202)$ and vice versa, so if $a = 196$ , $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), P(a+3), P(a+4), P(a+5), P(a+6)\}$ is fragrant, as desired. Thus, $b = 6$ is the smallest such positive integer value of $b$ such that there exists a non-negative integer $a$ for which the set $\{P(a+1), P(a+2), \cdots, P(a+b)\}$ is fragrant, as desired. $\blacksquare$

Lemma: If  $x \equiv  n, n^2 \pmod {P(n)}$ , then  $P(x) \equiv 0 \pmod {P(n)}$ .
Proof: If  $x \equiv n \pmod {P(n)}$  this is obviously true. If  $x \equiv n^2 \pmod {P(n)}$  then \[P(x) = n^4 + n^2 + 1 = (n^4+n^3+n^2) - (n^3+n^2+n) + (n^2+n+1) \equiv 0 \pmod { n^2+n+1} \equiv 0 \pmod {P(n)}.\]

Thus \[n \equiv 1 \pmod {3} \implies P(n) \equiv 0 \pmod {3}\]\[n \equiv 2,4 \pmod {7} \implies P(n) \equiv 0 \pmod {7}\]\[n \equiv 3,9 \pmod {13} \implies P(n) \equiv 0 \pmod {13}\]\[\cdots\] \[n \equiv 7,49 \pmod {57} \implies P(n) \equiv 0 \pmod {57} \text{ or } n \equiv 7,11 \pmod {19} \implies P(n) \equiv 0 \pmod {19}\]. Let  $i>1$  be a positive integer, then note \[ P(a+i)-P(a+1) = (2a+i+2)(i-1) \] and \[ P(a+1) \equiv P(a+i) \equiv a^2+3a+3 \pmod{2a+i+2}. \] So  $\gcd \left(P(a+1),P(a+i \right)>1$  iff  $\gcd \left(a^2+3a+3,2a+i+2 \right)>1$ . With the Euclidean Algorithm, we easily calculate \begin{align} \gcd \left(a^2+3a+3,2a+4 \right) &= \gcd(1,a+2),
 \gcd \left(a^2+3a+3,2a+5 \right) &= \gcd(a+6,-7),  \gcd \left(a^2+3a+3,2a+6 \right) &= \gcd(a+3,3),  \gcd \left(a^2+3a+3,2a+7 \right) &= \gcd(6-a,19) \end{align} for  $i=2,3,4$ . So  $(1)$  implies that  $\gcd{(P(a+1),P(a+2))}=1$  for all  $a \in \mathbb{N}_0$ . Then  $(2)$  to  $(4)$  implies  $P(a+1)$  shares a common factor with  $P(a+2),P(a+3),P(a+4)$  respectively, iff  $a \equiv 1 \pmod 7$ ,  $a \equiv 0 \pmod 3$ ,  $a \equiv 6 \pmod {19}$ . The factors they'd share would then be  $7$ , $3$  or  $19$ .
With that it is easy to show that  $b=1,2,3,4,5$  do not work. It is also not hard to show that  $b=6$  works. We want to construct  $a$ , such that \begin{align*} \gcd(P(a+1),P(a+5)) &=19,
  \gcd(P(a+2),P(a+4)) &=7,
  \gcd(P(a+3),P(a+6)) &=3. \end{align*} So with the above observations, this yields \begin{align*} a &\equiv 6 \pmod{19},
 a &\equiv 0 \pmod{7},
 a &\equiv 1 \pmod{3}. \end{align*} But the **Chinese Remainder Theorem** ensures that there is one such number. Done.

so  $x \equiv 2 \pmod{7}.$  Thus  $a \equiv 0 \pmod{7}.$  Similarly,  $P(a+3)$  must be buddies with  $P(a+1),$  implying that  $a \equiv 6 \pmod{7},$  contradiction. &= \gcd(y^2 + y + 1, 6y + 12) 
&= \gcd(y^2 + y + 1, 3y + 6).
\end{align*}

\begin{align*}
\gcd(P(y), P(y+3) &= \gcd(y^2 + y + 1, y+2) 
&= \gcd(y^2 + y + 1 - (y^2 + y - 2), y + 2) 
&= \gcd(3, y+2) \ne 1,
\end{align*}

stem_md: The equation  $$ (x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-2016)=(x-1)(x-2)\cdots (x-2016) $$  is written on the board, with  $2016$  linear factors on each side. What is the least possible value of  $k$  for which it is possible to erase exactly  $k$  of these  $4032$  linear factors so that at least one factor remains on each side and the resulting equation has no real solutions?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>If you remove  $k \le 2015$  linear factors, by the Pigeonhole Principle, at least one of the factors will appear on both sides, giving us a real root. Otherwise, you remove exactly one instance for each root. To show that  $k=2016$  is achievable, you start by examining smaller cases. With  $4$  linear terms,  $(x-1)(x-4)=(x-2)(x-3)$  has no real roots. For  $8$  linear terms,  $(x-1)(x-4)(x-6)(x-7) = (x-2)(x-3)(x-5)(x-8)$  boils down to a linear function, whereas  $(x-1)(x-4)(x-5)(x-8) = (x-2)(x-3)(x-6)(x-7)$  boils down to a quadratic with no real roots. This motivates the conjecture that  $(x-1)(x-4)(x-5)(x-8)...(x-2013)(x-2016) = (x-2)(x-3)(x-6)(x-7)...(x-2014)(x-2015)$  has no real roots. Let's prove it.

Suppose the left side was called  $A(x)$  and the right side was called  $B(x)$ . Suppose we removed linear factors in a way so that  $A(x)$  has the roots  $\equiv 0, 1\pmod{4}$  and  $B(x)$  has the roots  $\equiv 2, 3 \pmod{4}$ , so that it like just like the equation right above.
Of course, none of the integers in the set  $\{1, 2, 3, 4, ..., 2015, 2016\}$  are going to be roots. If  $x$  was in  $(2k+1, 2k+2)$  for some integer  $k$ , then  $A(x)$  would be negative and  $B(x)$  would be positive, so they would never be equal. If  $x$  was in  $(4k, 4k+1)$ , then we could pair off the terms as  $(x-(4a+1))(x-(4a+4))$  and  $(x-(4a+2))(x-(4a+3))$ , noting that they are both positive, but the product coming from  $B(x)$  is always  $2$  greater than the product coming from  $A(x)$ . Hence,  $B(x) > A(x)$  would hold.

The only case that remains is  $x \in (4k+2, 4k+3)$ , where  $A(x)$  and  $B(x)$  are both negative. Then if we can show that the magnitude of  $A(x)$  is greater than the magnitude of  $B(x)$ , then we would be finished. Comparing specifically the linear terms  $x$  lies between, we see that  $(x-(4k+1))(x-(4k+4))$  is going to be at least  $9$  times the value of of  $(x-(4k+2))(x-(4k+3))$ ; equality attained precisely at  $x=4k+2.5$ . For the rest of the products on either side, notice that the farther we stray  $g$  into  $\pm \infty$ , the closer the fraction  $\frac{(x-(4g+2))(x-(4g+3))}{(x-(4g+1))(x-(4g+4))}$  gets to  $1$  from the upper side.

The key claim is that the product  $U = \frac{3\cdot 4}{2\cdot 5} \times \frac{7\cdot 8}{6\cdot 9}\times ... \times \frac{(4g-1)\cdot (4g)}{(4g-2)\cdot (4g+1)}\times ...$  is bounded above by  $3$  (or actually something even less than that).

Then the worst case scenario on the right side would be attained by tending  $x$  to  $4k+3$ , the worst case scenario on the left side would be attained by tending  $x$  to  $4k+2$ , the worst case scenario for the inside would be at  $x=4k+2.5$ , but the products on both sides of the rational function  $\frac{B(x)}{A(x)}$  at this  $x$  would be finite version of the infinite product  $U$ , which can only be strictly less than  $3$ . Multiplying these together would give a product strictly less than  $9$ , which is not enough to overpower the  $\frac{1}{9}$  from the worst case scenario on the inside by setting  $x=4k+2.5$ .

Equivalently, we would like to show that  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} -\ln{(4n-2)}+\ln{(4n-1)}+\ln{(4n)}-\ln{(4n+1)}$  is bounded above by  $\ln{3}$ .
Noting that the summand is monotonic decreasing, we can use rectangle sums to identify an upper bound of   $$ \ln(1.2)+\int_{1}^{\infty} -\ln{(x-\frac{1}{2})}+\ln{(x-\frac{1}{4})}+\ln{(x)}-\ln{(x+\frac{1}{4})}\text{ }dx $$  The indefinite integral would be equal to   $$ -[(x-\frac{1}{2})\ln{(x-\frac{1}{2})}-(x-\frac{1}{2})]+[(x-\frac{1}{4})\ln{(x-\frac{1}{4})}-(x-\frac{1}{4})]+[x\ln{(x)}-x]-[(x+\frac{1}{4})\ln{(x+\frac{1}{4})}-(x+\frac{1}{4})] $$  which can be simplified as   $$ x[-\ln{(x-\frac{1}{2})}+\ln{(x-\frac{1}{4})}+\ln{(x)}-\ln{(x+\frac{1}{4})}]+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \ln{(x-\frac{1}{2})}-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \ln{(x-\frac{1}{4})}-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \ln{(x+\frac{1}{4})} $$  Notice that for any positive constant  $C$ ,   $$ \lim_{x \to \infty} x\cdot (\ln{(x+C)}-\ln{(x)}) = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln{(x+C)}-\ln{(x)}}{1/x} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1/(x+C)-1/x}{-1/x^2} = x-\frac{x^2}{x+C} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{Cx}{x+C} = C $$  Using this on pairs of terms on the left huge addend, we see that when we evaluate  $x$  to  $\infty$ , the huge term preceded by an  $x$  as a factor will have a limit of  $\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4} = 0$ . Meanwhile, the right side is much simpler, where we don't have the existence of an  $x$ , so  $\lim_{x \to \infty} \ln{(x+C)} - \ln{(x)} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \ln{\frac{x+C}{x}} = 0$ , so we can apply that to a sum of  $\frac{1}{4}\cdot (\ln{(x-\frac{1}{2})}-\ln{(x-\frac{1}{4})})$  and  $\frac{1}{4}\cdot (\ln{(x-\frac{1}{2})}-\ln{(x+\frac{1}{4})})$  to get  $0+0 = 0$ . So the result of the definite integral when evaluated at  $\infty$  will be  $0$ .
