well , the algebra of finding the  $f$  has become standard i feel , so we have  $f(x)+f\left(1-\frac{1}{x}\right)=\arctan(x)$  ,  $f\left(1-\frac{1}{x}\right)+f\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right)=\arctan\left(\frac{x-1}{x}\right)$  ,  $f\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right)+f(x)=\arctan\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right)$  
Now solving these simultaneous  equations we get  $2f(x)=\arctan(x)-\arctan\left(\frac{x-1}{x}\right)+\arctan\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right)$  

We have  $2\int_{0}^{1} f(x)dx=\underbrace{\left(\int_{0}^{1}\arctan(x)dx+\int_{0}^{1} \arctan\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right)dx\right)}_{\displaystyle :=I_{1}}-\overbrace{\left(\int_{0}^{1} \arctan\left(\frac{x-1}{x}\right)\right)}^{ \displaystyle :=I_{2}}$  ,

Now a quick note to see that  $\int_{0}^{1}f(g(x))dx=\int_{0}^{1} f(g(1-x))dx$ , using this we proceed now: $I_{1}=\left(\int_{0}^{1}\arctan(x)dx+\int_{0}^{1} \arctan\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)dx\right)=\left(\int_{0}^{1}\arctan(x)dx+\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\pi}{2}dx-\int_{0}^{1} \arctan(x)dx\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}$  $I_{2}=\int_{0}^{1} \arctan\left(\frac{x-1}{x}\right)dx=\int_{0}^{1} \arctan\left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right)dx=\int_{0}^{1} \frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\left(\frac{x-1}{x}\right)dx=\frac{\pi}{2}-I_{2} \implies I_{2}=\frac{\pi}{4}$ so  $\int_{0}^{1} f(x)dx=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \implies \int_{0}^{1}f(x)dx=\boxed{\frac{3\pi}{8}}$ .  $\square$

<details><summary>Another</summary>$\int_0^1f(x)\,dx+\int_{0}^1f\left(1-\frac{1}{x}\right)\,dx=\int_0^1 \arctan x\,dx \overset{x=1/x}\Longleftrightarrow \int_0^1 f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,dx+\int_0^1 f(1-x)\,dx=\int_0^1 \arctan \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,dx$ Note that  $\int_{0}^1f(1-x)\,dx=\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$  and that  $\int_0^1 f\left(1-\frac{1}{x}\right)\,dx=\int_0^1 f\left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right)\,dx$  (this is used later). $\int_0^1 \arctan x+ \arctan \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,dx=2\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx+\int_0^1 \left[f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+f\left(1-\frac{1}{x}\right)\right]\]\,dx$  $f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+f\left(1-\frac{1}{x}\right)=\arctan x \overset{x=x/(x-1)}\Longleftrightarrow f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+ f\left(1-\frac{1}{x}\right)=\arctan  \left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right)\,dx$  $\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\pi}{2}-\int_0^1 \arctan \left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right)\right]\,dx=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\boxed{\frac{3\pi}{8}}$</details>

By the mapping  $x\mapsto 1-\frac1x$  3 times, we have  $ f(x) = \frac{\arctan x + \arctan \left( \frac{1}{1-x} \right) - \arctan \left( 1- \frac 1x \right)}{2}$ . Now we observe that  $\arctan x + \arctan \left( \frac{1}{1-x} \right) = \frac\pi2 - \arctan(1-x) + \arctan x$  and integrating this part of the integral by substitution yields  $\frac\pi2$ . But we also have  $\int_0^1\arctan\left(\frac{1-x}x\right)\,dx=\frac\pi4$ , by reflecting the graph of  $\arctan\left(\frac{1-x}x\right)$  in the line  $x=\frac12$ . So we have the answer  $\boxed{\frac{3\pi}{8}}$
Yes. My comment above was not a complete solution, but just pointing at an alternative way to finish without integration by parts.

I think it's worth mentioning that the group of transformations  $\left\{x,\frac{x-1}{x},\frac{1}{1-x},1-x,\frac{x}{x-1},\frac{1}{x}\right\}$  has a nice geometric meaning: these are transformations of [cross-ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-ratio) of four points given by permuting these points. The subgroup  $\left\{x,\frac{x-1}{x},\frac{1}{1-x}\right\}$  then corresponds to even permutations.

Substituting, \begin{align*} x=\frac{1}{1-x} &\implies f(\frac{1}{1-x})+f(x)=\arctan (\frac{1}{1-x}).  x=1-\frac{1}{x} & \implies f(1-\frac{1}{x})+f(\frac{1}{1-x})=\arctan (1-\frac{1}{x}). \end{align*} Combining the three equations yields:   $$ 2f(x)=\arctan x+\arctan (\frac{1}{1-x})+\arctan (\frac{1-x}{x}). $$   Integrating this, \begin{align*} 2\int_0^1 f(x) \text dx &=\int _0^1 \arctan x \text dx+\int_0^1 \arctan (\frac{1}{1-x})\text dx+\int_0^1 \arctan (\frac{1-x}{x}) \text dx  &= \int_0^1 \arctan x \text dx +\frac{\pi}{2} -\int_0^1 \arctan (1-x) \text dx +\int_0^1 \arctan \frac{x}{1-x} \text dx  &= \int_0^1 \arctan x \text dx +\frac{\pi}{2} -\int_0^1 \arctan x \text dx +\frac{\pi}{2} -\int_0^1 \arctan (\frac{1-x}{x})\text dx.\end{align*} And so we get the answer   $$ \int_0^1 f(x)\text dx= \frac{3\pi}{8}. $$

stem_md:
Suppose that  $G$  is a finite group generated by the two elements  $g$  and  $h,$  where the order of  $g$  is odd. Show that every element of  $G$  can be written in the form
\[g^{m_1}h^{n_1}g^{m_2}h^{n_2}\cdots g^{m_r}h^{n_r}\]
with  $1\le r\le |G|$  and  $m_n,n_1,m_2,n_2,\dots,m_r,n_r\in\{1,-1\}.$  (Here  $|G|$  is the number of elements of  $G.$ )
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2016 Contests/2016 Putnam/1349021.json

candidates:
First we can get rid of the  $1 \le r \le |G|$  condition. The intuition behind this for me was graph theory based, like if you have a walk you can always reduce it to a path.

Suppose  $x = g^{m_1}h^{n_1}\ldots g^{m_s}h^{n_s}$  with  $s$  minimal. If  $s > |G|$ , then by the pigeonhole principle we must have  $g^{m_1}h^{n_1}\ldots g^{m_i}h^{n_i} = g^{m_1}h^{n_1} \ldots g^{m_j}h^{n_j}$  for some  $i < j$ . Then we can write  $x = g^{m_1}h^{n_1} \ldots g^{m_i} h^{n_i} g^{m_{j+1}} h^{n_{j+1}} \ldots g^{m_s} h^{n_s}$ , which contradicts the minimality of  $s$ . Therefore we have  $s \le |G|$ , as desired.

So if each  $x\in G$  can be expressed as some finite alternating product of  $\{g,g^{-1}\}$  and  $\{h,h^{-1}\}$  then we are done. Call such a product a  $(g,h)$ -product and define a  $(h,g)$ -product analogously with the roles of  $g$  and  $h$  swapped. We can make the following trivial observations:

i) if  $x \in G$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product then  $x^{-1}$  has an  $(h,g)$ -product.

ii) If  $x,y \in G$  each have a  $(g,h)$ -product then  $xy$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product

Now note that if we show  $g^2$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product we are done, since the order of  $g$  is odd, so we get by ii) that  $g = (g^2)^{\frac{|g|+1}{2}}$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product, then since  $g^{-1}h$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product, applying ii) again we get  $h = gg^{-1}h$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product. Then since  $g$  and  $h$  generate  $G$ , we get that each element of  $G$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product as desired.

Then the key observation which I missed during the contest is the following:

iii) If  $x \in G$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product then  $x$  has an  $(h,g)$ -product as well

Indeed, note that  $x^{-1} = x^{|x|-1}$ , so  $x^{-1}$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product. Then by i),  $x$  has an  $(h,g)$ -product, as desired. From here, it's easy, because we note  $h^{-1}g$  has an  $(h,g)$ -product and so a  $(g,h)$ -product, and  $g^2 = ghh^{-1}g$ , so  $g^2$  has a  $(g,h)$ -product, as desired.

I tried thinking about this in various sophisticated ways, and solved it quickly once I stopped doing that. First of all the condition  $1 \le r \le |G|$  is a bit of a red herring. Indeed, if  $S$  is any set of generators of a finite group  $G$ , then every element of  $G$  is a product of at most  $|G|$  elements of  $S$ . This is because if we let  $G_a$  be the elements expressable as a product of  $a$  or fewer such elements, then  $|G_{a+1}| > |G_a|$  until  $G_a$  is all of  $G$ . Therefore  $G_{|G|} = G$ . Indeed  $G_{|G|-|S|+1} = G$ .

So now the problem is simply to show that  $gh$ ,  $g^{-1}h$ ,  $gh^{-1}$ , and  $g^{-1} h^{-1}$  generate  $G$ . In fact,  $gh$  and  $g^{-1}h$  will do. Let  $H$  be the subgroup they generate. Note that  $(gh) \cdot (g^{-1}h)^{-1} = g^2 \in H$ . Since the order of  $g$  is odd we have  $g \in H$ . Since  $gh \in H$  we also have  $h \in H$ , and we're done.

Consider a directed graph whose vertices are elements of  $G$  where we draw edges  $v \to vgh$ ,  $v \to vgh^{-1}$ ,  $v \to vg^{-1} h$ , and  $v \to vg^{-1} h ^{-1}$  for every vertex  $v \in G$ .

The problem asks to show that there is a directed path of length at most  $|G|$ , starting from the identity  $1 \in G$  to any other element of  $G$ .  Of course, the shortest path if it exists will have this length, and consequently it suffices just to show that there is any path, i.e.\ that all vertices can be reached from  $1$ .  

Assume for contradiction some proper subset  $S$  of the vertices contains  $1$  and moreover  $Sgh = S$ ,  $Sgh^{-1} = S$ ,  $Sg^{-1} h = S$ ,  $Sg^{-1} h^{-1} = S$ .  Consequently, \[ S = (Sgh)(g^{-1} h)^{-1} = Sg^2. \] So  $Sg^{2k} = S$  for any  $k$  by induction, and since  $g$  has odd order,  $Sg = S$ .  And now  $S = (Sg)(g^{-1} h) = Sh$ .  But  $S = Sg = Sh$  is impossible for proper subsets  $S$  since  $g$  and  $h$  were supposed to generate  $G$ .

Obviously  $(gh)^{|G|} = 1$ , so the trivial element is written like that. 

Now, let  $|g| = 2d+1$  for some  $d$ . Then, since  $h = g^{-1} * gh$ , we see that  $h \in \langle g, gh \rangle$ . Thus,  $G = \langle g, gh \rangle$ .
Now, consider  $\langle g^{-1}h, gh \rangle$ , we have that  $(gh (g^{-1}h)^{-1})^{d+1} = (gh h^{-1}g)^{d+1} = (g^2)^{d+1} = g^{2d+2} = g$ . Thus,  $g \in \langle g^{-1}h, gh \rangle$ . Which means that  $G = \langle g, gh \rangle = \langle g^{-1}h, gh \rangle$ .

Since,  $G$  is finite,  $(gh)^{-1} = (gh)^m$  and  $(g^{-1}h) ^{-1} = (g^{-1}h)^n$ ,  for some  $n, m \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ .
Hence, every element in  $\langle g^{-1}h, gh \rangle$  (aka  $G$ ), has the form  $(gh)^{a_1}(g^{-1}h)^{b_1} \cdots (gh)^{a_k}(g^{-1}h)^{b_k}$ , for some positive integers  $k$ , and positive integers  $a_i$ 's,  $b_i$ 's. But we can spread out those exponents and get some series of  $g^{\epsilon_i}h^{\delta_i}$  that has  $\epsilon_i$  and  $\delta_i$  as 1 or -1.

First we show that the problem is true if we drop the  $1 \le r \le |G|$  condition. We wish to show that any element of  $G$  can be written as a finite product of  $gh, gh^{-1}, g^{-1}h, g^{-1}h^{-1}$ . Since  $G$  is finite,  $(g^{-1}h)^{-1} = h^{-1}g$  is a positive power of  $g^{-1}h$ , so  $(gh)(h^{-1}g) = g^2$  is representable, and since  $g$  has odd order,  $g$  is a power of  $g^2$ , so  $g$  is representable too. Now  $h = (g)(g^{-1}h)$  is representable too, so the entirety of  $G$  is representable.

Now we solve the problem. First, note that  $1 = (gh)^{|G|}$  is OK, and now suppose  $a$  is a nontrivial element of  $G$ . Let
\[a = (g^{m_1} h^{n_1}) \cdots (g^{m_r} h^{n_r})\]
be a valid representation of  $a$  with  $r$  minimal; since  $a$  is nontrivial,  $r \ge 1$ . By the minimality of  $r$ , the partial products  $(g^{m_1} h^{n_1}) \cdots (g^{m_k} h^{n_k})$  with  $1 \le k \le r$  are all distinct, ensuring  $r \le |G|$  as desired.

We can relax the size constraint by noticing that for any sequence of length longer than  $|G|$  that generates an element  $x$ , by Pigeonhole there exist two prefixes that are identical, thus we can strictly decrease the length of the sequence.

Now denote by  $S$  the set of all elements in  $G$  that can be generated as such. The condition implies  $Sgh = S$  and  $Sg^{-1} h = S$ , so any linear combination of  $gh$  and  $g^{-1}h$  can be generated, in particular   $$ S = (Sgh)(g^{-1}h)^{-1} = Sg^2. $$   But as the order of  $g$  is odd, this implies  $Sg = S$  and also  $Sh = S$ . By definition  $S = G$  now.

Let  $A_j = \{ g^{m_1} h^{n_1} \cdots g^{m_j} h^{n_j} \mid m_1,\cdots,n_r \in \{1,-1\}\}$ Then  $|A_j| \le |A_{j+1}|$ .

If  $|A_j| < |A_{j+1}|$  for all  $j=1,\cdots,r-1$  then we are done. Otherwise suppose  $|A_i| = |A_{i+1}|$ . Then 

Observe   $$ A_{i+1} = A_igh = A_i gh^{-1} = A_i g^{-1}h = A_i g^{-1}h^{-1} = ghA_i = gh^{-1}A_i = g^{-1}h^{-1}A_i = g^{-1}hA_i $$  From  $A_i gh = A_ig^{-1}h$  we can see that  $A_ig = A_ig^{-1}$ . This implies that  $A_i=A_ig^2$ . Since  $ord(g)$  is odd,  $A_i = A_ig$ . Similarly  $gA_i = A_i$ .

Similarly we can also get  $g^2 (hA_i) = hA_i$ , so  $ghA_i=g^{ord(g)+1}hA_i = hA_i$ . This implies that  $hA_i = A_ih = A_{i+1}$  and  $h^2A_i = A_i = A_ih^2$  ( in particular one can check that  $A_{i+2} = A_i$ . ) 

Now suppose  $x\in G$ , then there exists  $c_1,d_1,\cdots,c_k,d_k$  such that   $$ x=g^{c_1} h^{d_1} \cdots g^{c_k} h^{d_k} $$    $$ x\in A_i \iff h^{d_1+\cdots+d_k} \in A_i $$    $$ x\in A_{i+1} \iff h^{d_1+\cdots+d_k} \in A_{i+1} \iff h^{d_1+\cdots+d_k-1} \in A_i  $$  At least one of these two is true; wlog  $d_1+\cdots+d_k$  is even, then  $h^{d_1+\cdots+d_k}\in A_i \iff h^2 \in A_i \iff (gh)^{2k} \in A_i \iff i \text{ even } $ And similarly the second statement is true iff  $i$  is odd.

Call an element *representable* if it can be written in the above form, and *$r$ -representable* if it does so with at most length  $r$ . We claim that all representable elements are at most  $|G|$ -representable. For the sake of contradiction, suppose otherwise. Thus, some element
\[x=g^{m_1}h^{n_1}\dots h^{m_r},\]
is  $r$ -representable, where  $r>|G|$ , and  $r$  is minimal. By Pigeonhole, there exist two indices  $i<j\le r$  such that
\[g^{m_1}h^{n_1}\dots h^{m_i}=g^{m_1}h^{n_1}\dots h^{m_j}.\]
Thus,
\[x=g^{m_1}h^{n_1}\dots h^{m_i}g^{m_{j+1}}\dots h^{m_r}.\]
This means that  $x$  is also  $r+j-i$ -representable, which violates our minimal assumption, a contradiction.

Notice that if  $x$  is representable and  $y$  is representable, then  $xy$  is representable. Thus, it suffices to show that  $g$ ,  $g^{-1}$ ,  $h$ , and  $h^{-1}$  are representable. Notice that
\[(gh)(g^{-1}h)^{|G|-1}=gh(g^{-1}h)^{-1}=ghh^{-1}g=g^2.\]
Thus,  $g^2$  is representable. Since  $\operatorname{ord} g$  is odd, we have that
\[(g^2)^{(\operatorname{ord} g+1)/2}=g,\]
so  $g$  is representable. Then,
\[g^{\operatorname{ord} g-1}=g^{-1},\]
so  $g^{-1}$  is representable. Finally,
\[g^{-1}(gh)=h,\]
so  $h$  is representable, and likewise  $h^{-1}$ .

Consider the directed graph formed by vertices as elements of the group and  $v\in G$  is connected to  $v\to vgh, v\to vgh^{-1}, v\to vg^{-1}h, v\to vg^{-1}h^{-1}.$  It suffices to prove the graph is connected, as we can just take any walk around, and it is guaranteed to have less than or equal to  $|G|$  in size. 
Suppose that the graph was disconnected, and a connected subgraph that contained  $1$  was  $S.$  By the rules, we have  $Sgh = S = Sg^{-1}h,$  so then by right multiplication, we have  $Sg^2 = S.$  However,  $Sg^{o(g)} = S,$  but  $2\nmid o(g),$  implying that  $Sg = S.$  Furthermore,  $S=Sg(g^{-1}h) = Sh,$  so then  $S = Sg = Sh.$  This implies that  $S = G,$  as  $G$  is generated by  $g, h.$

stem_md: Find the smallest constant  $C$  such that for every real polynomial  $P(x)$  of degree  $3$  that has a root in the interval  $[0,1],$ \[\int_0^1|P(x)|\,dx\le C\max_{x\in[0,1]}|P(x)|.\]
solution_md:
Here's a proof that does not need the Simpson quadrature rule.

We can ignore the case  $P\equiv0$ . Firstly, we may assume that  $P(x)>0$  for  $x\in(0,1)$ :
*<u>Idea:</u> Split the interval  $[0,1]$  using the roots of  $P$ .*
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Suppose that  $C_0$  is the smallest constant such that if  $\deg Q\leq3$  and  $Q(x)>0$  for  $x\in(0,1)$ , we have
\[\int_0^1\!Q(x)\,dx\leq C_0\max_{x\in[0,1]}Q(x)\]
Clearly  $C_0\leq C$ .

Conversely, if  $\deg P\leq3$  and  $P$  has roots  $r_1,\ldots,r_n\in(0,1)$ , then
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1\!|P(x)|\,dx&=\int_0^{r_1}\!|P(x)|\,dx+\int_{r_1}^{r_2}\!|P(x)|\,dx+\cdots+\int_{r_n}^1\!|P(x)|\,dx
&\leq r_1C_0\max_{x\in[0,r_1]}|P(x)|+(r_2-r_1)C_0\max_{x\in[r_1,r_2]}|P(x)|+\cdots+(1-r_n)C_0\max_{x\in[r_n,1]}|P(x)|
&\leq[r_1+(r_2-r_1)+\cdots+(1-r_n)]C_0\max_{x\in[0,1]}|P(x)|
&=C_0\max_{x\in[0,1]}|P(x)|.
\end{align*}
Hence  $C\leq C_0$ , so  $C_0=C$ .</details>

We may assume that  $P(1)=0$ , and  $P(\alpha)=1=\max_{x\in[0,1]}P(x)$  for some  $\alpha\in[0,1)$ . We now claim that there exists a cubic  $P_0(x)=1-\frac{x(x-b)^2}{(1-b)^2}$ , with  $b\in[0,1]$ , such that  $P\leq P_0$  on  $[0,1]$ :
*<u>Idea:</u> Push  $1-P$  downwards until it has two roots; since it is nonnegative, it must be of the form  $kx(x-b)^2$ .*
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Consider
\[\lambda=\inf_{x\in[0,1]}\frac{1-P(x)}{(1-x)(x-\alpha)^2}\geq0,\]
and let  $P_0(x)=P(x)+\lambda(1-x)(x-\alpha)^2$ . Then we have  $P_0(1)=0$ ,  $P_0(\alpha)=1$ , and  $P\leq P_0\leq1$  on  $[0,1]$  by our choice of  $\lambda$ .


<u>Case 1:</u>  $(x-\alpha)^3$  divides  $1-P_0$ . 

Then  $1-P_0$  is a constant multiple of  $(x-\alpha)^3$ . Combined with  $1-P\geq0$  on  $[0,1]$ , this gives  $\alpha=0$  and  $P_0(x)=1-x^3$ , which is of the desired form with  $b=0$ .

<u>Case 2:</u>  $(x-\alpha)^3$  does not divide  $1-P_0$ .

Then  $\frac{1-P_0(x)}{(x-\alpha)^2}$  is nonnegative on  $[0,1]$ , continuous except at  $\alpha$ , and bounded away from 0 in a neighbourhood of  $\alpha$ . Now
\[\inf_{x\in[0,1]}\frac{1-P_0(x)}{(1-x)(x-\alpha)^2}=\lambda-\lambda=0,\]
so  $\inf_{x\in[0,1]}\frac{1-P_0(x)}{(x-\alpha)^2}=0$ . Thus  $1-P_0$  has another root in  $[0,1)$  other than  $\alpha$ .

Hence  $1-P_0$  is nonnegative on  $[0,1]$ , and has two distinct roots on  $[0,1)$ , say  $0\leq a\leq b<1$ . It is easy to see that  $b$  is a double root and  $a=0$ , so  $1-P_0(x)=kx(x-b)^2$  for some  $k>0$  and  $b\in(0,1)$ . Combined with  $P_0(1)=0$ , we have  $k=\frac1{(1-b)^2}$ , so  $P_0(x)=1-\frac{x(x-b)^2}{(1-b)^2}$ .</details>

We have now reduced the question to a one-variable inequality:
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1\!P(x)\,dx&\leq\int_0^1\!P_0(x)\,dx
&=\int_0^1\!(1-\frac{x(x-b)^2}{(1-b)^2})\,dx
&=1-\frac1{(1-b)^2}\int_0^1\!(x^3-2bx^2+b^2x)\,dx
&=1-\frac1{(1-b)^2}\left(\frac14-\frac{2b}3+\frac{b^2}2\right)
&=1-\frac{3-8b+6b^2}{12(1-b)^2}
&=\frac{6c^2+4c-1}{12c^2}\qquad(c\coloneqq1-b)
&\leq\frac{6c^2+(4c^2+1)-1}{12c^2}\qquad(\mbox{AM-GM})
&=\frac56.
\end{align*}
Equality holds when  $c=\frac12\implies b=\frac12$ , and  $P(x)=P_0(x)=1-x(2x-1)^2$ . Hence  $\boxed{C=\frac56.}$

The key to this problem: Simpson's rule. Specifically, the fact that Simpson's rule integrates every polynomial of degree at most  $3$  exactly.

If  $P(x)$  is identically zero, the inequality is trivially true for any  $C$ . Assume otherwise; there are at most finitely many roots  $0\le r_1,r_2,\cdots,r_n\le 1$  in the interval. Let  $M=\max_{x\in[0,1]}P(x)$ .

On an interval  $[r_j,r_{j+1}]$ ,  $P$  doesn't change sign, and
\begin{align*}\int_{r_j}^{r_{j+1}} |P(x)|\,dx &= \left|\int_{r_j}^{r_{j+1}} P(x)\,dx\right| = \left|\frac{r_{j+1}-r_j}{6}\left(P(r_j)+4P\left(\frac{r_j+r_{j+1}}{2}\right)+P(r_{j+1})\right)\right|
\int_{r_j}^{r_{j+1}} |P(x)|\,dx &\le \frac{r_{j+1}-r_j}{6}|0+4M+0| = \frac46M\cdot(r_{j+1}-r_j)\end{align*}
On the initial interval  $[0,r_1]$  (possibly empty, but that isn't actually a problem),  $P$  doesn't change sign, and
\begin{align*}\int_{0}^{r_{1}} |P(x)|\,dx &= \left|\int_{0}^{r_{1}} P(x)\,dx\right| = \left|\frac{r_{1}-0}{6}\left(P(0)+4P\left(\frac{0+r_1}{2}\right)+P(r_{1})\right)\right|
\int_{0}^{r_{1}} |P(x)|\,dx &\le \frac{r_1}{6}|M+4M+0| = \frac56M\cdot r_1\end{align*}
On the final interval  $[r_n,1]$  (again possibly empty),  $P$  doesn't change sign, and
\begin{align*}\int_{r_n}^{1} |P(x)|\,dx &= \left|\int_{r_n}^{1} P(x)\,dx\right| = \left|\frac{1-r_n}{6}\left(P(r_n)+4P\left(\frac{r_n+1}{2}\right)+P(1)\right)\right|
\int_{r_n}^{1} |P(x)|\,dx &\le \frac{1-r_n}{6}|0+4M+M| = \frac56M\cdot(1-r_n)\end{align*}
Sum these:
\begin{align*}\int_0^1 |P(x)|\,dx &\le \frac56M\cdot r_1 + \frac46M\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\cdot(r_{j+1}-r_j) + \frac56M\cdot(1-r_n)
&\le \frac56M\cdot r_1 +\frac46M\cdot(r_n-r_1)+\frac56M\cdot(1-r_n)
&\le \frac56M (r_1 + r_n - r_1 + 1-r_n) -\frac16 M(r_n-r_1)
\int_0^1 |P(x)|\,dx &\le\frac56M\end{align*}

So, there's a constant that works. Is it the best possible? Well, the procedure gives us a hint: if we cut down to one nonempty interval, putting the sole root at an endpoint, then we have equality if  $P$  takes its maximum at both the midpoint and the other endpoint. One such function is  $A(x)=1-x(2x-1)^2=1-x+4x^2-4x^3=(1-x)(1+4x^2)$ , which has maximum value  $1$  achieved at  $0$  and  $\frac12$ , and integral  $1-\frac12+\frac43-\frac44=\frac56$ . By example,  $\frac56$  is the best possible constant, and we're done.

Let  $x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots$  be the sequence such that  $x_0=1$  and for  $n\ge 0,$ \[x_{n+1}=\ln(e^{x_n}-x_n)\]
(as usual, the function  $\ln$  is the natural logarithm). Show that the infinite series
\[x_0+x_1+x_2+\cdots\]
converges and find its sum.
solution_md:
I used a similar approach to @edwood:

Define the partial sum   $$ s_n=\sum_{i=0}^n x_i $$  Then, by induction, we have   $$ x_{n+1} = \ln(e-s_n) $$  Therefore   $$ s_{n+1} = s_n + x_{n+1} = s_n + \ln(e-s_n) $$  Now, we have a recurrence relation for  $s_n$ . Then, we can prove that  $s_n$  is strictly increasing by showing that  $x_n>0$ . We can also prove that  $s_n$  is less than  $e-1$  by induction. This proves that the series converges: it is strictly increasing and bounded.

Now that we know that the partial sums converges, and all of the individual terms are positive, it follows that the individual terms must go to zero:   $$ \lim_{n\to\infty} x_n = 0 $$  Using our relation above,   $$ \lim_{n \to \infty} \ln(e-s_n) = 0 $$  , and then it follows that   $$ \boxed{\lim_{n \to \infty} s_n = e-1} $$

Note that from the inequality  $e^x\geq 1+x$  we obtain that  $e^x-x\geq 1$  for all real  $x$ , so in particular \[x_{n+1}=\ln(e^{x_n}-x_n) \geq \ln 1 = 0.\] Combining this with  $x_0=1$  yields that all the  $x_i$  are positive.  As a result, we have \[x_{n+1}=\ln(e^{x_n}-x_n)\leq\ln(e^{x_n}) = x_n.\] So  $\{x_i\}_{i=0}^\infty$  is a nonincreasing sequence of real numbers which is bounded below; by a well-known result from real analysis, this means that the sequence  $\{x_i\}_{i=0}^\infty$  converges.

Let  $S=\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n$ .  Note that rewriting the original condition yields  $e^{x_{n}} - e^{x_{n+1}} = x_n$ ; sending  $n$  to infinity and using the fact that  $\exp$  is continuous gives \[\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n = \lim_{n\to\infty}(e^{x_n}-e^{x_{n+1}}) = e^S - e^S = 0,\] i.e.  $S=0$ .  Finally, note that for any  $k\geq 1$ , \begin{align*}x_0+x_1+\cdots+x_k &= \left(e^{x_0}-e^{x_1}\right)+\left(e^{x_1}-e^{x_2}\right)+\cdots+\left(e^{x_k}-e^{x_{k+1}}\right)&=e^{x_0}-e^{x_{k+1}} = e - e^{x_{k+1}}.\end{align*} Now I wasn't sure if sending  $k$  to infinity here was enough to conclude that the sum is  $e-1$  by Putnam standards, so to stay safe I used an  $\varepsilon$  argument for rigor.  Specifically, let  $\varepsilon > 0$ .  Note that since  $x_n\to 0$  as  $n\to\infty$ , there exists  $K\geq 0$  such that  $n\geq K$  implies that  $x_n<\ln(\varepsilon + 1)$ .  Thus, for all  $k\geq K$  we have \begin{align*}|x_0+\cdots+x_k - (e-1)|&=|\left(e-e^{x_{k+1}}\right) - (e-1)| = |1-e^{x_{k+1}}|&=e^{x_{k+1}}-1<e^{\ln(\varepsilon + 1)}-1 = (\varepsilon + 1) - 1 = \varepsilon,\end{align*} where here the third equality comes from the fact that  $x_{k+1}\geq 0$ . We begin by noting  $x_{n+1} = \log(e^{x_n} - x_n) \ge \log 1 = 0$ , owing to  $e^t \ge 1+t$ .  So  $x_n \ge 0$  for all  $n$ .

That means that  $z_n\to 0$  extremely fast - faster than geometrically fast. (As fast as a Newton's method root finding.) And that's how fast  $x_n\to 0,$  so the sum of the  $x_n$  converges very rapidly (we could quote the ratio test).

Here's another way to show convergence: let  $y_n=e^{x_n}$ , so  $y_{n+1}=f(y_n)$ , where  $f(x)=x-\log x$ . What I just said was not just that  $x_n\to 0,$  but that it does so very rapidly, faster than geometrically fast. Thus  $\{x_n\}$  is a bounded and decreasing sequence and therefore  $\lim_{n \to \infty}x_n$  exists. Thus,  $e^a = e^a-a$ , which implies that  $a = 0$  and thus   $$ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x_k = \lim_{k \to \infty}(e-e^{x_{n+1}}) = e-1. $$</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Given  $x_0=1$  ,  $x_{n+1} = ln (e^{x_n} - x_n) $ .**Claim 1: All  $x_i $ s are positive.****Proof:**  $x_0=1>0$  . Let  $x_n >0$  .  $x_{n+1}= ln (e^{x_n} - x_n) > ln 1 = 0$  (As  $ln $  is an increasing function ). 
           Here we use the inequality  $e^x \geq x+1$  . (Short  proof : Consider the function  $f (x)= e^x -x-1$  .  $f (0)= 0$  and  $f'(x)= e^x-1>0$  for  $x>0$ . So  $f (x) >f (0)=0$  for  $x>0$ )**Claim 2: The sequences  $t_n = e^{x_n} $  and  $x_n $  is decreasing .****Proof:** Note that  $e^{x_{n+1}} = e^{x_n} - x_n $  and as  $x_n >0$  we have  $e^{x_{n+1}} < e^{x_n}$  . And as exponential  is increasing function we have  $x_{n+1} < x_n $  . 

Hence  $x_n $  is decreasing and  $0 < x_n <1$  . So  $\lim x_n =L $ (say) is finite and  $\geq 0$ .Now using continuity of exponential function ,  $\lim_{x \to L } e^x = e^L$  hence  $\lim e^{x_n}= e^L $ . Now using  $e^{x_{n+1}} = e^{x_n} - x_n$  and taking limits on both sides we get  $e^L= e^L -L $  ie  $L=0$  (we could  spilt the limit on RHS as both the limits exist). Hence  $\lim e^{x_n} = 1$ . 
So now note that partial sum is just this   $s_n = \sum_{i=0}^n x_i = e^{x_0} - e^{x_n} = e - e^{x_n} $  using  $e^{x_{n+1}} = e^{x_n} - x_n $  and hence  $s_n $  is increasing and bounded above by e (as  $e^x >0$ ). Hence it converges to a limit , that limit being the required sum of the infinite series. Hence  $\lim s_n = \lim (e - e^{x_n}) = e  - \lim e^{x_n} = e -1 $  . So the sum of the infinite series is  $e-1$  .</details>

Let $x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots$ be the sequence such that $x_0=1$ and for $n\ge 0,$ \[x_{n+1}=\ln(e^{x_n}-x_n)\] (as usual, the function $\ln$ is the natural logarithm). Show that the infinite series \[x_0+x_1+x_2+\cdots\] converges and find its sum.
Putnam 2016 B1**Answer.** The series $x_0+x_1+\dots$ converges to the limit $e-1$ . First we show that $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ converges to the limit zero. - Proceed inductively to see if $x_n \ge 0$ then $e^{x_n}-x_n \ge 1$ so $x_{n+1} \ge 0$ too. Together with $x_0>0$ we see $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is bounded below by $0$ . - Observe that $x_{n+1}=\log (e^{x_n}-x_n) \le \log e^{x_n}=x_n$ since $x_n \ge 0$ , for all $n$ , so $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is strictly decreasing. - It is now clear that $(x_n)_n$ converges to a limit $L \ge 0$ . Thus, $(e^{x_n})_n$ also converges; to the limit $e^L$ . Now, for any $\varepsilon>0$ we can find an integer $N(\varepsilon)>0$ such that for all $n>N(\varepsilon)$ we have $$ |e^{x_{n+1}}-e^{x_n}|<\varepsilon $$ so $|x_n|<\varepsilon$ leading to $L=0$ , as desired. Now we see that $s_n=\sum^n_{i=0} x_n$ is a strictly increasing sequence. We'll show that it is convergent. Observe that for $x$ in a neighbourhood of $0$ , $e^x-x=1+\mathcal{O}(x^2)$ while $\log(1+x)=\mathcal{O}(x)$ so we see for $n$ sufficiently big, $\left | \frac{x_{n+1}}{x_n} \right |=\mathcal{O}(x_n)<1$ hence proving the convergence. Finally, we evaluate this limit $\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} s_n=s$ . Note that $x_n=\log(e-s_{n-1})$ for all $n \ge 1$ (proof by induction); so we have $$ 0=\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} x_n=\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \log(e-s_{n-1})=\log(e-s) $$ hence $s=e-1$ as desired. $\blacksquare$

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Manipulating and telescoping, we see that  $e-e^{x_n}=x_0 + x_1 + \dots x_{n+1}$ . Note  $x_n$  approaches  $0$  over time due to the behavior of  $\ln(e^x-x)$ . So this is  $e-1$</details>

Suppose we have proved that  $x_i>0$  for some  $i\geq 0$  then  $e^{x_{i+1}}=e^{x_i}-i>1$  and it follows that  $x_{i+1}>0$ . Thus by induction  $x_n>0$  for all  $n$ . Now  $e^{x_{n+1}}=e^{x_n}-x_n>e^{x_n}$  and so  $x_{n+1}>x_n$ . Thus  $\{x_n\}$  is a decreasing sequence of positive numbers and so  $\lim_{n\to \infty} x_n$  exists and suppose it equals  $x$ . We have   $$ e^x=\lim_{n\to \infty}e^{x_{n+1}}=\lim_{n\to\infty}(e^{x_n}-x_n)=e^x-x $$   and so  $x=0$ . Now we get   $$ \sum_{n=1}^m x_n=\sum_{n=1}^m (e^{x_n}-e^{x_{n+1}})=e-e^{x_{m+1}}\to e-e^0=e-1 $$   as  $m\to \infty$ .

Pretty awesome problem. Notice that the given equation yields $e^{x_{n+1}} = e^{x_n} - x_n$ for every index $n$ , so summing, we have \[x_0+x_1+\cdots+x_n = e^{x_0} - e^{x_{n+1}}\] for every index $n$ .**Claim:** $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = 0$ . *Proof:* Consider the above equation instead written in the form \[e^{x_{n+1}} = e - x_0 - x_1 - \cdots - x_n.\] Because the sequence of partial sums $\{x_n\}$ is strictly increasing and bounded above by $e$ , it has a finite limit. Thus $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = 0$ . $\blacksquare$ Hence our desired sum equals \[L = \lim_{n\to \infty} e - e^{x_{n+1}} = e - 1.\]

We claim that $s_n\to e-1$ . Where $s_n$ denotes the partial sum $s_n=x_0+x_1+\cdots+x_n$ . Bruh this $\ln$ seems to annoy us so we rewrite $x_{n+1}=\ln (e^{x_n}-x_n)$ as, $e^{x_{n+1}}=e^{x_n}-x_n.$ Let us write few equations in this manner namely, \begin{align*} e^{x_{n+1}}&=e^{x_n}-x_n. e^{x_{n}}&=e^{x_{n-1}}-x_{n-1}. &\vdotswithin{=} e^{x_1}&=e^{x_0}-x_0. \end{align*} Aha! adding all of the above equation yields us, $$ \sum_{0\le i\le n}e^{x_i}-\sum_{1\le i\le n+1}e^{x_i}=e-e^{x_{n+1}}=s_n. $$ This result gives us a hint that in order to prove the convergence of $s_n$ , we might want to prove the convergence of $x_n$ first. **Claim 1.** $x_n\to 0.$ *Proof.* Begin by noticing that $(x_n)_{n\ge 0}$ is bounded below by $0$ as the function $\ln(e^x-x)$ can take the least value of $0$ over $\mathbb{R}$ . Also one might see that $\Delta x_n<0$ hence by **Monotone Convergence Theorem** we say $(x_n)_{n\ge 0}$ converges to a point a say $\ell$ . Computing the value of $\ell$ is easy as we have previously seen that $e^{x_{n+1}}=e^{x_n}-x_n$ meaning $e^{\ell}=e^{\ell}-\ell$ which forces $x_n\to 0$ . Recall that $e-e^{x_{n+1}}=s_n$ , which implies $s_n\to e-1$ . $\square$

<details><summary>Storage</summary>$\textbf{Claim :}$   $x_{n+1} = \ln (e-1-x_1-x_2 - \cdot \dots \cdot -  x_n)$ .   $\textit{Proof.}$  We proceed using induction.  The base case is trivial and is left for brevity.  Assume that it works for  $n$ , we will show that it works for  $n+1$ .  $x_{n+1} = \ln (e^{x_n} - x_n) = \ln( e^{\ln (e-1-x_1-x_2 - \cdot \dots \cdot - x_{n-1})} - x_n) = \ln (e - 1 - x_1 - x_2 - \cdot \dots \cdot - x_n)$ .    $\textbf{Claim :}$   $x_{n} \geq 0$  for all  $n \in \mathbb{N}$ .   $\textit{Proof.}$   $x_{n+1} = \ln (e^{x_n} - x_n)$ . We claim that  $e^{x} - x\geq 1$  and we are done! Note that  $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x} \left( e^x - x \right) = e^{x} - 1 \geq 0 \; \forall \; x \geq 0$ . So the minimum value of  $e^{x} - x$  is  $1$  for positive reals. Now we can finish this with induction. If  $x_{n}$  is positive then so is  $x_{n+1}$  and we already know that  $x_0 = 1$ .   $\textbf{Claim :}$   $\{ x_n \}_{n \geq 1}$  is a decreasing sequence.   $\textit{Proof.}$  We proceed using induction.  The base case is trivial and is left for brevity.  Assume that it works for  $n$ , we will show that it works for  $n+1$ .  $x_{n+1} = \ln(e-1-x_1-x_2 - \cdot \dots \cdot -  x_n) < \ln(e-1-x_1-x_2 - \cdot \dots \cdot -  x_{n-1}) = x_n$  since  $x_n \geq 0$ .   So  $\{ x_n \}_{n \geq 1}$  is a decreasing sequence bounded below by  $0$ , so it must be convergent.   $L \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} \ln \left( e^{x_n} - x_n \right) = \ln \left( e^L - L \right)$ . So  $e^L = e^L - L$ , or,  $L = 0$ .  So,  $0 = \lim_{n \to \infty} x_{n+1} = \ln \left( e - \left( \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=0}^{n} x_i \right) \right)$ . So,  $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=0}^{n} x_i = e-1$ .</details>

stem_md:
Define a positive integer  $n$  to be *squarish* if either  $n$  is itself a perfect square or the distance from  $n$  to the nearest perfect square is a perfect square. For example,  $2016$  is squarish, because the nearest perfect square to  $2016$  is  $45^2=2025$  and  $2025-2016=9$  is a perfect square. (Of the positive integers between  $1$  and  $10,$  only  $6$  and  $7$  are not squarish.)

For a positive integer  $N,$  let  $S(N)$  be the number of squarish integers between  $1$  and  $N,$  inclusive. Find positive constants  $\alpha$  and  $\beta$  such that
\[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{S(N)}{N^{\alpha}}=\beta,\]
or show that no such constants exist.
solution_md:
<details><summary>B2 solution</summary>Note that  $\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\frac{S(n)}{n^{\alpha}} = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\frac{S(n^4)}{n^{4\alpha}}$ . This simplifies things considerably.

Now note that between  $n^2 + 1$  and  $(n+1)^2$ , inclusive, there are precisely  $2\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + 1$  squarish numbers:  $(n+1)^2$  itself, and each of the pairs  $(n^2 + k^2, (n+1)^2 - k^2)$  where  $k \geq 1$  and  $n^2 + k^2 < (n+1)^2 - k^2 \iff k^2 < n + \frac{1}{2} \implies k^2 \leq n \implies k \leq \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor$ . This shows the above result. Thus

\[S(n^4) = \sum_{i = 0}^{n^2-1}2\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + 1\]

But for any  $k$ ,  $\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor = k \iff n^2 \leq k < (n+1)^2$ , so there are precisely  $2k+1$   $n$  that give  $k$ . It follows that

\[S(n^4) = \sum_{i = 1}^{n}(2i-1)^2\]

Furthermore 

\[1^2 + 3^2 + \ldots + (2n-1)^2 = (1^2 + 2^2 + \ldots + (2n)^2) - 4(1^2 + 2^2 + \ldots + n^2) = \frac{4n^3-n}{3}\]

From which it follows that  $\boxed{\alpha = \frac{3}{4}, \beta = \frac{4}{3}}$ .</details>

It is easy to find exact forms for  $S(a^4)$ , which ends up being  $4/3 a^3 + O(a^2)$ . Then notice for  $a^4 \leq N \leq (a+1)^4$  we have  $$ \frac{S(a^4)}{(a+1)^3} \leq \frac{S(N)}{N^{3/4}} \leq \frac{S((a+1)^4)}{a^3} $$  So by comparing lead coefficients of the left and right, they both approach  $4/3$ . Result follows by squeezing.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>We first calculate  $S(k^2)$  for a positive integer  $k$ . We can partition any interval  $[n^2,(n+1)^2)$  as  $[n^2,n^2+n)$  and  $[n^2+n+1,(n+1)^2)$ . The squarish numbers are in a one-to-one correspondence with the numbers  $n^2+0,n^2+1,\ldots,n^2+r^2$ . In the first interval we have  $n^2+r^2 \leq n^2+n$  and so  $n \geq r^2$ , or  $r \leq \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor$ . Thus there are  $\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor+1$  such numbers here. Similarly for the interval  $[n^2+n,(n+1)^2)$  the squarish numbers are in a one-to-one correspondence with the numbers  $(n+1)^2-1^2,(n+1)^2-2^2,\ldots,(n+1)^2-r^2 \geq n^2+n+1$ . We again get  $r \leq \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor$ , but since we don't count  $(n+1)^2$ , there are  $\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor$  total squarish numbers here. Thus, in any interval  $[n^2,(n+1)^2)$  there are  $2 \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor+1$  squarish numbers. Now observe that   $$ S(k^2) \leq S(N) \leq S((k+1)^2). $$   We have \begin{align*}S(k^2) &= (2\lfloor \sqrt{1} \rfloor+1)+(2\lfloor \sqrt{2} \rfloor+1)+\cdots+(2\lfloor \sqrt{k-1} \rfloor+1)+1& = 2(\lfloor \sqrt{1} \rfloor+\lfloor \sqrt{2}\rfloor+\cdots+\lfloor \sqrt{k-1}\rfloor)+k.\end{align*} Now we may make the floor functions disappear by using the following inequality:   $$ 2(\sqrt{1} +\sqrt{2}+\cdots+\sqrt{k-1})+k-2(k-1) \leq S(k^2) \leq 2(\sqrt{1} +\sqrt{2}+\cdots+\sqrt{k-1})+k. $$   Now, we would like to relate this to the Riemann sum for  $\sqrt{x}$  on  $[0,1]$  and so we divide by  $k\sqrt{k}$  to get   $$ \dfrac{2(\sqrt{1} +\sqrt{2}+\cdots+\sqrt{k-1})+k-2(k-1)}{k\sqrt{k}} \leq \dfrac{S(k)}{k\sqrt{k}} \leq \dfrac{2(\sqrt{1} +\sqrt{2}+\cdots+\sqrt{k-1})+k}{k\sqrt{k}} $$   and since  $\int_{0}^1 \sqrt{x} dx = \dfrac{2}{3}$ , we find after taking the limit as  $k \to \infty$  and applying the Squeeze Theorem that   $$ \lim_{k \to \infty}\left(\dfrac{S(k^2)}{(k^2)^{\frac{3}{4}}}\right) = \dfrac{4}{3} \implies \lim_{N \to \infty}\left(\dfrac{S(N)}{N^{\frac{3}{4}}}\right) = \dfrac{4}{3}. $$</details>

**Answer.**  $\alpha=\tfrac{3}{4}, \beta=\tfrac{4}{3}$ .

For each  $n \ge 1$  define  $T(n)$  as   $$ T(n) \overset{\text{def}}{:=} \left | \{n^2+x^2 \mid 0 \le x \le \sqrt{n}\} \cup \{n^2+n+x \mid 1 \le x<\sqrt{n}\} \right| $$   then  $T(n)=2\sqrt{n}+\mathcal{O}(1)$ . In fact, it is clear that   $$ S(N)=\sum^{k}_{m=1} T(m) $$   with  $k$  the largest integer satisfying  $(k+1)^2 \le N$ . Consequently, we have   $$ S(N)=2\left(1+\sqrt{2}+\dots+\sqrt{N}\right)+\mathcal{O}(N). $$   However, it is clear that  $\int^k_{0} \sqrt{x} \, dx \sim \sqrt{1}+\dots+\sqrt{N}$  because of Riemann sums. Clearly, we obtain   $$ S(N)=\frac{4}{3}N^{\frac{3}{4}}+\mathcal{O}(N). $$   Now it is clear what  $\alpha, \beta$  must be, which is what we just claimed.

Partition  $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$  into intervals of the form  $[n^2-n+1, n^2+n]$  for  $n \geq 1$ . There are  $\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + \lfloor \sqrt{n-1} \rfloor +1$  squarish integers in any of these intervals.
For any  $N=n^2+n$ , we thus have  $S(N)=n+ \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + 2 \left( \lfloor \sqrt{1} \rfloor + \lfloor \sqrt{2} \rfloor + \cdots + \lfloor \sqrt{n-1} \rfloor \right)$ .
We have  $S(N) = n+ \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + 2 \left( \lfloor \sqrt{1} \rfloor + \lfloor \sqrt{2} \rfloor + \cdots + \lfloor \sqrt{n-1} \rfloor \right) \leq n+ \sqrt{n}+ 2 \left( \sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2} + \cdots + \sqrt{n-1} \right)$  $\leq n+\sqrt{n} + 2 \int_1^n \sqrt{x} dx = n+\sqrt{n} + \frac{4}{3} (n^\frac{3}{2}-1) \leq \frac{4}{3} n^\frac{3}{2} + n+\sqrt{n}$ , 
and  $S(N) = n+ \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor + 2 \left( \lfloor \sqrt{1} \rfloor + \lfloor \sqrt{2} \rfloor + \cdots + \lfloor \sqrt{n-1} \rfloor \right) \geq n- \sqrt{n}+ 2 \left( \sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2} + \cdots + \sqrt{n-1} + \sqrt{n} \right) - (2n-1)$  $ \geq -n-\sqrt{n}+1 +2 \int_0^n \sqrt{x} dx \geq \frac{4}{3}n^{\frac{3}{2}}-n-\sqrt{n}$ .

Now for  $N$  not of the form  $n^2+n$ , assume  $n^2+n < N < (n+1)^2+n+1$ . Then   $$ \frac{\frac{4}{3}n^{\frac{3}{2}}-n-\sqrt{n}}{(n+2)^\frac{3}{2}} \leq \frac{S(n^2+n)}{(n+2)^\frac{3}{2}} < \frac{S(N)}{N^\frac{3}{4}} < \frac{S((n+1)^2+n+1)}{n^\frac{3}{2}} \leq \frac{\frac{4}{3}(n+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}+n+1+\sqrt{n+1}}{n^\frac{3}{2}} $$  but the limit to infinity of the left and right hand sides are both  $\frac{4}{3}$ , so we have that  $\alpha = \frac{3}{4}, \beta = \frac{4}{3}$  satisfy the condition.  $\square$

Here's a quick outline. Clearly  $S(N)$  is nondecreasing. In particular, we evaluate 
\[S\left(n^2+2n\right) = n+2\sum_{k=1}^n \left \lfloor \sqrt k \right \rfloor \approx n + 2\int_1^n \sqrt x\ \mathrm dx = \frac 43 n^{3/2} + \mathcal O(n).\] Thus, for each positive integer  $x$  and  $k = \lfloor \sqrt x \rfloor$ , we have  $S\left(k^2+2k\right) \leq S(x) \leq S\left((k+1)^2+2k+1\right)$  which approximates  $S(x)$  within  $\mathcal O(k) = \mathcal O\left(\sqrt x \right)$ . So  $S(n) \approx \frac 43 n^{3/4}$  works.

stem_md: Suppose that  $S$  is a finite set of points in the plane such that the area of triangle  $\triangle ABC$  is at most  $1$  whenever  $A,B,$  and  $C$  are in  $S.$  Show that there exists a triangle of area  $4$  that (together with its interior) covers the set  $S.$
solution_md:
Let  $\triangle{ABC}$  be the triangle with the greatest area out of all of the triangles formed by the points. Let  $\ell_C$  be the line through  $C$  parallel to line  $AB,$  let  $\ell_B$  be the line through  $B$  parallel to line  $AC,$  and let  $\ell_A$  be the line through  $A$  parallel to line  $BC.$  Also, let  $A'$  be the intersection of  $\ell_B$  and  $\ell_C$  and define  $B'$  and  $C'$  similarly. 

If some point  $D$  lies outside of  $\triangle{A'B'C'},$  then it must lie outside at least two of the angles  $\angle{A'B'C'}, \angle{B'C'A'},$  or  $\angle{C'A'B'},$  say  $\angle{A'B'C'}$  and  $\angle{B'C'A'}.$  However, this implies that the altitude from  $D$  to  $\overline{BC}$  has greater length than the altitude from  $A$  to  $\overline{BC},$  implying that   $$ [DBC]>[ABC], $$   contradiction. 

Hence, all points in the collection must be on the boundary or in the interior of  $\triangle{A'B'C}.$  Now, by the given information in the problem,  $[ABC] \le 1,$  so by congruent triangles,  $[A'B'C] \le 4,$  concluding the proof.  $\square$

Choose a triangle  $ABC$  with vertices in  $S$  whose area is the maximum area. (There is such a thing since there are finitely many triangles.) Draw line  $L_1$  through  $A$  parallel to  $\overline{BC}.$   Then if  $D$  is any other point in  $S,$   $D$  cannot be on the opposite side of  $L_1$  from  $B$  and  $C.$  If it were, then  $\triangle DBC$  would have the same base and a greater altitude than  $\triangle ABC$  and hence a greater area; that is not permitted by the maximality of  $\triangle ABC.$  Repeat by drawing line  $L_2$  through  $B$  parallel to  $\overline{AC}$  and line  $L_3$  through  $C$  parallel to  $\overline{AB}.$  In each case, any point  $D\in S$  must lie on the side of that line towards the original triangle. The three lines we drew intersect to form  $\triangle XYZ$  which must contain all of  $S.$   $\triangle XYZ$  is similar to  $\triangle ABC$  and can be decomposed into four congruent copies of  $\triangle ABC.$  Hence  $\mathrm{area}(\triangle XYZ)=4\cdot \mathrm{area}(\triangle ABC)\le 4$  and we are done.

stem_md: Let  $A$  be a  $2n\times 2n$  matrix, with entries chosen independently at random. Every entry is chosen to be  $0$  or  $1,$  each with probability  $1/2.$  Find the expected value of  $\det(A-A^t)$  (as a function of  $n$ ), where  $A^t$  is the transpose of  $A.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>B4 solution</summary>Let  $X = M - M^T$ , so that

\[X = \begin{pmatrix}0 & x_{0,1} & x_{0,2} & \ldots  x_{1,0} & 0 & x_{1,2} & \ldots  x_{2,0} & x_{2,1} & 0 & \ldots  \hdots & \hdots & \hdots & \ddots\end{pmatrix}\]

where  $x_{i,j} = -x_{j,i}$ . Let  $S_{2n}$  denote the symmetric group of  $2n$  elements. Then

\[\text{det} X = \sum_{P \in S_{2n}}(-1)^{\text{inv}(P)}\prod_{i=0}^{2n-1}x_{i,P(i)}\]

and thus by Linearity of Expectation

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{det} X] = \sum_{P \in S_{2n}}(-1)^{\text{inv}(P)}\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=0}^{2n-1}x_{i,P(i)}\right]\]

But  $x_{i,j}$  is independent to all other elements except  $x_{j,i}$ . It follows that  $\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=0}^{2n-1}x_{i,P(i)}\right] = 0$  unless the product is of the form  $\prod_i x_{i,P(i)}x_{P(i),i}$ . In particular,

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{det} X] = \sum_{\substack{P \in S_{2n}  P(P(x)) = x  P(x) \neq x}}\sum_{P \in S_{2n}}(-1)^{\text{inv}(P)}\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i}x_{i,P(i)}x_{P(i),i}\right]\]

But 

\[\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i}x_{i,P(i)}x_{P(i),i}\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i}-x_{i,P(i)}^2\right] = \left(-frac{1}{2}\right)^n\]

and  $\text{inv}(P) \equiv n \pmod 2 \implies (-1)^{\text{inv}(P)} = (-1)^n$ . It follows that 

\[(-1)^{\text{inv}(P)}\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i}x_{i,P(i)}x_{P(i),i}\right] = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\]

and thus

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{det} X] = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\#(P \in S_{2n} | P(P(x)) = x, P(x) \neq x)\]

Let  $f(n)$  denote the above cardinality. Then  $P(1) = 2, \ldots, 2n$ , and by symmetry there are an equal number of permutations in each group. Thus  $f(n) = (2n - 1)f(n - 1)$ , and further  $f(1) = 1$ . It follows that  $f(n) = (2n-1)!!$ , and finally

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{det}(X)] = \boxed{\frac{(2n-1)!!}{2^n}}\]</details>

I don't want to repeat all the ideas from my contest-day writeup (plus I dont think my solution is worded well enough to get more than a point) so here's the basic idea. Note that $B = A - A^t$ is skew-symmetric (i.e. $B^t = -B$ ) so (writing $B = \{b_{i,j}\}_{i,j=1}^{2n}$ ) we have $b_{ii} = 0$ and $b_{ij} = -b_{ji}$ for all appropriate $i$ and $j$ . Now recall the permutation definition of determinant, i.e. \[\det B = \sum_{\sigma\in S_{2n}}\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^{2n}b_{i\sigma(i)}.\] By linearity of expectation, \[\mathbb E[\det B] = \mathbb E\left[\sum_{\sigma\in S_{2n}}\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^{2n}b_{i\sigma(i)}\right] = \sum_{\sigma\in S_{2n}}\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i=1}^{2n}b_{i\sigma(i)}\right].\] Suppose $\sigma$ does not consist of only two-cycles, i.e. $\sigma(i)=j$ but $\sigma(j)\neq i$ for some $i\in[2n]$ . Then toggling the values of $a_{i\sigma(i)}$ and $a_{\sigma(i)i}$ essentially negates the product (i.e. it changes the value of $b_{i\sigma(i)}$ but not of any other term), and so the expected value of the product is zero for that $\sigma$ . So the only terms we care about are those of the form \[(-1)^n(-c_1^2)(-c_2^2)\cdots (-c_n^2) = c_1^2c_2^2\cdots c_n^2,\] where $c_i\in\{-1,0,1\}$ . (Remember, $b_{ij} = -b_{ji}$ for all $i$ and $j$ .) Now each of the $c_i$ behave independently, so it suffices to compute the expected value of $c_1^2$ and then raise this to the $n$ th power. This can be shown to be $\tfrac12$ by a simple calculation, so the expected contribution of this term to the overall sum is $(\tfrac12)^n$ . There are \[\dfrac{1}{n!}\binom{2n}2\binom{2n-2}2\cdots\binom{2}2 = \dfrac{(2n)!}{2^nn!}\] elements of $S_{2n}$ consisting of $n$ 2-cycles, and so scaling upward gives the requested answer as $\tfrac{(2n)!}{4^nn!}$ . Now the key claim is that if  $\sigma(i) = j$  but  $\sigma(j) \neq i$ , then the term  $x_{ij}$  appears exactly once in the product but  $x_{ji}$  does not appear at all. Therefore, we only need to consider  $\sigma$  of the form \[ \sigma = (a_1 \; b_1)(a_2 \; b_2) \dots (a_n \; b_n) \] i.e.\ the  $\sigma$  which consist entirely of two-cycles.  WLOG  $a_k < b_k$ . Let  $a_{ij}$ ,  $1 \le i, j \le n$ , denote the entries of  $A$ . By the expansion of determinant and linearity of expectation
\[\mathbb{E}[\det(A - A^{t})] = \sum_{\sigma} (-1)^{\text{sgn}(\sigma)} \mathbb{E}[(a_{1\sigma(1)} - a_{\sigma(1)1}) \cdots (a_{n\sigma(n)} - a_{\sigma(n)n})].\]
Note that if  $i \neq j$ ,  $x_{ij} = a_{ij} - a_{ji}$  follows the probability distribution of  $X$  where
\[P(X = x) = \begin{cases*} \tfrac{1}{4} & if  $x = 1$  \tfrac{1}{2} & if  $x = 0$  \tfrac{1}{4} & if  $x = -1$ \end{cases*}\]
and moreover the variables  $x_{ij}$  ( $1 \le i < j \le n$ ) are independent. (Of course  $x_{ii} = 0$  with probability 1.) A key observation is that  $\mathbb{E}[x_{ij}] = 0$  for  $i \neq j$ .

For each permutation  $\sigma$  we shall find
\[(-1)^{\text{sgn}(\sigma)} \mathbb{E}[(a_{1\sigma(1)} - a_{\sigma(1)1}) \cdots (a_{n\sigma(n)} - a_{\sigma(n)n})] = (-1)^{\text{sgn}(\sigma)} \mathbb{E}[x_{1 \sigma(1)} \cdots x_{n \sigma(n)}].\]
If  $\sigma$  has a fixed point  $i$  then the product is always zero, so henceforth assume  $\sigma$  is fixed-point-free. If some  $x_{ij}$  appears to the first power in the product, then the expected value is zero.

Thus, we may focus on the  $\sigma$  for which each  $x_{ij}$  appearing in the product appears at least twice. So,  $x_{i \sigma(i)}$  appears, then  $x_{\sigma(i) i}$  must appear as well.

This means  $\sigma$  must be a product of  $n$  disjoint 2-cycles  $(i_k \; j_k)$  for  $1 \le k \le n$ . Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
& & (-1)^{\text{sgn}(\sigma)} \mathbb{E}[(a_{1\sigma(1)} - a_{\sigma(1)1}) \cdots (a_{n\sigma(n)} - a_{\sigma(n)n})]
& = & (-1)^n \mathbb{E}[x_{i_1 j_1} \cdots x_{i_k j_k} x_{j_1 i_1} \cdots x_{j_k i_k}]
& = & (-1)^n \mathbb{E}[x_{i_1 j_1} x_{j_1 i_1}]^n
& = & (-1)^n \mathbb{E}[-x_{i_1 j_1}^2]^n
& = & (-1)^n (-\tfrac{1}{2})^n
& = & \tfrac{1}{2^n}.
\end{eqnarray*}
It is easy to observe that there are  $(2n - 1) (2n - 3) \cdots (1) = (2n - 1)!!$  such permutations  $\sigma$ . So the final answer, by linearity of expectation, is  $\tfrac{(2n - 1)!!}{2^n}$ .

Replace  $2n$  with  $n$ . 
Let  $B=A-A^t$ . Then  $B$  is a skew-symmetric matrix, so  $b_{ij} = -b_{ji}$  for  $i\not = j$ , and  $b_{ii}=0$  for all  $i$ . Now for all  $i<j$ , we have
\[ b_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 &\qquad  p=1/4  0&\qquad p=1/2  -1 &\qquad p=1/4,\end{cases}\]
and then  $b_{ji}=-b_{ij}$ . 
Note that the entire set  $\{b_{ij}\}_{i<j}$  are pairwise independent. This will be very important. 

We have by linearity that
\[ \mathbb{E}[\det B] = \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \mathbb{E}[\text{sgn}(\pi) \cdot b_{1,\pi(1)}b_{2,\pi(2)}\cdots b_{n,\pi(n)}]. \]
We will analyze the above expression for some fixed  $\pi$ . Firstly, if any of  $b_{i,\pi(i)}$  is 0, then the entire product is 0. 

Let  $k$  be the number of pairs  $(i,\pi(i))$  where  $(\pi(i),i)$  is also in the product. Pair these up, and if  $k<n/2$ , then there will be some terms  $\prod_{i\in S} b_{i,\pi(i)}$  for some set  $S$  that are left over. But then the  $(i,\pi(i))$ 's in  $S$  are independent of everything else, so their expectation is 0, since independent variables are multiplicative in expectation and  $\mathbb{E}[b_{i,\pi(i)}]=\tfrac14(1) + \tfrac14(-1)=0$  for  $i\in S$ . So all  $\pi$  with  $k<n/2$  make the product have 0 expectation.

Now consider the  $\pi$  with  $k=n/2$ . That means all  $n$  terms pair up into 2-cycles. Call these  $\pi$  \textit{friendly}. Each one products to  $b_{i,\pi(i)}b_{\pi(i),i} = -1$ . So the value of the product is  $(-1)^{n/2}$ . And  $\text{sign}(\pi) = (-1)^{n/2}$  since there are  $n/2$  2-cycles. So the overall summand is  $(-1)^n=1$ . 

So we have
\[ \mathbb{E}[\text{sgn}(\pi) b_{1,\pi(1)}\cdots b_{n,\pi(n)}] = \begin{cases} 0 &\quad \text{if  $\pi$  is not friendly, or any of  $b_{i,\pi(i)}$  is 0} 
1 &\quad \text{if  $\pi$  is friendly, and all of  $b_{i,\pi(i)}$  are nonzero.}\end{cases}\]
Conditioned on  $\pi$  being friendly, the probability that  $b_{i,\pi(i)}$  are all nonzero is  $(1/2)^{n/2}$ , since the 2 values in each pair are not independent. So
\[ \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \mathbb{E}[\text{sgn}(\pi) \cdot b_{1,\pi(1)}b_{2,\pi(2)}\cdots b_{n,\pi(n)}] = \sum_{\text{friendly  $\pi$ }} \frac{1}{2^{n/2}}= \frac{1}{2^{n/2}} \cdot (\text{\# friendly  $\pi$ }).\]
The number of friendly  $\pi$  is  $(n-1)!!$  since the smallest non-picked number has  $n-1$  choices to pair with, then the next smallest non-picked number has  $n-3$  choices to pair with, and so on, till the last non-picked number has 1 choice. (This map is clearly a bijection.) So the answer is 
\[ \frac{(n-1)!!}{2^{n/2}}.\]

stem_md: Find all functions  $f$  from the interval  $(1,\infty)$  to  $(1,\infty)$  with the following property: if  $x,y\in(1,\infty)$  and  $x^2\le y\le x^3,$  then  $(f(x))^2\le f(y) \le (f(x))^3.$
solution_md:
Let $g(x)=\log f(e^x)$ ; so we are solving this problem.
Find all functions $g \colon \mathbb R^+ \to \mathbb R^+$ such that \[\frac yx \in [2,3] \implies \frac {g(y)}{g(x)} \in [2,3]\]
See that $g(2x) \ge 2g(x)$ and $g(3x) \le 3 g(x)$ . **Claim:** We have $g(2x)=2g(x)$ . **Proof:** Assume for some $\varepsilon>0$ we have $g(2a)=(2+\varepsilon)g(a)$ for some $a$ . \[(2+\varepsilon) 2^{n-1} \le \frac{g(2^na)}{g(a)} \le 3^{\lfloor{\log_3(2^n) \rfloor}+1}=2^n \cdot 3^{1-\{n \log_3 2 \}} \implies 1+\frac{\varepsilon}2 \le 3^{1-\{n \log_3 2 \}}\] By Kronecker's theorem, we have $\{n \log_3 2 \}$ is dense in $(0,1)$ so RHS can as close to $1$ as we want to get that contradiction. $\square$ **Claim:** We have $g(3x)=3g(x)$ . **Proof:** Similar proof as before. $\square$ **Claim:** $g$ is strictly increasing. **Proof:** Say $g(a) \ge g(b)$ but $a0$ can be as small as possible (again Kronecker's theorem) so \[1 \le \frac{g(b)}{g(a)} \left(\frac ab + \frac{\varepsilon}2 \right)\] which can't be true as $\varepsilon \to 0$ . $\square$ Now by scaling assume $g(1)=1$ so $g(2^n3^m)=2^n3^m$ for any $n$ , $m \in \mathbb Z$ . Again it is dense in $\mathbb R^+$ (by Kronecker's theorem). Now as $g$ is increasing and by simple bounding, we get $g(x)=x$ is forced (which works). So all in all the only solutions are $\boxed{f(x)=x^{\alpha}} \text{ where } \alpha \in \mathbb R^+$

Since  $2x_1 - 1$  is always odd,  $f(x_1, x_2)$  contains exactly  $x_2 - 1$  powers of  $2$  in its prime factorization, hence,  $f(x_1, x_2)$  is a binary number with  $x_2 - 1$  trailing zeroes. Since every positive integer can be uniquely expressed in binary, in particular, every positive integer with  $x_2 - 1$  powers of  $2$  in its prime factorization can be uniquely expressed in the form  $(2x_1 - 1) \cdot 2^{x_2 - 1},$  since  $2x_1 - 1$  can obviously take on any arbitrary odd value. Let  $E_k$  be the set of positive integers with  $k$  powers of  $2$  in its prime factorization. Since the family of sets  $\{ E_k \}_{k \geq 0}$  is disjoint (as a given positive integer obviously can't have both  $a$  and  $b$  powers of  $2$  in its prime factorization where  $a \neq b$ ) and covers the entirety of  $\mathbb{N}$  (as every positive integer has a finite number of powers of  $2$  in its prime factorization), it follows that  $f$  is bijective.  

Observe that from the lemma and the fact that  $S$  is absolutely convergent (which can be derived from a bounding argument using the fact that  $|S_k| = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k2^n + 1} < \frac{1}{k} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k2^n} = \frac{2}{k^2}$  for each  $k$  hence  $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} |S_k| < 2 \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^2},$  the RHS which is known to converge to  $\frac{\pi^2}{3},$  hence the LHS is convergent) we can express  $S$  in the alternate equivalent form  $S = \sum_{b=1}^{\infty} T_{2b-1}.$  
We have $T_{2b - 1} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} S_{(2b-1) \cdot 2^k} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{(2b-1) \cdot 2^k -1}}{(2b-1) \cdot 2^k} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(2b-1) \cdot 2^k \cdot 2^n + 1}.$  
Since the exponent  $(2b-1) \cdot 2^k - 1$  is even only for  $k = 0$  and odd for all  $k > 0,$  we can rewrite this as $T_{2b - 1} = \frac{1}{2b-1} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(2b-1)2^n + 1} - \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2b-1} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(2b-1) \cdot 2^k \cdot 2^n + 1}.$ Rearranging the terms of the above summation using the distributive property, we obtain $T_{2b - 1} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left ( \frac{1}{2b-1} - \sum_{n=1}^{k} \frac{1}{(2b-1) 2^k} \right ) \frac{1}{(2b-1)2^k + 1}.$  
Note that by the finite geometric series formula,  $\sum_{n=1}^{k} \frac{1}{(2b-1) 2^k} = \frac{1}{2b-1} - \frac{1}{(2b-1) 2^k}$ . Hence, for each  $k$  the coefficient  $\frac{1}{2b-1} - \sum_{n=1}^{k} \frac{1}{(2b-1) 2^k}$  equals  $\frac{1}{(2b-1) 2^k}$  and we can simplify the whole expression for  $T_{2b - 1}$  to  $T_{2b - 1} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(2b-1) 2^k} \cdot \frac{1}{(2b-1)2^k + 1}.$ Since we established from the Lemma that  $S = \sum_{b=1}^{\infty} T_{2b-1},$  we can rewrite  $S$  as  $S = \sum_{k= 1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k} \cdot \frac{1}{k+1},$  which is a well-known telescoping sum that converges to  $S = \boxed{1}.$</details>

stem_md: Determine all functions  $f: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$  which satisfy the inequality  $$ f(a^2) - f(b^2) \leq \left( f(a) + b\right)\left( a - f(b)\right), $$  for all  $a,b \in \mathbb R$ .
solution_md:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ which satisfy the inequality $$ f(a^2) - f(b^2) \leq \left( f(a) + b\right)\left( a - f(b)\right), $$ for all $a,b \in \mathbb R$ .
Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion $f(x^2)-f(y^2)\le (f(x)+y)(x-f(y))$ $P(y,x)$ $\implies$ $f(x^2)-f(y^2)\ge -(f(y)+x)(y-f(x))$ And so $-(f(y)+x)(y-f(x))\le (f(x)+y)(x-f(y))$ Which is new assertion $Q(x,y)$ : $f(x)f(y)\le xy$ $Q(1,-1)$ $\implies$ $f(1)f(-1)\le -1<0$ and so one of $f(1)$ or $f(-1)$ is $>0$ and the other is $<0$ Adding $Q(1,x)$ and $Q(1,-x)$ , we get $f(1)(f(x)+f(-x))\le 0$ Adding $Q(-1,x)$ and $Q(-1,-x)$ , we get $f(-1)(f(x)+f(-x))\le 0$ And so (see three lines above) $f(-x)=-f(x)$ $Q(x,-y)$ $\implies$ $f(x)f(y)\ge xy$ And so $f(x)f(y)=xy$ and so (setting there $y=1$ and since $f(1)\ne 0$ ) : $f(x)=ax$ for some real $a$ Plugging this back in originel equation, we get $a^2=1$ and so two solutions : $\boxed{\text{S1 : }f(x)=x\quad\forall x}$ $\boxed{\text{S2 : }f(x)=-x\quad\forall x}$

Let  $P(a,b)$  be the given assertion. $P(0,0)\Rightarrow f(0)^2\le0\Rightarrow f(0)=0$  $P(x,0)\Rightarrow f(x^2)\le xf(x)$  $P(0,x)\Rightarrow-f(x^2)\le-xf(x)\Rightarrow f(x^2)\ge xf(x)$ So  $f(x^2)=xf(x)$ , hence  $f$  is odd. Now  $P(x,y)$  gives the new assertion  $Q(x,y):f(x)f(y)\le xy$ . $Q(x,-y)\Rightarrow-f(x)f(y)\le-xy\Rightarrow f(x)f(y)\ge xy$ So equality holds in  $Q(x,y)$ , so  $f(x)=\frac1{f(1)}x$  after setting  $y=1$ . Then  $x=1$  yields the solutions  $\boxed{f(x)=x}$  and  $\boxed{f(x)=-x}$ , which both work.

stem_md: Let be a natural number  $ n\ge 2 $  and  $ n $  positive real numbers  $ a_1,a_n,\ldots ,a_n $  that satisfy the inequalities   $$  \sum_{j=1}^i a_j\le a_{i+1} ,\quad \forall i\in\{ 1,2,\ldots ,n-1 \} .  $$  Prove that  $$  \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \frac{a_k}{a_{k+1}}\le n/2 .  $$
solution_md:
This is an old question.
Let  $x_{1}=a_{1},x_{i}=a_{i+1}-\sum_{j=1}^{i} a_{j}(2\leq i\leq n)$  , then  $x_{i}\geq 0$  ,  $x_{i+1}-x_{i}=a_{i+1}-2a_{i}.$ So we have  $2\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{a_{i}}{a_{i+1}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(1-\frac{x_{i+1}-x_{i}}{a_{i+1}})=n-1-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{x_{i+1}-x_{i}}{a_{i+1}}=n-\frac{x_{1}}{a_{1}}-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{x_{i+1}-x_{i}}{a_{i+1}}=n-\frac{x_{n}}{a_{n}}-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}x_{i}(\frac{1}{a_{i}}-\frac{1}{a_{i+1}})\leq n.$ The last step is because  $a_{i}\leq a_{i+1}$  , which is obvious.

stem_md: We say that a rational number is *spheric* if it is the sum of three squares of rational numbers (not necessarily distinct). Prove that:**a)**  $ 7 $  is not spheric.**b)** a rational spheric number raised to the power of any natural number greater than  $ 1 $  is spheric.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Sa</summary>Suppose there exists rational numbers  $x,y,z$  such that  $$ 7=x^2+y^2+z^2 $$  Let  $k$  be the smallest positive integer such that  $kx,ky,kz$  are all integers. Let  $a=kx$ ,  $b=ky$  and  $c=kz$ . Since  $k$  is minimal, this means  $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ .

We have:  $$ 7k^2=a^2+b^2+c^2 $$  All perfect squares are either  $0,1,4$  modulo  $8$ .

stem_md:
In order to study a certain ancient language, some researchers formatted its discovered words into expressions formed by concatenating letters from an alphabet containing only two letters. Along the study, they noticed that any two distinct words whose formatted expressions have an equal number of letters, greater than  $ 2, $  differ by at least three letters.
Prove that if their observation holds indeed, then the number of formatted expressions that have  $ n\ge 3 $  letters is at most  $ \left[ \frac{2^n}{n+1} \right] . $
solution_md:
Denote by  $S$  be the set of all binary strings of length  $n$ . Of course  $|S|=2^n$ . Let  $S'\subset S$  be the set of our formatted expressions of length  $n$ . For any  $s'\in S'$ , denote by  $W(s')$  the set of all binary strings of length  $n$  which differ from  $s'$  in at most one bit.  $W(s')$  consists of  $s'$  itself plus another  $n$  strings, each one differs from  $s'$  only in the  $i$ -th bit,  $i=1,2,\dots,n$ . Hence  $|W(s')|=n+1$ .
	
	Let  $s_1',s_2'\in S', s_1'\neq s_2'$ . Then  $W(s_1')\cap W(s_2')=\emptyset$ . Indeed, if  $s_0\in W(s_1')\cap W(s_2')$ , it would mean  $s'_1$  and  $s'_2$  differ in at most two bits, so they cannot be both in  $S'$ , a contradiction.
	Thus,  $W(s'),s'\in S'$  are disjoint sets, each one of  $n+1$  elements. Hence 
	  $$ |S'|\leq \left\lfloor \frac{|S|}{n+1}\right \rfloor =\left \lfloor\frac{2^n}{n+1}\right \rfloor $$

stem_md: Let be a real number  $ a, $  and a function  $ f:\mathbb{R}_{>0 }\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}_{>0 } . $  Show that the following relations are equivalent. $ \text{(i)}\quad\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}_{>0 } \implies\left( \lim_{x\to\infty } \frac{f(x)}{x^{a+\varepsilon }} =0\wedge \lim_{x\to\infty } \frac{f(x)}{x^{a-\varepsilon }} =\infty \right) $  $ \text{(ii)}\quad\lim_{x\to\infty } \frac{\ln f(x)}{\ln x } =a $
solution_md:
$(i)\implies (ii)$  Let  $\epsilon >0$ .     
From the epsilon-delta definition of the limit we have that  $\exists n_1, n_2 >0$  such that  $\frac{f(x)}{x^{a+\epsilon}}<1,\forall x>n_1$  and  $\frac{f(x)}{x^{a-\epsilon}}>1,\forall x> n_2$ .  Let  $N=\max\{n_1,n_2\}$ .    
We have that   $$ x^{a-\epsilon} <f(x)<x^{a+\epsilon},\forall x>n \implies a-\epsilon < \frac{\ln(f(x))}{\ln x}< a+\epsilon,\forall x>n. $$  Since  $\epsilon$  was chosen arbitrarily, the conclusion follows.      $(ii) \implies (i)$  Let  $\epsilon >0$ .    
Again, from the epsilon-delta definition of the limt we have that  $\exists N>0$  such that    $$ a-\frac{\epsilon}{2} <\frac{\ln(f(x))}{\ln x} < a+ \frac{\epsilon}{2},\forall x> N. $$     
Hence,  $x^{a-\frac{\epsilon}{2}}<f(x) < x^{a+\frac{\epsilon}{2}},\forall x>N $ . From here it follows that   $$ 0<\frac{f(x)}{x^{a+\epsilon}}<\frac{1}{x^{\frac{\epsilon}{2}}},\forall x>N \implies \lim_{x\to \infty}\frac{f(x)}{x^{a+\epsilon}}=0 $$  and that   $$ \frac{f(x)}{x^{a-\epsilon}}>x^{\frac{\epsilon}{2}},\forall x>N \implies  \lim_{x\to \infty}\frac{f(x)}{x^{a-\epsilon}}=\infty  $$

stem_md: Find all functions,  $ f:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} , $  that have the properties that  $ f^2 $  is differentiable and  $ f=\left( f^2 \right)' . $
solution_md:
First note that  $f$ , being a derivative, has the IVP. Now suppose  $f(p)\not=0$  Then  $f^2(p)\not=0$  and since  $f^2$  is continuous we have  $f(x)\not=0$  on a nhbd of  $p$ . By the IVP it follows that  $f(x)$  has the same sign as  $f(p)$  in that nbhd.
Hence  $f$  itself is diff in that nbhd, since it equals  $\pm \sqrt{f^2}$  with a fixed sign. Then  $f=2ff'\implies f'=1/2$ . Hence  $f(x)=x/2+c_p$   in a nhbd of  $p$ . Note that this implies that  $f$  is continuous on  ${\bf R}$ , since it is surely continuous in points where  $f(p)=0$ .
Now suppose that  $f(a)=f(b)=0$  with  $a<b$ . If  $f(c)>0$  for some  $c\in (a,b)$ , then we can take  $c\in [a,b]$  such that  $f(c)>0$  is maximal.
Then  $c\in (a,b),f(c)>0$  hence  $f$  is strictly increasing in a nbhd of  $c$ . Contradiction. Hence  $f(x)\le 0$  on  $[a,b]$  and also  $f(x)\ge 0$  on  $[a,b]$ . Hence  $f=0$  on  $[a,b]$ .
It follows that  $f$  is of the following type: $f(x)=x/2+c$  if  $x\le a, f(x)=0$  if  $a\le x\le b$  and  $f(x)=x/2+d$  if  $x\ge b$ .
Here the eventualities  $a=-\infty, a=b,b=\infty$  are allowed.

stem_md: Let  $A$  be a ring and let  $D$  be the set of its non-invertible elements. If  $a^2=0$  for any  $a \in D,$  prove that:**a)**  $axa=0$  for all  $a \in D$  and  $x \in A$ ;**b)** if  $D$  is a finite set with at least two elements, then there is  $a \in D,$   $a \neq 0,$  such that  $ab=ba=0,$  for every  $b \in D.$ *Ioan Băetu*
solution_md:
a) Let  $G:=(A,+)$  be the additive group structure of  $A$ . Fix  $a\in D$ . Consider the group endomorphism  $\varphi:G\to G$  given by  $x\mapsto axa$ . For a unit  $x$ , since  $ax$  is not a unit, it follows that  $axax=(ax)^2=0$  so  $axa=0$ . Hence  $A^\times\subseteq\ker\varphi$ .

Assume FTSOC there exists  $x\in A\setminus\ker\varphi$ . Then  $x$  is not a unit. Since  $a\in\ker\varphi$ , it follows that  $a+x\not\in\ker\varphi$  so  $a+x$  is not a unit. Thus  $ax+xa=(a+x)^2=0$  so  $\varphi(x)=axa=a(ax+xa)=0$ , contradicting the choice of  $x$ .  $\square$ b) Let  $a=a_1\cdots a_k$  be the longest nonzero product of elements in  $D$ . It exists since  $D$  is finite, and the  $a_i$  are distinct by part a). Clearly  $a\in D$  since  $a_1a=0$ . If there exists  $b\in D$  such that  $ab$  or  $ba$  is nonzero,  $ab$  or  $ba$  would be a longer nonzero product of elements in  $D$ , contradicting the maximality of  $a$ . Thus  $ab=ba=0$  for all  $b\in D$ , so this choice of  $a$  works.  $\square$

stem_md: Let  $K$  be a finite field with  $q$  elements,  $q \ge 3.$  We denote by  $M$  the set of polynomials in  $K[X]$  of degree  $q-2$  whose coefficients are nonzero and pairwise distinct. Find the number of polynomials in  $M$  that have  $q-2$  distinct roots in  $K.$ *Marian Andronache*
solution_md:
Clearly any polynomial in  $M$  cannot have  $0$  as a root since it has nonzero constant term. Let  $K^\times=:\langle g\rangle$ .**Lemma.** For an integer  $r$ ,
\[
\sum_{a\in K^\times}a^r=
\begin{cases}
-1 & \mathrm{if}\ q-1\mid r
0 & \mathrm{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
*Proof.* If  $q-1\mid r$ , then  $a^r=1$  for all  $a\in K^\times$  so the sum equals  $-1$ . Otherwise, we have
\[
\sum_{a\in K^\times}a^r=\sum_{i=0}^{q-2}g^{ri}=\frac{(g^r)^{q-1}-1}{g^r-1}=0
\]
by Lagrange.  $\square$ Note that for  $f\in M$  and
\[
f(x)=:\sum_{i=0}^{q-2}a_ix^i,
\]
we have
\[
f(g^r)=\sum_{i=0}^{q-2}a_i(g^i)^r=\sum_{a\in K^\times}\pi(a)a^r
\]
for a permutation  $\pi$  of  $K^\times$ . Furthermore,  $f$  is determined uniquely by  $\pi$  since  $a_i=\pi(g^i)$ . So we are counting the number of permutations  $\pi$  such that
\[
b_\pi(r):=\sum_{a\in K^\times}\pi(a)a^r=0
\]
for all positive integers  $r\leq q-1$ , with one exception. Consider the  $(q-1)\times(q-1)$  matrix  $T$  over  $K$  given by  $t_{ij}=j^i$ . Then
\[
T
\begin{pmatrix}
\pi(1)
\pi(2)
\pi(3)
\vdots
\pi(q-1)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1^1 & 2^1 & 3^1 & \cdots & (q-1)^1
1^2 & 2^2 & 3^2 & \cdots & (q-1)^2
1^3 & 2^3 & 3^3 & \cdots & (q-1)^3
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots
1^{q-1} & 2^{q-1} & 3^{q-1} & \cdots & (q-1)^{q-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\pi(1)
\pi(2)
\pi(3)
\vdots
\pi(q-1)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
b_\pi(1)
b_\pi(2)
b_\pi(3)
\vdots
b_\pi(q-1)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It is easy to see that
\[
T^{-1}=-
\begin{pmatrix}
1^{-1} & 1^{-2} & 1^{-3} & \cdots & 1^{-(q-1)}
2^{-1} & 2^{-2} & 2^{-3} & \cdots & 2^{-(q-1)}
3^{-1} & 3^{-2} & 3^{-3} & \cdots & 3^{-(q-1)}
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots
(q-1)^{-1} & (q-1)^{-2} & (q-1)^{-3} & \cdots & (q-1)^{-(q-1)}
\end{pmatrix}
\]
by Lemma. If  $b_\pi(i)\neq 0$  only when  $i=c$ , then
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\pi(1)
\pi(2)
\pi(3)
\vdots
\pi(q-1)
\end{pmatrix}
=T^{-1}
\begin{pmatrix}
b_\pi(1)
b_\pi(2)
b_\pi(3)
\vdots
b_\pi(q-1)
\end{pmatrix}
\]
equals  $b_\pi(c)$  times column  $c$  of  $T^{-1}$ . This vector contains all elements of  $K^\times$  as entries iff  $\gcd(c,q-1)=1$ . Since there are  $q-1$  choices for  $b_\pi(c)$ , there are  $\boxed{(q-1)\varphi(q-1)}$  such permutations  $\pi$ .  $\square$

stem_md: Find all the positive integers  $p$  with the property that the sum of the first  $p$  positive integers is a four-digit positive integer whose decomposition into prime factors is of the form  $2^m3^n(m + n)$ , where  $m, n \in N^*$ .
solution_md:
If sum is  $\frac{p(p+1)}{2}=2^m3^n (m+n)$  then $1000 \leq 2^m 3^n (m+n) \leq 3^{m+n} (m+n) \to m+n \geq 5$  $10000 > 2^m 3^n (m+n)\geq 2^{m+n} (m+n) \to m+n \leq 9$ And as  $2,3 \not |m+n \to m+n=5,7$  $m+n=5$ Then only possible variant is  $3^5*5$  but  $\frac{p(p+1)}{2}=3^5*5$  has no solutions $m+n=7$  $p(p+1)=7*2^{m+1} 3^n$  and  $2000 \leq p(p+1) <20000 \to 45 \leq p \leq 140$ One of  $p$  or  $p+1$  is in form  $7*2^a*3^b$  so possible variants are  $56,63,84,112,126$  but as other number from pair  $\{p,p+1\}$  should be in form  $2^c 3^d$  then only  $p=63$  is suitable
And  $p(p+1)=63*64=2*2^5*3^2*7$  is solution

stem_md:
If  $a, b$  and  $c$  are the length of the sides of a triangle, show that  $$ \frac32 \le  \frac{b + c}{b + c + 2a}+
 \frac{a + c}{a + c + 2b}+
 \frac{a + b}{a + b + 2c}\le \frac53. $$
solution_md: Use Radon's Inequality for both sides. Define the sum as  $S$ .  $$ S=\sum_{cyc}{\left(\dfrac{b}{b+c+2a}+\dfrac{c}{b+c+2a}\right)}\geq \dfrac{2(a+b+c)^2}{a^2+b^2+c^2+3(ab+bc+ca)}\geq \dfrac{3}{2} $$  For the other side, it sufficies to prove  $$ 3-S=\sum_{cyc}{\dfrac{2a}{b+c+2a}}\leq \dfrac{4}{3} $$  But  $$ \sum_{cyc}{\dfrac{2a}{b+c+2a}}\geq \dfrac{(a+b+c)^2}{a^2+b^2+c^2+ab+bc+ca}\geq \dfrac{4}{3} $$    $$ \Longleftrightarrow a(b+c-a)+b(c+a-b)+c(a+b-c)\geq 0 $$  as desired.

stem_md: Determine the positive integers expressible in the form  $\frac{x^2+y}{xy+1}$ , for at least  $2$  pairs  $(x,y)$  of positive integers
solution_md:
We will begin with an auxiliary result:
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
All ordered pairs of positive integers  $(x,y)$  satisfying  $xy+1|x^2+y$  are one of the forms  $(a^2,a),(1,a),(a-1,a)$ , where  $a\in\mathbb N$ .**Proof:** Suppose  $(x,y)$  is a solution. Then  $\frac{x^2+y}{xy+1}$  is an integer, say  $k$ . We have   $$ xy+1|x^2+y\iff xy+1|x^2y^2+y^3=(x^2y^2-1)+(y^3+1)\iff xy+1|y^3+1. $$  Thus the problem reduces to finding divisors of  $y^3+1$  which are  $1\pmod{y}$ . Two trivial factors are  $1$  and  $y^3+1$ ; the first factor gives no solution; whereas the second factor leads to  $(x,y)=(y^2,y)$ , which is a solution for all  $y\in\mathbb N$ . Now suppose  $xy+1$  is a nontrivial factor of  $y^3+1$ . Note that if  $xy+1$  is a factor of  $y^3+1$  which is  $1\pmod{y}$ , then so is  $\frac{y^3+1}{xy+1}$ , so we can assume WLOG  $xy+1\le \sqrt{y^3+1}<y^{\frac{3}{2}}+1\implies $   $x<y^{\frac12}\implies x^2<y.$  Then   $$ k=\frac{x^2+y}{xy+1}\le \frac{2y}{x y+1}\implies kxy+k<2y....(\star ) $$  But if  $k\ge 2$ , then  $kxy+k\ge 2y+2>2y$ , contradicting  $(\star)$ . So   $$ k=1\implies x^2+y=xy+1\implies x^2-xy+y-1=0\implies (x-1)(x-y+1)=0. $$   The lemma is now immediate.  $\square$ ------------------------------------------------------------------------
Coming back to the main problem, we note that by our lemma, the only positive integer values that  $\frac{x^2+y}{xy+1}$  can take are:  $$ \left\{\begin{array}{lc}\text{For} (x,y)=(a^2,a), & \frac{x^2+y}{xy+1}=a
\text{For} (x,y)=(1,a), & \frac{x^2+y}{xy+1}=1
\text{For} (x,y)=(a-1,a), & \frac{x^2+y}{xy+1}=1.\end{array}\right. $$  So if  $a\ne 1$ , then  $\frac{x^2+y}{xy+1}$  takes the value  $a$  only once: for  $(x,y)=(a^2,a)$ . But it takes the value  $1$  for infinitely many pairs, so the only possible integer is  $\boxed{1}$ .

Let  $\frac{x^2 + y}{xy + 1} = k$ . Rearranging we get  $x^2 - kxy + (y - k) = 0$ . Now let  $(x,y) \in \mathbb{N}^2$  be the solution to this equation which minimizes  $x$ . Let the other root be  $x_1 \in \mathbb{Z}$ . By Vieta we have  $x + x_1 = ky$  and  $xx_1 = y-k$ .
Now if  $y - k = 0$ , we have  $(x,y) = (k^2 , k)$  which is a solution for every  $k \in \mathbb{Z^+}$ .
If  $y - k < 0$ , then since  $x > 0$ , we have  $x_1 < 0$ , so  $y^2 < ky = x + x_1 < x \implies x > y^2$ .
But note that  $xy + 1 \mid x^2 + y \implies xy + 1 \mid x^2y + y^2 \implies xy + 1 \mid y^2 - x$ .
Since  $x > y^2$ , we must have  $xy + 1 \leq x - y^2 \implies xy + y^2 + 1 \leq x$ , but that is clearly a contradiction.
If  $y - k > 0$ , then  $x_1 > 0$ . By our assumption,  $x_1 \geq x$ . Now note that  $2x \leq x + x_1 = ky < y^2$ , implying  $x < y^2 / 2$ .
Now note that  $xy + 1 \mid y^2 - x \implies xy + 1 \leq y^2 - x \implies x(y+1) < x(y+1) + 1 \leq y^2 \implies x \leq y - 1$ .
We have  $ky = x + x_1 \leq x_1 + y - 1 \implies x_1 \geq ky - y + 1$ .
So,  $y - k = xx_1 \geq x(ky - y + 1) \geq (ky - y + 1) \implies k(y+1) \leq 2y - 1 \implies k \leq 2 - \frac{3}{y+1} < 2$ .
For  $k = 1$ , it is easy to see that the pairs  $(1,a)$  work for all  $a \geq 1$ , thus the only answer is  $k = 1$ .

Lemma: Let  $l=\inf_{n \geq 1} \frac{f(n)}{n}$  ( $l$  exists because  $\forall n \geq 1,$   $\frac{f(n)}{n} \geq 1$ ). Then  $ \underset{n  \to \infty}{\lim}\frac{f(n)}{n}=l$ .
Proof: $\forall m,n \geq 1$ ,  $f(m+n) \leq f(m)+f(n)$ , by induction,  $\forall m,n \geq 1$ ,  $f(mn) \leq mf(n)$ .
Let  $\epsilon > 0$ . By definition of  $l$ , there exist  $m \geq 1$  such that  $l \leq \frac{f(m)}{m} \leq l+ \frac{\epsilon}{2}$ . Let  $n \geq 1$ , write  $n = qm +r$  where  $0 \leq r<m$ , we have: $l \leq \frac{f(n)}{n} = \frac{f(qm+r)}{n} \leq \frac{f(qm)+f(r)}{n} \leq \frac{qf(m)+f(r)}{n} \leq \frac{(l+\frac{\epsilon}{2})qm}{n}+\frac{d}{n} \leq l+\frac{\epsilon}{2}+\frac{d}{n}$  where  $d=\underset{0 \leq i<m}{\max}f(i)$ . 
But  $\frac{d}{n} \underset{n \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} 0$ , So there exist  $N > 1$ , s.t.  $\forall n \geq N$ ,  $\frac{d}{n}<\frac{\epsilon}{2}$ . 
Therefore,  $\forall n>N$ ,  $l \leq \frac{f(n)}{n} \leq l + \epsilon$ . Done.

Using the lemma, there exist  $n_0 \geq 1$  s.t.  $\forall n \geq n_0$ ,  $|f(n) - ln| < \frac{n}{2}$ . Take  $n, m \geq n_0$ : $|f(m+n)-f(m)-f(n)| \leq |f(m+n)-l(m+n)|+|f(m)-lm|+|f(n)-ln| < m+n$ , hence  $|\frac{f(m)+f(n)}{f(m+n)}-1|<\frac{m+n}{f(m+n)} \leq 1$ , it follows that  $f(m+n)=f(m)+f(n)$ .

Then $f((k+1)x)=(k+1)f(x)$ for all $x$ . Contradiction! Then exists infinites $n$ such that $f((k+1)n)=(k+1)f(n)$ Let $q$ an arbitrary positive integer, then: $$ P(n,q): f(n+q) \mid f(n)+ f(q) \implies (k+1)f(n+q) \mid (k+1)f(n)+ (k+1)f(q) $$ $$ P((k+1)n,(k+1)q): f((k+1)(n+q)) \mid f((k+1)n)+f(q(k+1)) \implies (k+1)f(n+q) \mid (k+1)f(n)+f(q(k+1)) $$ Combining both: $$ (k+1)f(n+q) \mid f(q(k+1))-(k+1)f(q) $$ But $(k+1)f(n+q)$ is unbounded when $n$ varies so $f(q(k+1))-(k+1)f(q)=0$ for any $q$ , so we are done. $\square$ This gives us the answer because the claim is true when $k=2$ so it's true for any $k$ , then $f(k)=f(1)k$ :D

The condition $f(m) \ge m$ implies that $f$ is unbounded. Now ignore $f(m) \ge m$ , and use the fact that $f$ is unbounded instead. [rule] Denote $g(T)$ by the smallest positive integer $j$ that satisfies $$ f(j) \ge T > \max(\{f(1), f(2), f(3), \dots, f(j - 1)\}), $$ where we define $\max(\varnothing) = 0$ . For every positive integer $T$ , the value of $g(T)$ is well-defined since $f$ is unbounded (Intuitively, $g(T)$ is the first time the function $f$ exceeds $T$ in value). The function $g$ must also satisfies $g(x) \ge g(y)$ whenever $x \ge y$ , and surely $g$ is also unbounded. Let $C = f(1)$ . For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ , define $N_k$ using the following algorithm: - Start with $N_k = (2k+1)C$ . - If $g(N_k) \le k$ , increment the value of $N_k$ . Repeat this step. The algorithm will end because $g$ is unbounded, so $g(N_k)$ eventually will be greater than $k$ . Now, define $m_k = g(N_k)$ . We have the following estimate: $$ f(m_k) \ge N_k \ge (2k+1)C. $$ [rule]**Claim 01.** $f(i) + f(m_k - i) = f(m_k)$ for each $1 \le i < m_k$ . *Proof.* By definition of $m_k$ , $f(i) + f(m_k - i) < f(m_k) + f(m_k) = 2f(m_k)$ . Since $f(i) + f(m_k-i)$ is a multiple of $f(m_k)$ , so $f(i) + f(m_k - i) = f(m_k)$ . $\square$ [rule]**Claim 02.** $f(m_k - t) = f(m_k) - tC$ for every $t \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots, k \}$ . *Proof.* By the construction of $m_k$ , we have $m_k = g(N_k) > k$ . Therefore, $m_k - k \in \mathbb{N}$ . We are going to prove the claim using induction on $t$ . The base case $t=0$ is obvious. Now, let's assume $f(m_k - t) = f(m_k) - tC$ for $t = i$ . Consider the following: \[ f(m_k - i) | f(m_k - (i + 1)) + f(1). \] If $\frac{f(m_k - (i + 1)) + f(1)}{f(m_k - i)} \ge 2$ , then $f(m_k - (i + 1)) \ge 2f(m_k - i) - C = 2(f(m_k) - Ci) - C \ge f(m_k)$ , a contradiction (The last inequality is the consequence of $f(m_k) \ge (2k+1)C \ge (2i+1)C$ ). Therefore, $\frac{f(m_k - (i + 1)) + f(1)}{f(m_k - i)} = 1$ , i.e. $f(m_k - (i + 1)) = f(m_k - i) - f(1) = f(m_k) - (i + 1)C$ . $\square$ [rule] Combining both claims, we obtain $f(i) = f(m_k) - f(m_k - i) = f(m_k) - (f(m_k) - Ci) = Ci$ for every $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ . Since $k$ can be arbitrarily large, therefore $f(n) = Cn$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ . $\blacksquare$

Let  $P(m,n)$  denote the assertion that  $f(m+n)|f(m)+f(n)$ .

Since  $\frac{f(2^k)}{2^k}$  cannot keep getting smaller by at least a factor of 2, hence it is eventually constant, i.e.  $f(2^{k+r})=2^kf(2^r)$  for some  $r$  and all  $k\ge 0$ . Take  $r$  to be minimal.

Note   $$ 2^kf(2^r)=f(2^{k+r})\le f(2^r)+f(2^r(2^k-1))\le\cdots\le 2^kf(2^r) $$  Thus equality must hold everywhere so  $f(2^r(2^k-i))=(2^k-i)f(2^r)$  for all  $i<2^k$ . Since  $k$  can be anything,  $f(n2^r)=nf(2^r)$  for all  $n$ .

Now  $f(m+n2^r)|f(m)+nf(2^r)$  and  $f(m+2^r)+(n-1)f(2^r)$ . 
If  $f(m+2^r)-f(m)-f(2^r)\ne 0$ , then  $|m+n2^r|\le f(m+n2^r)\le |f(m+2^r)-f(m)-f(2^r)|$ , contradiction since the LHS is unbounded.
Hence  $f(m+2^r)=f(m)+f(2^r)$  for all  $m$ .

If  $r=0$  then we are done,  $f$  is linear and  $f(m)=cm$ , which works.

Else  $P(2^{r-1},n2^{r}-2^{r-1}): nf(2^r)|2f(2^{r-1})+(n-1)f(2^r)$ , so it divides  $2f(2^{r-1})-f(2^r)$ . Since the LHS is unbounded,  $2f(2^{r-1})=f(2^r)$ , which contradicts the minimality of  $r$ .

stem_md:
A set  $S=\{ s_1,s_2,...,s_k\}$  of positive real numbers is "polygonal" if  $k\geq 3$  and there is a non-degenerate planar  $k-$ gon whose side lengths are exactly  $s_1,s_2,...,s_k$ ; the set  $S$  is multipolygonal if in every partition of  $S$  into two subsets,each of which has at least three elements, exactly one of these two subsets in polygonal. Fix an integer  $n\geq 7$ .
(a) Does there exist an  $n-$ element multipolygonal set, removal of whose maximal element leaves a multipolygonal set?
(b) Is it possible that every  $(n-1)-$ element subset of an  $n-$ element set of positive real numbers be multipolygonal?
solution_md:
<details><summary>observation</summary>$S$  is polygonal if and only if  $2\max\{s_1, s_2, \ldots , s_k\} < s_1+s_2+\cdots +s_k$ .</details>
I'll edit this post if I get time after finishing up finals stuff.

EDIT: <details><summary>a</summary>Consider the set  $S$  of size  $n$  defined as  $S=\{2,4, \ldots ,2^{n-4},  2^{n-3}, 2^{n-3}, 2^{n-3}, 2^{n-2}-1\}$ . When this set is divided into two pieces either one set has three  $2^{n-3}$ 's, or one set has two  $2^{n-3}$ 's. In addition, that set can either have  $2^{n-2}-1$  or not have it. No matter which of the 4 cases, it is easy to see that set is polygonal by the above hidden observation. The other set is not polygonal because it only contains distinct powers of two or near powers of two, and so by the geometric series summation formula the sum of all except the largest element is smaller than the largest element always, so by the observation again it is not polygonal. Thus, this set is multipolygonal.

Now if we remove  $2^{n-2}-1$  by almost identical logic the remaining set is also multipolygonal so this set works.</details>

stem_md: Determine the planar finite configurations  $C$  consisting of at least  $3$  points, satisfying the following conditions; if  $x$  and  $y$  are distinct points of  $C$ , there exist  $z\in C$  such that  $xyz$  are three vertices of equilateral triangles
solution_md:
Consider two points in  $C$  with the largest distance. Clearly there must be a third that forms an equilateral triangle with these two. I claim that these three points form the convex hull of  $C$  and there are no more points on the convex hull. Suppose not; then there exists a point  $P$  that is outside of or on this triangle. Clearly  $P$  must be in the reuleaux triangle determined by these three points or else it contradicts the maximality assumed at the start. Furthermore, let the vertex of this triangle furthest from  $P$  be  $A$ . Then in order for  $A, P$  to have a third point in  $C$  that makes an equilateral triangle, this third point  $P'$  must be  $P$  rotated  $60^{\circ}$  clockwise or counterclockwise w.r.t  $A$ . But clearly then  $P'$  does not lie in the previous reuleaux triangle, which contradicts maximality of the distance of the two points first chosen.

Now we know that any additional points must be strictly inside this maximal equilateral triangle. However, again if we have another point  $P$  inside, then  $A,P$  must have another point  $P'$  in  $C$  such that  $P'$  is the image of  $P$  under a  $60^{\circ}$  rotation w.r.t  $A$ , but this means  $P'$  does not lie in the equilateral triangle, contradiction.

Thus, the only configuration possible is three points that form an equilateral triangle.

stem_md: Given a prime  $p$ , prove that the sum  $\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor \frac{q}{p} \rfloor}{k^{p-1}}$  is not divisible by  $q$  for all but finitely many primes  $q$ .
solution_md: By finite differences,  $\sum_{i=1}^n n^{p-1}$  is a degree  $p$  polynomial with leading coefficient  $\tfrac{1}{p}$ . By Lagrange interpolation, can be written in the form  $P(n)/p!$  for some integer polynomial  $P$ . Now, ignoring  $q=p$ , if  $q$  divides the sum then it should divide  $P(-\{q/p\})$ . If infinitely many  $q$  exist then  $P(-k/p)$  should be zero for some  $k \in \{1,\ldots,p-1\}$ , but the leading coefficient of  $P$  cannot be divisible by  $p$  since  $\nu_p(p!)=1$ , which is a contradiction by rational root theorem.  $\blacksquare$
