stem_md:
The ratio of prime numbers  $p$  and  $q$  does not exceed 2 ( $p\ne q$ ).
Prove that there are two consecutive positive integers such that 
the largest prime divisor of one of them is  $p$  and that of the other is  $q$ .
solution_md:
That's not really hard but I still get stucked for hours. WLOG, suppose $p < q < 2p$ . $\boxed{\textbf{Lemma.}\; \text{Given natural numbers}\; m > 1, n\; \text{where}\; \gcd(m, n) = 1,\; \text{there exists unique positive integer} \; 1\le n < m \;\text{satisfy}\; a.n\equiv 1\pmod{m}}$
SketchBezout's lemma kills it immediately.
Since $p$ and $q$ are prime numbers, we have $\gcd(p, q) = 1$ then the lemma tells us that there is $1\le a < q$ satisfy $a.p \equiv 1\pmod{q}$ **Case 1.** $1\le a \le p$ then consider two consecutive natural numbers: $a.p$ and $a.p - 1$ . Here, $1\le a\le p$ hence $a.p$ has the largest prime divisor which is $p$ . And $a.p - 1 < q^{2} \implies \frac{ap - 1}{q} < q \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$ means all prime divisors of $ap - 1$ doesn't exceed $q$ . We're done.**Case 2.** $p < a < q$ . Note that $(q - a).p \equiv -1\pmod{q}$ and $1\le q - a < q$ Consider $(q - a)p$ and $(q - a)p + 1$ . Firstly, we have $p\mid (q - a)p$ and $q\mid (q - a)p + 1$ . On other hand, $q - p < p < a \implies q - a < p$ then the largest prime divisor of $(q - a)p$ is $p$ . And $(q - a)p + 1 < q^{2} \implies \frac{(q - a)p + 1}{q} < q$ and we're done. :) What a beautiful problem

Now assume  $q \geq 5$ . Let  $1 \leq t \leq q-1$  be such that  $t \equiv \frac{-1}{p} \pmod{q}$ . 
Now we consider two cases. If  $t$  is odd, then  $\frac{pt + 1}{2q}$  is an integer. Furthermore we have  $\frac{pt + 1}{2q} < \frac{2qt + 1}{2q} = t + \frac{1}{2q}$ , implying that  $\frac{pt + 1}{2q} \leq t$ .
Now consider the numbers  $pt , pt + 1$ . Clearly  $t < q < p$ , so the largest prime factor of  $pt$  is  $p$ . Also, since  $\frac{pt + 1}{2q} \leq t < q$ , the largest prime factor of  $pt + 1$  is  $q$ . Thus we are done in this case.
Let  $t$  be even. Then,  $r = q - t$  is odd. We have  $r = q - t \equiv -t \equiv \frac{1}{p} \pmod{q}$ . So we have  $q \mid pr - 1$ .
Now we proceed similarly. Since  $r$  is odd, we have  $pr - 1$  is even, and so  $\frac{pr - 1}{2q}$  is an integer.
So,  $\frac{pr - 1}{2q} < \frac{2qr - 1}{2q} = r - \frac{1}{2q}$ , implying that  $\frac{pr - 1}{2q} \leq r - 1 \leq q - 2$ .
Now we consider the numbers  $pr - 1 , pr$ . Clearly since  $r < q < p$ , largest prime divisor of  $pr$  is  $p$ . Also , since  $\frac{pr - 1}{2q} \leq q - 2$ , we have that the largest prime divisor of  $pr - 1$  is  $q$ . We are done in this case as well.

stem_md:
Is there a positive integer  $N>10^{20}$  such that all its decimal digits are odd, 
the numbers of digits 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 in its decimal representation are equal, 
and it is divisible by each 20-digit number obtained from it by deleting 
digits? (Neither deleted nor remaining digits must be consecutive.)
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The answer is affirmative.

We'll construct  $N>10^{20}$  so that  $A\mid N$  for all  $20$ -digit number  $A$  consists of only digits  $1,3,5,7,9$ .
Among those  $A$ s, let  $A_0$  be (one of) number with highest  $\nu_5 (A)$ .
Then let  $A_0'$  be the number formed by placing some digits  $1,3,5,7,9$  on the left of  $A_0$  so that there're equal no. of each digit.
It's clear that  $5^{\nu_5 (A)}\mid A_0'$  for all  $20$ -digit number  $A$  consists of only digits  $1,3,5,7,9$ .
Then, for each  $20$ -digit number  $A$  consists of only digits  $1,3,5,7,9$ , there exists positive integer  $t_A$  that   $$ \frac{A}{5^{\nu_5 (A)}} \mid \overline{\underbrace{A_0'A_0'...A_0'}_{t_A}}, $$   which exists by Pigeonhole and note that  $\gcd ( \frac{A}{5^{\nu_5 (A)}},10) =1$ .
Finally, choose  $N=\overline{\underbrace{A_0'A_0'...A_0'}_{T}}$  where  $T=\mathrm{lcm}{(t_A)}$ .</details>

stem_md:
A cube stands on one of the squares of an infinite chessboard. 
On each face of the cube there is an arrow pointing in one of the four directions 
parallel to the sides of the face. Anton looks on the cube from above and 
rolls it over an edge in the direction pointed by the arrow on the top face. 
Prove that the cube cannot cover any  $5\times 5$  square.
solution_md:
I think that I have a nice solution!

Suppose that the cube can cover a  $5\times 5$  square. Since the cube has  $6$  faces, then after at most  $6$  moves, Anton will see one face again. Hence, there is a number  $a\le 6$ , such that movement of the cube repeats every  $a$  moves (a move is determined by going forward, backwards, to the left, or to the right). WLOG, suppose that the first move the cube does is heading north. We'll check the following  $3$  cases:

<u>Case 1:</u> The  $a^{\text{th}}$  move is going south. Then we notice that after  $2a$  moves, the cube goes back to where it started. Thus, the set of the squares the cube touches is  $2a\le 12<25$ . Contradiction!

<u>Case 2:</u> The  $a^{\text{th}}$  move is going east/west. Then we notice that after  $4a$  moves, the cube goes back to where it started. Thus, the set of the squares the cube touches is  $4a\le 24<25$ . Contradiction!

<u>Case 3:</u> The  $a^{\text{th}}$  move is going north. Then we notice that the cube will always move north at the  $ka^{\text{th}}$  move ( $k\in\mathbb{N}$ ). Let  $(a,b)$  and  $(a+p,b+q)$  be the coordinates of the squares where the cube started moving and where it is after  $k$  moves. It is obvious that  $|p|+|q|\le 6$ . The  $ka^{\text{th}}$  move will always place the cube on  $(a+kp,b+kq)$ . Now just notice that the cube can't touch all  $4$  corner squares of the  $5\times 5$  square. Contradiction!

All things considered, we conclude that the cube can't cover any  $5\times 5$  square.

stem_md: Positive numbers are written in the squares of a 10 × 10 table. Frogs sit in five squares and cover the numbers in these squares. Kostya found the sum of all visible numbers and got 10. Then each frog jumped to an adjacent square and Kostya’s sum changed to  $10^2$ . Then the frogs jumped again, and the sum changed to  $10^3$  and so on: every new sum was 10 times greater than the previous one. What maximum sum can Kostya obtain?
solution_md:
The maximum is  $10^6$ This can be achieved by having  $\frac{1}{1000}$  in all squares except the top 2 by 3, and then having  $10^1-\frac{94}{10000}$ ,  $10^2-\frac{94}{10000}$ , ...,  $10^6-\frac{94}{10000}$  in a cyclic order, and have the frogs jump around in a circle.

We shall now prove  $10^7$  is unattainable.

In the increase from  $10^1$  to  $10^2$  there is an increase of 90. As 5 squares were revealed and 5 taken away, at least one of the revealed squares must have a value strictly greater than  $\frac{90}{6} = 15$ . However as the total value after is only 100, the square must have value at most 100.
Therefore the square has value in the range  $(15,100)$ . 
Similarly for the other jumps up to  $10^6$  to  $10^7$  we must have squares in the ranges:  $(1.5*10^2,10*10^2)$ ,  $(1.5*10^3,10*10^3)$ , ...,  $(1.5*10^6, 10*10^6)$ . These 6 squares are in non-intersecting ranges, so they must all be unique. However as there are only 5 frogs, at least one of the squares must be visible at all times, which is impossible as even the smallest possible value, 15, creates too big of a sum for the first position. Therefore, Kostya cannot get a sum of  $10^7$ , so the maximal value is  $\boxed{10^6}$ .

stem_md: The flights map of air company   $K_{r,r}$  presents several cities. Some cities are connected by a direct (two way) flight, the total number of flights is m. One must choose two non-intersecting groups of r cities each so that every city of the first group is connected by a flight with every city of the second group. Prove that number of possible choices does not exceed  $2*m^r$  .
solution_md:
Consider all pairs  $(A, B)$  satisfying the following:



- There exists two disjoint groups of cities  $P, Q$ , each of size  $r$ .
- $A$  consists of  $r$  flights. No two flights share the same city, be that origin or destination. All flights in  $A$  connect a city in  $P$  to a city in  $Q$ .
- $B$  is the ordered pair  $(P, Q)$ .


Any such pair is considered *relevant*.

Now, consider any  $r$  flights. It belongs to at most  $2^r$  relevant pairs. To see this, note that if they are not disjoint (some city belongs to two flights), then clearly they don't belong in any relevant pair. And if they are disjoint, then we can obtain  $P, Q$  by picking, for each flight, which city is in  $P$  (and the other will be in  $Q$ ). There are  $2^r$  such  $P, Q$ . It's possible that not all of them will work, but we know there are at most  $2^r$  choices.

On the other hand, consider any valid choices of  $P, Q$  such that every city in  $P$  is connected to every city in  $Q$ . Any such  $P, Q$  belongs in  $r!$  relevant pairs: permute the cities in  $Q$  and pair them up with cities in  $P$  in that order to give the desired  $r$  flights.

Suppose there are  $k$  ways to pick  $P, Q$  as desired. Then we have  $k \cdot r! \le 2^r \cdot m^r$  by double-counting the number of relevant pairs as described above. Since  $2^r \le 2 \cdot r!$ , we have  $k \le 2 \cdot m^r$ .

stem_md: Find all functions from positive integers to itself such that  $f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)+f(c)+f(d)$  for all  $c^2+d^2=2ab$
solution_md:
Find all functions from positive integers to itself such that $f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)+f(c)+f(d)$ for all $c^2+d^2=2ab$
Let $P(x,y,z,t)$ be the assertion $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)+f(z)+f(t)$ true $\forall x,y,z,t\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ such that $2xy=z^2+t^2$ Let $a=f(1)$ and $b=f(3)$ $P(x,x,x,x)$ $\implies$ $f(2x)=4f(x)$ So $f(2)=4a$ , $f(4)=16a$ , $f(6)=4b$ and $f(8)=64a$ $P(4,1,2,2)$ $\implies$ $f(5)=25a$ $P(9,1,3,3)$ $\implies$ $f(9)=99a-2b$ Let positive integer $x\ge 3$ $P(10x^2+10,1,2x+4, 4x-2)$ $\implies$ $f(10x^2+11)=f(10x^2+10)+f(1)+f(2x+4)+f(4x-2)$ $P(10x^2+10,1,2x-4, 4x+2)$ $\implies$ $f(10x^2+11)=f(10x^2+10)+f(1)+f(2x-4)+f(4x+2)$ Subtracting, we get $f(2x+4)+f(4x-2)=f(2x-4)+f(4x+2)$ , which is : Assertion $Q(x)$ : $f(2x+1)=f(2x-1)+f(x+2)-f(x-2$ true $\forall$ integer $x\ge 3$ $Q(3)$ $\implies$ $f(7)=49a$ $Q(4)$ $\implies$ $f(9)=4b+45a$ and so $4b+45a=99a-2b$ and so $b=9a$ and $f(9)=81a$ So $f(n)=n^2a$ $\forall n\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9\}$ And $Q(x)$ allows simple induction for all odd $n$ (and even $n$ are obtained from odd ones) And so $\boxed{f(x)=ax^2\quad\forall x\in\mathbb Z_{>0}}$ which indeed is a solution, whatever is $a\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$

stem_md:
Consider a regular polygon  $A_1A_2\ldots A_{6n+3}$ . The vertices  $A_{2n+1}, A_{4n+2}, A_{6n+3}$  are called *holes*. Initially there are three pebbles in some vertices of the polygon, which are also vertices of equilateral triangle. Players  $A$  and  $B$  take moves in turn. In each move, starting from  $A$ , the player chooses pebble and puts it to the next vertex clockwise (for example,  $A_2\rightarrow A_3$ ,  $A_{6n+3}\rightarrow A_1$ ). Player  $A$  wins if at least two pebbles lie in holes after someone's move. Does player  $A$  always have winning strategy?

*Proposed by Bohdan Rublov*
solution_md:
It is all about seeing how  $3(2n+1)$  is relevant, beautiful problem though.

First consider the arcs  $\widehat{A_{2n+1}A_{4n+2}}, \widehat{A_{4n+2}A_{6n+3}}, \widehat{A_{6n+3}A_{2n+1}}$ , call our pebbles to be  $P_1, P_2, P_3$  so that  $P_1 \in \widehat{A_{6n+3}A_{2n+1}}, \; P_2 \in \widehat{A_{2n+1}A_{4n+2}}$  and  $P_3 \in \widehat{A_{4n+2}A_{6n+3}}$ .

On the first move  $A$  will move  $P_1$  so that now the distance between  $P_2$  and  $P_1$  is only  $2k$ , meaning that from now on the set of moves will be the following:

- Pair  $(P_2, P_3)$  so that whenever  $B$  moves one of these, then  $A$  will move the other one. (1)
- If  $B$  moves  $P_1$  at any point, then so will  $A$ . (2)

The idea is that the nearest distance from a hole of  $P_2$  and  $P_3$  is preserved once  $A$ 's turn is finished, meaning that situation (1) cannot be done forever as if  $B$  enters a hole, then  $A$  will as well and thus win.

Therefore at some point having situation (2) moves is forceful, which means that  $P_1$  will move two steps clockwise upon the finish of  $A$ 's turn, we will then reach point where  $P_1$  catches up to  $P_2$  or both  $P_2, P_3$  end up in holes.

Of course  $B$  cannot allow the later meaning that at some point  $P_1$  will be in the same vertex as  $P_2$ .
If this happend and it's  $B$ 's turn then it is over because  $A$  changes strategy to:

-Pair  $(P_1,P_2)$ , if  $B$  moves one, then  $A$  will move the other one.

This way we guarantee both of them reaching the same hole at some point.

Now if it was  $A$ 's turn when  $P_1,P_2$  shared the same vertex, then  $A$  will move  $P_3$  and we may now change  $A$ 's strategy as seen above.

Therefore in any case, we end up making  $A$  win, thus we are done :cool:.

stem_md:
Let  $S = \{1, \dots, n\}$ .  Given a bijection  $f : S \to S$  an *orbit* of  $f$  is a set of the form  $\{x, f(x), f(f(x)), \dots \}$  for some  $x \in S$ .  We denote by  $c(f)$  the number of distinct orbits of  $f$ .  For example, if  $n=3$  and  $f(1)=2$ ,  $f(2)=1$ ,  $f(3)=3$ , the two orbits are  $\{1,2\}$  and  $\{3\}$ , hence  $c(f)=2$ .

Given  $k$  bijections  $f_1$ ,  $\ldots$ ,  $f_k$  from  $S$  to itself, prove that \[ c(f_1) + \dots + c(f_k) \le n(k-1) + c(f) \] where  $f : S \to S$  is the composed function  $f_1 \circ \dots \circ f_k$ .

*Proposed by Maria Monks Gillespie*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>By induction on  $k$ , it suffices to prove the result for  $k=2$ , i.e.,  $c(f_1\circ f_2)\ge c(f_1)+c(f_2)-n$ . We will prove this by induction on  $n$ . 

The base case  $n=1$  is clear. Now assume the result is true for all lesser  $n$ . By definition,  $f_1$  and  $f_2$  are permutations of  $S$ , so their orbits correspond to their cycles when written in cycle notation. Thus the orbits of  $f_1$  form a partition of  $S$ ; call this partition  $P_1$ . Similarly, let  $P_2$  be the partition of  $S$  formed by the orbits of  $f_2$ . If  $c(f_1)+c(f_2)\le n+1$ , then the result is immediate, so assume that  $c(f_1)+c(f_2)\ge n+2$ . **Lemma.** Given two partitions  $P_1$ ,  $P_2$  of  $S$  satisfying  $|P_1|+|P_2|\ge n+2$ , there exists a proper subset  $R$  of  $S$  such that:
(i)   $R$  is the union of  $p_1$  parts of  $P_1$  and the union of  $p_2$  parts of  $P_2$ , for some  $p_1$  and  $p_2$ (ii)  $|R|\ge p_1+p_2-1$ .  

<details><summary>Proof</summary>We can construct  $R$  using the following algorithm:

Step 1: Start with an arbitrary part  $A$  of  $P_1$  and color it red. Then color blue all the parts in  $P_2$  that contain an element from  $A$ . 

Now continue this process: at each step, color red all the parts in  $P_1$  that contain an element from a blue part (other than the parts already colored red), and then color blue all the parts in  $P_2$  that contain an element from a red part (other than the parts already colored blue). (These are performed sequentially, not simultaneously.) The process terminates when there is no need to color additional parts in  $P_1$  red at the beginning of a step. Let  $|R|(t)$ ,  $p_1(t)$ , and  $p_2(t)$  denote the number of elements in a red part at the end of step  $t$ , the number of red parts at the end of step  $t$ , and the number of blue parts at the end of step  $t$ , respectively. We claim that  $|R|(t)\ge p_1(t)+p_2(t)-1$  for all  $t$  for which the process has not terminated at the beginning of step  $t$ , which we will prove by induction.

For the base case  $t=1$ , we have  $|R|(1)=|A|$ ,  $p_1(1)=1$ , and  $p_2(1)\le |A|$ , so indeed  $|R|(1)\ge p_1(1)+p_2(1)-1$ . Now assume the claim is true for all lesser  $t$ . Recall that at step  $t$ , we color red all the parts in  $P_1$  that contain an element from a blue part. Let  $N$  be the set of "new" elements in a blue part from step  $t-1$ . Note that we color at most  $|N|$  new parts red. But we color exactly  $p_1(t)-p_1(t-1)$  new parts red, so 
\[
p_1(t)-p_1(t-1)\le |N|.\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad(1)
\]
Also, from step  $t-1$  to step  $t$  we increase the number of elements in a red part by  $|R|(t)-|R|(t-1)$ , so the number of "new" elements in a red part is  $|R|(t)-|R|(t-1)-|N|$ . Next, we color blue all the parts in  $P_2$  that contain an element from a red part (other than the parts that are already colored blue); note that we color at most  $|R|(t)-|R|(t-1)-|N|$  new parts blue. But we color exactly  $p_2(t)-p_2(t-1)$  new parts blue, so
\[
p_2(t)-p_2(t-1)\le |R|(t)-|R|(t-1)-|N|.\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad(2)
\]
Adding  $(1)$  and  $(2)$  yields  $p_1(t)+p_2(t)-p_1(t-1)-p_2(t-1)\le |R|(t)-|R|(t-1)$ , so
\begin{align*}
|R|(t)\ge |R|(t-1)-p_1(t-1)-p_2(t-1)+p_1(t)+p_2(t)\ge p_1(t)+p_2(t)-1
\end{align*}
where we used the inductive hypothesis  $|R|(t-1)\ge p_1(t-1)+p_2(t-1)-1$ . This completes the proof of the claim.

Now observe that this process terminates, as otherwise  $S$  would have to have arbitrarily many elements. Moreover, letting  $R$  be the union of the red parts in  $P_1$  at the end of the step just before termination (or the union of the blue parts in  $P_2$ ; they are the same set) satisfies (i), and it satisfies (ii) by the above claim. It only remains to show that  $R$  is a *proper* subset of  $S$ . But this is immediate: if  $R=S$ , then  $n=|S|=|R|\ge p_1+p_2-1=|P_1|+|P_2|-1\ge n+1$ , contradiction. This completes the proof of the lemma.</details>

Since  $|P_1|=c(f_1)$  and  $|P_2|=c(f_2)$ , the lemma applies. Note that  $R$  is an invariant subset of  $f_1$  and  $f_2$ , i.e., the image of  $R$  under  $f_1$  and  $f_2$  is itself. Therefore  $R$  is an invariant subset of the permutation  $f_1\circ f_2$ , which implies that  $R$  can be partitioned into some number of orbits of  $f_1\circ f_2$ . In particular,  $R$  consists of at least one orbit.

Next, let  $f_1'$  and  $f_2'$  be the functions that result from restricting the domain of  $f_1$  and  $f_2$  to  $S\backslash R$ , respectively. By property (i) of  $R$ , it follows that  $f_1':S\backslash R\to S\backslash R$  and  $f_2': S\backslash R\to S\backslash R$  are permutations of  $S\backslash R$ . Moreover,  $c(f_1')=c(f_1)-p_1$  and  $c(f_2')=c(f_2)-p_2$ . So by the inductive hypothesis, 
\begin{align*}
c(f_1'\circ f_2')&\ge c(f_1')+c(f_2')-|S\backslash R|
&=c(f_1)+c(f_2)-p_1-p_2-|S\backslash R|
&=c(f_1)+c(f_2)-p_1-p_2-(n-|R|)
&=c(f_1)+c(f_2)+(|R|-p_1-p_2)-n
&\ge c(f_1)+c(f_2)-n-1
\end{align*}
where the last step follows from property (ii) of  $R$ . Hence,  $c(f_1\circ f_2)\ge 1+c(f_1'\circ f_2')\ge c(f_1)+c(f_2)-n$  as desired. This completes the induction and the proof.</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Lemma: Let  $G_1$  and  $G_2$  be two graphs on  $n$  vertices such that  $G_1$  has  $c_1$  connected components and  $G_2$  has  $c_2$  connected components. Then  $G_1\cup G_2$  has at least  $c_1+c_2-n$  connected components.

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Suppose that  $G_1\cup G_2$  is connected. It suffices to show that given a fixed  $G_1$ , the maximum number of connected components  $G_2$  can have is  $n+1-c_1$ . Consider a graph  $G$  with  $c_1$  vertices, where each vertex corresponds to a connected component of  $G_1$ , and we connect two vertices in  $G$  if in  $G_2$ , there exists an edge between the vertices of their corresponding connected components in  $G_1$ .  $G$  clearly must be connected since  $G_1\cup G_2$  is connected. Now, consider a spanning tree  $G'$  of  $G$ .  $G'$  has  $c_1-1$  edges and the corresponding edges of  $G'$  must exist in  $G_2$ , so there exists a subgraph of  $G_2$  with no cycles and at least  $c_1-1$  edges. Hence,  $G_2$  has at least  $n-(c_1-1)=n+1-c_1$  connected components, as desired.

If  $G_1\cup G_2$  is not all connected, then we will prove the result with strong induction. The base case of  $n=1$  is clearly true. Now, split  $G_1\cup G_2$  into two disjoint subgraphs  $X$  and  $Y$  with  $x>0$  and  $y>0$  vertices respectively. If  $c_x$ ,  $c_y$ ,  $c_{1,x}$ ,  $c_{2,x}$ ,  $c_{1,y}$ , and  $c_{2,y}$  are the number of connected components of  $X$ ,  $Y$ ,  $G_1$  in  $X$ ,  $G_2$  in  $X$ ,  $G_1$  in  $Y$ , and  $G_2$  in  $Y$  respectively, then by induction we have that  $c_x\geq c_{1,x}+c_{2,x}-x$  and  $c_y\geq c_{1,y}+c_{2,y}-y$ . Thus,  $G_1\cup G_2$  has  $c_x+c_y\geq c_{1,x}+c_{2,x}+c_{1,y}+c_{2,y}-x-y=c_1+c_2-n$  connected components, as desired.</details>

Note that  $H_1$  has  $c(f_1)$  connected components and  $H_2$  has  $c(f_2)$  connected components. Consider the graph  $H_1\cup H_2$ . Clearly, any orbit of  $f_1\circ f_2$  must be contained in  $H_1\cup H_2$ , so the number of orbits of  $f_1\circ f_2$  is at least the number of connected components of  $H_1\cup H_2$ , which is at least  $c_1+c_2-n$ , as desired.</details>

Lemma.  $s(g)$  is the minimum amount of swaps needed to turn the identity bijection into  $g$ .
Proof:
It is easy to see that we can create a cycle of length  $c$  in  $c - 1$  swaps by induction. Doing this for each cycle,  $c_1$  through  $c_l$ , of  $g$ , yields  $\sum_{i = 1}^l (c_i - 1) = \left(\sum_{i = 1}^l c_i\right) - l = n - l$ , and  $l = c(g)$  so it is possible to write  $g$  in  $n - c(g)$  swaps. Now we show that this is the minimum.

To do this, simply notice that each swap either links two disjoint cycles together or breaks one complete cycle apart; the net result is that  $c(g)$  changes by  $1$ . To get from the identity to  $g$ , we need to join cycles at least  $n - c(g)$  times, so there must be at least that many swaps. And thus, since  $s(f)$  is the length of the minimal sequence of swaps to make  $f$ , certainly  $s(f)$  is at most equal to that quantity.</details>

<details><summary>Graph theory!</summary>Define a connected component of a graph  $G$  to be a subgraph such that any edge going through a vertex of  $G$  has its other endpoint in a vertex in  $G$ . Moreover, there does not exist two subgraphs  $G_1, G_2$  of  $G$  such that  $G_1, G_2$  had disjoint vertices and no edge ran between  $G_1, G_2$ . The problem hinges on this lemma:**Lemma**: Suppose  $A, B$  are directed graphs on  $n$  vertices. Let  $E(G)$  be the number of connected components on a graph  $G$ . Then  $E(A)+E(B)\le n+E(A\cup B)$ . (Note that some edges might loop at a vertex).

<u>Proof:</u> Let a single vertex be a vertex that is its own connected component. Define a multi-edge to be an edge that is part of a connected component with at least 2 vertices. Suppose that there were  $x$  single-vertices in  $B$ . Then any other connected component of  $B$  goes through at least  $2$  vertices, and thus  $x+2(E(B)-x)\le n$ . In other words,  $x\ge 2E(B)-n$ . In other words, the number of pairs of vertices with an edge running between them is at most  $E(B)-x\le n-E(B)$ . 

Now consider the graph  $A$ , and repeatedly add edges from graph  $B$ . Each multi-edge can connect at most 2 connected components of  $A$ , reducing  $E(A)$  by 1. When the process terminates,  $E(A)$  has been reduced by at most  $n-E(B)$ , and thus  $E(A\cup B)\ge E(A)-(n-E(B))=E(A)+E(B)-n$ , proving the lemma.  $\blacksquare$ We will prove  $c(f_1)+c(f_2)\le n+c(f_1\circ f_2)$ ; then the result holds by induction on  $k$ . 

Let  $G(f)$  for any  $f:S\rightarrow S$  be the directed graph such that an edge goes from  $V_1$  to  $V_2$  iff  $f(V_1)=V_2$ . Consider the connected components of  $G(f_1)\cup G(f_2)$ . Suppose that  $C_1, C_2$  were two such connected components, and there existed an edge of  $G(f_1\circ f_2)$  that ran from  $C_1$  to  $C_2$ . Then it would follow that either an edge of  $G(f_1)$  or  $G(f_2)$  ran between  $C_1$  and  $C_2$ , contradicting that  $C_1$  and  $C_2$  were connected components of  $G(f_1)\cup G(f_2)$ . 

It therefore follows that  $E(G(f_1\circ f_2))\ge E(G(f_1)\cup G(f_2))$ . Suppose this were not true. Then it would mean that for some two connected components of  $G(f_1)\cup G(f_2)$ , there is an edge of  $G(f_1\circ f_2)$  running between the two components by Pigeonhole, which was proven to be false. But then by our lemma,  $E(G(f_1\circ f_2))\ge E(G(f_1)\cup G(f_2))\ge E(G(f_1))+E(G(f_2))-n$ . Finally, observe that  $c(f)=E(G(f))$  for a function  $f:S\rightarrow S$ . Thus  $c(f_1\circ f_2)\ge c(f_1)+c(f_2)-n$ , and the problem is proven, as desired.  $\square$</details>

If  $\tau_2 \cdots \tau_k$  is written as a product of disjoint cycles, then left multiplication by  $\tau_1$  either joins two cycles or breaks one cycle into two. In either case, \[c(\tau_1 \cdots \tau_k) \ge c(\tau_2 \cdots \tau_k) - 1 \ge n - k,\] where the last step follows from the inductive hypothesis. This completes the proof.

I liked this problem a lot (no idea why :P). Anyway here's my solution: Consider the symmetric group  $S_n$  whose elements are all the bijections from  $S$  to itself. It is well known that every element of  $S_n$  can be written as a product of disjoint cycles. Let  $f$  be an element of  $S_n$  with  $P$  fixed points, and which can be written as a product of  $D$  disjoint cycles (of length at least  $2$ ). Then one can easily see that we have  $c(f)=P+D$ . Consider the following key claim-**CLAIM** Let  $\eta$  be a cycle of length  $z \geq 2$ . Then  $\eta$  can be converted into the identity permutation in  $z-1$  steps.

<u>*Proof of Claim*</u> Even though the claim is intuitively quite clear, I'll give a brief sketch. The proof proceeds by induction on  $z$ . For  $z=2$  the result is obvious. Assume that the result is true for  $z$ . Then in a  $z+1$ -cycle, simply interchange one of the elements to get a permutation consisting of a  $z$ -cycle and a fixed element. Now apply the inductive hypothesis to get the desired result.  $\Box$ -----
Let  $\sigma$  be the identity element of  $S_n$ . Also let  $\ell(\zeta)$  denote the length of a cycle  $\zeta$  of  $f$ . Then, by our Claim,  $f$  can be converted into  $\sigma$  in   $$ \sum_{i=1}^D (\ell(\zeta)-1)=(n-P)-D=n-c(f) $$  steps. Keeping this in mind, we define the function  $d:S_n \times S_n \rightarrow \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$  as follows-


- $d(\sigma,f)=d(f,\sigma)$  is the minimum number of steps required to convert  $f$  to  $\sigma$ , i.e.  $d(f,\sigma)=n-c(f)$  $\text{ }$
- $d(f,g)=d(f,\sigma)+d(\sigma,g)$

Note that, because of the way in which we defined the function  $d$ , it must be a metric function, or specifically it must follow the triangle inequality. Now, consider the  $k$  bijections given to us. Then, using the above analysis, we get that   $$ d(f_1,\sigma)+d(f_2,\sigma)+ \dots +d(f_k,\sigma) \geq d(f_1 \circ f_2 \circ \dots \circ f_k, \sigma) \Rightarrow c(f_1) +c(f_2)+ \dots + c(f_k) \leq n(k-1) + c(f) \quad \blacksquare $$  P.S. But the number of connected components of  $G$  is precisely  $m$ , yielding the result.  $\square$

Let  $ABC$  be a scalene triangle with circumcircle  $\Omega$ , and suppose the incircle of  $ABC$  touches  $BC$  at  $D$ .  The angle bisector of  $\angle A$  meets  $BC$  and  $\Omega$  at  $E$  and  $F$ .  The circumcircle of  $\triangle DEF$  intersects the  $A$ -excircle at  $S_1$ ,  $S_2$ , and  $\Omega$  at  $T \neq F$ .  Prove that line  $AT$  passes through either  $S_1$  or  $S_2$ .

*Proposed by Evan Chen*

Here's the pedestrian solution:

Assume for simplicity  $AB < AC$ .  Let  $K$  be the contact point of the  $A$ -excircle on  $BC$ ; also let ray  $TD$  meet  $\Omega$  again at  $L$ .  From the fact that  $\angle FTL = \angle FTD = 180^{\circ} - \angle FED$ , we can deduce that  $\angle FTL = \angle ACF$ , meaning that  $F$  is the reflection of  $A$  across the perpendicular bisector  $\ell$  of  $BC$ .  If we reflect  $T$ ,  $D$ ,  $L$  over  $\ell$ , we deduce  $A$ ,  $K$  and the reflection of  $T$  across  $\ell$  are collinear, which implies that  $\angle BAT = \angle CAK$ .

Now, consider the reflection point  $K$  across line  $AI$ , say  $S$ .  Since ray  $AI$  passes through the  $A$ -excenter,  $S$  lies on the  $A$ -excircle.  Since  $\angle BAT = \angle CAK$ ,  $S$  also lies on ray  $AT$ .  But the circumcircles of triangles  $DEF$  and  $EFK$  are congruent (from  $DF = KF$ ), so  $S$  lies on the circumcircle of  $\triangle DEF$  too.  Hence  $S$  is the desired intersection point.

Of course,  $T$  is actually the [contact point of the mixtilinear incircle](https://www.mit.edu/~evanchen/handouts/Mixt-GeoGuessr/Mixt-GeoGuessr.pdf). :)

SolutionWLOG $AC>AB$ , and define $S$ as the intersection of $AT$ and the $A$ -excircle such that $T$ is between $A$ and $S$ . It is well-known that $T$ is the contact point of the $A$ -mixtilinear incircle on $\Omega$ , so that a compositional transformation of inversion centered at $A$ with power $AB\cdot AC$ and reflection about the $A$ -angle bisector sends $T$ to the tangency point of the $A$ -excircle on $BC$ , $T'$ . However, since the excircle is symmetric about the $A$ -angle bisector, this implies that $A$ is equidistant from $S$ and $T'$ , so that $$ AS=AT'\Longrightarrow AS\cdot AT=AT\cdot AT'=AB\cdot AC=AE\cdot AF $$ so that $S, T, E$ and $F$ lie on a circle. However, $D$ lies on a circle with $T, E$ , and $F$ , so we're done $.\:\blacksquare\:$

Here is a sketch of my solution:

We will denote by  $I$  the incenter of  $\triangle{ABC}$  and by  $J$  we will denote the point where the  $A$ -excircle touches  $BC$ .Also let  $TD\cap\Omega\equiv L$ .

Hence   $$ \angle{ABT}=\angle{ABC}+\angle{DBT}=\angle{BTD}+\angle{DBT}=180^0-\angle{BDT}=180^0-\angle{AJB}=\angle{AJC}. $$  But  $\angle{ATB}=\angle{ACJ}$ ,so  $\triangle{BAT}\sim\triangle{JAC}$ .From here we obtain that lines  $AT,AJ$  are isogonal in  $\triangle{BAC}$ .Thus  $\angle{TAI}=\angle{I_aAJ}$ ,where  $I_a$  is the center of the  $A$ -excircle
By applying law of sines in  $\triangle{BAI},\triangle{ATB}$  and  $\triangle{AJI_a}$  we easily obtain  $\frac{AT}{AI}=\frac{AI_a}{AJ}$ .
But  $\angle{TAI}=\angle{I_aAJ}$ ,so  $\triangle{TAI}\sim\triangle{I_aAJ}$ .
Now let  $S\equiv AT\cap\odot(DEF)$ .PoP yields  $AT\cdot AS=AE\cdot AF\stackrel{\text{well known}}{=}AI\cdot AI_a$ ,so points  $T,S,I_a,I$  are concyclic.Hence  $\angle{AI_aS}=\angle{ATI}\stackrel{\triangle{TAI}\sim\triangle{I_aAJ}}{=}\angle{AI_aJ}$ ,but lines  $AT,AJ$  are symmetric wrt  $AI$ ,so  $\angle{AI_aS}=\angle{AI_aJ}$  implies  $I_aS=I_aJ$ .Therefore  $S$  lies on the  $A$ -excircle of  $\triangle{ABC}$ .This ends our proof,because  $AT\cap\odot(DEF)\equiv S$ (so  $S\in\odot(DEF)$ ) and  $S$  lies on the  $A$ -excircle of  $\triangle{ABC}$ ,meaning that  $S_1\in AT$  or  $S_2\in AT$ .

Let  $A=(1,0,0), B=(0,1,0), C=(0,0,1)$ .  For convenience, let  $s=\tfrac{a+b+c}{2}$ , and let  $s_a=s-a$ , and define  $s_b,s_c$  similarly.  Then it’s obvious that  $D=(0:s_c:s_b), E=(0:b:c),$  and  $F=(-a^2:b^2+bc:c^2+bc)$ .  First, let’s find the equation for  $(DEF)$ .  Let it be defined as per usual by \[a^2yz+b^2zx+c^2xy=(x+y+z)(ux+vy+wz).\]  The point  $D$  gives the equation \[a^2s_bs_c=(s_b+s_c)(s_cv+s_bw)\iff as_bs_c=s_cv+s_bw,\] since  $s_b+s_c=a$ .  Meanwhile,  $E$  gives \[a^2bc=(b+c)(bv+cw).\]  We’ll solve for  $v$  and  $w$  before inserting the somewhat messier  $F$  into our equation.  A simple application of Cramer’s rule shows that \[v=\left(\frac{acs_b}{b+c}\right)\left(\frac{(b+c)s_c-ab}{cs_c-bs_b}\right).\]  But  $cs_c-bs_b=(b+c)s_c-bs_c-bs_b=(b+c)s_c-ab$ , so  $v=\left(\frac{acs_b}{b+c}\right)$ .  Similarly  $w=\left(\frac{abs_c}{b+c}\right)$ .  Now we plug in  $F$ .  Since  $F$  is on the circumcircle also, the LHS of the circle equation is  $0$ ; hence, we must have \[-a^2u+abcs_b+abcs_c=0\iff u=bc.\]  So the equation of  $(DEF)$  is \[(b+c)(a^2yz+b^2zx+c^2xy)=(x+y+z)(bc(b+c)x+acs_by+abs_cz).\]  Next, we find the coordinates of  $T=(ABC)\cap(DEF)$ . Let  $T=(1:p:q)$  for some  $p,q$ .  From the circle equations, \[bc(b+c)+acs_bp+abs_cq=0\]\[a^2pq+b^2q+c^2p=0.\]The first gives\[p=-\frac{bs_cq}{cs_b}-\frac{b(b+c)}{as_b}.\]Plugging this into the second, we get \[\left(\frac{a^2bs_c}{cs_b}\right)q^2+(blah)q+\frac{bc^2(b+c)}{as_b}=0,\]for some linear term.  But we don’t care about it because we can use Vieta: since  $F$  is the other intersection point, one of the solutions corresponds to  $F$ , namely when  $q=-\frac{c(b+c)}{a^2}$ .  So the other  $q$  satisfies \[q\left(\frac{-c(b+c)}{a^2}\right)\left(\frac{a^2bs_c}{cs_b}\right)=\frac{bc^2(b+c)}{as_b},\] which simplifies to  $q=-\frac{c^2}{as_c}$ .  Similarly,  $p=-\frac{b^2}{as_b}$ .  So \[T=\left(1:-\frac{b^2}{as_b}:-\frac{c^2}{as_c}\right)=\left(-as_bs_c:b^2s_c:c^2s_b\right).\]  Now, define  $S_1’=AT\cap(DEF)$ , so our ultimate goal is to show that  $S_1’$  lies on the  $A$  excircle.  Let  $S_1’=(r:b^2s_c:c^2s_b)$  for some  $r$ .  Plugging into the equation for  $(DEF)$ , we know that \[(b+c)(a^2b^2c^2s_bs_c+b^2c^2s_br+b^2c^2s_cr)=(r+b^2s_c+c^2s_b)(bc(b+c)r+ab^2cs_bs_c+abc^2s_bs_c)\]\[(b+c)(ab^2c^2)(as_bs_c+r)=(r+b^2s_c+c^2s_b)(b+c)(bcr+abcs_bs_c)\]\[abc(as_bs_c+r)=(r+b^2s_c+c^2s_b)(as_bs_c+r)\]The second factor on each side corresponds to  $T$ , so we can divide it out to get  $r+b^2s_c+c^2s_b=abc$ .  Now, it’s easy to verify that  $b^2s_c+c^2s_b-abc=(b-c)^2s$  by direct expansion, so in fact  $r=-(b-c)^2s$ .  Then  $S_1’=(-(b-c)^2s:b^2s_c:c^2s_b)$ , and we just have to show that this lies on the  $A$  excircle.

This part of the calculation is the longest; but it’s also straightforward, since we know it has to reduce to  $0$  or we’ve done something wrong.  The  $A$  excircle has equation  $a^2yz+b^2zx+c^2xy=(x+y+z)(s^2x+s_c^2y+s_b^2z)$ , so we just have to verify that \[a^2b^2c^2s_bs_c-b^2c^2(b-c)^2s_bs-b^2c^2(b-c)^2s_cs=(b^2s_c+c^2s_b-(b-c)^2s)(-(b-c)^2s^3+b^2s_c^3+c^2s_b^3).\]Remembering that  $s_b+s_c=a$  and  $b^2s_c+c^2s_b-abc=(b-c)^2$ , both sides simplify giving \[a^2b^2c^2-ab^2c^2(b-c)^2s=abc(-(b-c)^2s^3+b^2s_c^3+c^2s_b^3)\]Cancelling  $abc$  on each side (yay!) we get \[bc(as_bs_c-(b-c)^2s)=-(b-c)^2s^3+b^2(s-c)^3+c^2(s-b)^2.\]Expanding on the right hand side, this is
\[bc(a(s-b)(s-c)-(b-c)^2s)=2bcs^3-3b^2cs^2-3bc^2s^2+6b^2c^2s-b^2c^3-b^3c^2.\]Now we can cancel  $bc$  on each side, so our equation has gone from degree  $8$  to degree  $3$ .  Our next goal is to cancel out a factor of  $s$  from each side, since we’re already close, and this will reduce the problem to degree  $2$ , which is extremely manageable.  We proceed by cancelling  $bc$ , expanding a bit on the left side, and simplifying: \[as^2-a(b+c)s-(b-c)^2s=2s^3-3bs^2-3cs^2+6bcs-bc(2s)\]\[\iff as-a(b+c)-(b-c)^2=2s^2-3(b+c)s+4bc.\]We now finish by moving the  $as$  term to the other side to kill off the  $s^2$  term. \[a(b+c)+(b-c)^2=(2s+2b+2c)s-2s^2-4bc\iff (b-c)^2=(2s-a)(b+c)-4bc\iff (b-c)^2=(b+c)^2-4bc,\]which is true.**Remarks.** A bash is relatively motivated.  Finding the equation of  $(DEF)$  is clearly going to be pretty easy, since we have two nice points on  $BC$ , so we don't have to solve a three-variable system.  Then we can normalize  $T$  to a convenient form and get a quadratic, which is easy to do with Vieta.  In finding  $S_1'$  we conveniently got a factor of  $as_bs_c+r$  on each side, so we didn't need to expand to a quadratic or use Vieta, although it wouldn't have been too much worse.  It was nice that  $S_1'$  had such a good form, because we're plugging it into a circle equation for the excircle, and even a slightly worse  $x$  coordinate would have been a pain.  Finally, in the last circle equation our goal is to pull out factors of whatever we can, so that we can get the degree down to something manageable. But the circumcircles of triangles $DEF$ and $EFK$ are congruent (from $DF = KF$ ), so $S$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle DEF$ too. Hence $S$ is the desired intersection point. First, I will prove the following key lemma: **Claim:** $T$ is the $A$ -mixtilinear intouch point. *Proof.* We proceed with phantom points. Let $T'$ be the $A$ -mixtilinear intouch point, and let $A'$ be the reflection of $A$ over the perpendicular bisector of $A'.$ It is well-known that $T', D,$ and $A'$ are collinear, so we have \begin{align*} \angle{MT'D} &= \angle{MT'A'} &= \angle{ACM} &= \angle{ACB}+\angle{BCM} &= 180^\circ - \angle{CBA}-\angle{BAC}+\angle{BAM} &= 180^\circ - \angle{KBA}-\angle{BAK} &= \angle{BKA} &= 180^\circ-\angle{BKM} &= 180^\circ - \angle{MKD}. \end{align*} This implies that $T'MKD$ is cyclic, so $T'=T,$ concluding the proof. $\blacksquare$ Now, invert around $A$ with radius $\sqrt{AB \cdot AC}.$ Let the image of $T$ be $S.$ It is well-known that $K$ and $M$ swap under this inversion, so we have $$ AS \cdot AT = AB \cdot AC = AK \cdot AM. $$ By the inverse of Power of a Point, this implies that $KSTM$ is cyclic. Also, since $T$ lies on the $A$ -mixtilinear incircle, $S$ must lie on its image, which is the $A$ -excircle. Hence, we know that $S$ lies on the $A$ -excircle, $(KMT),$ and line $AT,$ implying the desired result. $\square$

stem_md:
Let  $p$  be a prime number.  Let  $\mathbb F_p$  denote the integers modulo  $p$ , and let  $\mathbb F_p[x]$  be the set of polynomials with coefficients in  $\mathbb F_p$ .  Define  $\Psi : \mathbb F_p[x] \to \mathbb F_p[x]$  by \[ \Psi\left( \sum_{i=0}^n a_i x^i \right) = \sum_{i=0}^n a_i x^{p^i}. \] Prove that for nonzero polynomials  $F,G \in \mathbb F_p[x]$ , \[ \Psi(\gcd(F,G)) = \gcd(\Psi(F), \Psi(G)). \] Here, a polynomial  $Q$  divides  $P$  if there exists  $R \in \mathbb F_p[x]$  such that  $P(x) - Q(x) R(x)$  is the polynomial with all coefficients  $0$  (with all addition and multiplication in the coefficients taken modulo  $p$ ), and the gcd of two polynomials is the highest degree polynomial with leading coefficient  $1$  which divides both of them.  A non-zero polynomial is a polynomial with not all coefficients  $0$ .  As an example of multiplication,  $(x+1)(x+2)(x+3) = x^3+x^2+x+1$  in  $\mathbb F_5[x]$ .

*Proposed by Mark Sellke*
solution_md:
Let  $\mathbb{N}$  denote the set of natural numbers, including  $0$ . Let  $R$  be the ring consisting of the set of  $\mathbb{F}_p$ -polynomials
\[
\left\{a_n x^{p^n}+a_{n-1} x^{p^{n-1}}+\cdots+a_1 x^p+a_0x\mid n\in\mathbb{N};a_0,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb{F}_p\right\},
\]
with addition  $+$  and multiplication  $\circ$  (function composition). It is easy to check that  $R$  is a ring with additive identity  $0$  and multiplicative identity  $x$ . Let  $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$  denote the algebraic closure of  $\mathbb{F}_p$ .**Lemma 1.**  $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$  is isomorphic to  $R$  with isomorphism  $\Psi$ .

*Proof.* We first prove that  $\Psi:\mathbb{F}_p[x]\rightarrow R$  is a homomorphism:


- $\Psi(f+g)=\Psi(f)+\Psi(g)$  is trivial.
- We have  $\Psi(x^\alpha x^\beta)=x^{p^{\alpha+\beta}}=\left(x^{p^\alpha}\right)^{p^\beta}=\Psi(x^\alpha)\circ\Psi(x^\beta)$ . Clearly we also have  $\Psi(cx^\alpha)=c\Psi(x^\alpha)$  for any constant  $c$ . It follows that  $\Psi(fg)=\Psi(f)\Psi(g)$ .
- $\Psi(1)=x$  is trivial.
[/list]
Clearly  $\ker\Psi=\{1\}$  and  $\Psi$  is surjective so  $\Psi$  is an isomorphism.  $\square$ Let  $\overline{R}\supseteq R$  be the ring consisting of the set of  $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$ -polynomials
\[
\left\{a_n x^{p^n}+a_{n-1} x^{p^{n-1}}+\cdots+a_1 x^p+a_0x\mid n\in\mathbb{N};a_0,\ldots,a_n\in\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}\right\},
\]
with addition  $+$  and multiplication  $\circ$ . Let  $\tilde{\Psi}:\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}[x]\rightarrow\overline{R}$  be the extension of  $\Psi$  given by
\[
\sum_{i=0}^n a_i x^i\mapsto\sum_{i=0}^n a_i x^{p^i}.
\]
By the same argument as Lemma 1,  $\tilde{\Psi}$  is an isomorphism.**Lemma 2.** For  $f\in\overline{R}$  and all  $a,b\in\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$  and  $c\in\mathbb{F}_p$ , we have
[list=i]
- $f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)$ ,
- $f(ca)=cf(a)$ .
[/list]
*Proof.* The first part follows directly from freshman's dream. For the second part, note that  $c^{p^\alpha}=c$  for all  $a\in\mathbb{N}$  by FlT. The result immediately follows.  $\square$ **Lemma 3.** All  $f\in\overline{R}$  (viewed as a polynomial in  $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}[x]$ ) is separable.

*Proof.* The formal derivative of  $f$  is equal to the coefficient of  $x$  in  $f$ , which is in  $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$ . Thus the formal derivative of  $f$  is relatively prime with  $f$  so  $f$  is separable.  $\square$ For  $f\in\overline{R}$ , let
\[
Z(f):=\{r\in\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}\mid f(r)=0\}
\]
denote the set of roots of  $f$ . By Lemma 3, all the roots of  $f$  have multiplicity  $1$ . It follows that
\[
f(x)=\prod_{r\in Z(f)}(x-r).
\]**Lemma 4.** For all  $f\in\overline{R}$ ,  $Z(f)$  forms a vector space over  $\mathbb{F}_p$ , with addition and multiplication the same as that of  $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$ .

*Proof.* We first prove that  $Z(f)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$  is an abelian group:
[list]
- If  $r_1,r_2\in Z(f)$ , then  $f(r_1+r_2)=f(r_1)+f(r_2)=0$  by Lemma 2 so  $r_1+r_2\in Z(f)$ .
- $Z(f)$  is commutative because the additive group of  $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$  is abelian.
- $f(0)=0$  because  $f$  has no constant term. Thus  $0\in Z(f)$ .
- If  $r\in Z(f)$ , then  $f(-r)=-f(r)=0$  by Lemma 2 so  $-r\in Z(f)$ .

For all  $c\in\mathbb{F}_p$  and  $r\in Z(f)$ , we have  $f(cr)=cf(r)=0$  by Lemma 2 so  $cr\in Z(f)$ . Thus  $Z(f)$  is a vector space over  $\mathbb{F}_p$ .  $\square$ [rule]
From now on, " $=$ " will denote equality up to multiplication by a unit of  $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}[x]$ .**Lemma 5.** If  $F,G\in\overline{R},H\in\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}[x]$  and  $F(x)=H(G(x))$ , then  $H\in\overline{R}$ .

*Proof.* Assume for the sake of contradiction  $H\not\in\overline{R}$ . Then  $H$  has a  $cx^\alpha$  term where  $\alpha$  is not a power of  $p$ . Take the minimum such  $\alpha$ . Let
\[
G(x)=:a_nx^{p^n}+a_{n-1}x^{p^{n-1}}+\cdots+a_0x.
\]
Clearly the  $x^\alpha$  term of  $H(G(x))$  appears only in  $c(G(x))^\alpha$ , so it has coefficient  $ca_0^\alpha\neq 0$ . This implies that  $F$  has an  $x^\alpha$  term, a contradiction.  $\square$ **Lemma 6.** For nonzero polynomials  $F,G\in\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}[x]$ , we have  $G\mid F$  if and only if  $\tilde{\Psi}(G)\mid\tilde{\Psi}(F)$ .

*Proof.* Suppose  $F=HG$  for some  $H\in\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}[x]$ . Then  $\tilde{\Psi}(F)=\tilde{\Psi}(H)\circ\tilde{\Psi}(G)$ . Since  $\tilde{\Psi}(H)$  has no constant term, it follows that  $\tilde{\Psi}(G)\mid\tilde{\Psi}(F)$ .

Now let  $P:=\tilde{\Psi}(F)$  and  $Q:=\tilde{\Psi}(G)$ , and suppose  $Q\mid P$ . Then  $Z(Q)$  is a subspace of  $Z(P)$ . Let  $\alpha:=\dim Z(P)$  and  $\beta:=\dim Z(Q)$ . Let  $e_1,\ldots,e_\beta$  be a basis for  $Z(Q)$  and extend it to a basis  $e_1,\ldots,e_\alpha$  for  $Z(P)$ . We have
\begin{align*}
P(x)&=\prod_{r\in Z(P)}(x-r)
&=\prod_{c_1,\ldots,c_\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_p}\left(x-\sum_{i=1}^\alpha c_ie_i\right)
&=\prod_{c_{\beta+1},\ldots,c_\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_p}\prod_{c_1,\ldots,c_\beta\in\mathbb{F}_p}\left(\left(x-\sum_{i=\beta+1}^\alpha c_ie_i\right)-\sum_{j=1}^\beta c_je_j\right)
&=\prod_{c_{\beta+1},\ldots,c_\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_p}Q\left(x-\sum_{i=\beta+1}^\alpha c_ie_i\right)
&=\prod_{c_{\beta+1},\ldots,c_\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_p}\left(Q(x)-\sum_{i=\beta+1}^\alpha c_i Q(e_i)\right)
&=A(Q(x))
\end{align*}
where
\[
A(x):=\prod_{c_{\beta+1},\ldots,c_\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_p}\left(x-\sum_{i=\beta+1}^\alpha c_i Q(e_i)\right).
\]
By Lemma 5,  $A\in\overline{R}$  so  $P=A\circ Q$ . It follows that  $F=\tilde{\Psi}^{-1}(A)\cdot G$  so  $G\mid F$ , as desired.  $\square$ **Lemma 7.** Let  $\mathbb{F}$  be an algebraic extension of  $\mathbb{F}_p$ . For nonzero polynomials  $F,G\in\mathbb{F}[x]$ , we have  $G\mid F$  if and only if  $\tilde{\Psi}(G)\mid\tilde{\Psi}(F)$  (where divisibility is taken in  $\mathbb{F}[x]$ ).

*Proof.* Since  $\mathbb{F}$  is an algebraic extension, it is a subfield of  $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$ . Suppose  $F=HG$  for some  $H\in\mathbb{F}[x]$ . Then  $\tilde{\Psi}(F)=\tilde{\Psi}(H)\circ\tilde{\Psi}(G)$ . Since  $\tilde{\Psi}(H)$  has no constant term, it follows that  $\tilde{\Psi}(G)\mid\tilde{\Psi}(F)$ .

If  $\tilde{\Psi}(G)\mid\tilde{\Psi}(F)$ , by Lemma 6 we have  $F=GH$  for some  $H\in\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}[x]$ . Let
\begin{align*}
F(x)&=:a_\alpha x^\alpha+\cdots+a_0
G(x)&=:b_\beta x^\beta+\cdots+b_0
H(x)&=:c_\gamma x^\gamma+\cdots+c_0.
\end{align*}
Then  $a_0=b_0c_0$  so  $c_0\in\mathbb{F}$ . Assume we already have  $c_0,\ldots,c_i\in\mathbb{F}$ . Then
\[
b_{i+1}c_0+b_ic_1+\cdots+b_1c_i+b_0c_{i+1}=a_{i+1}\in\mathbb{F}
\]
(where we set  $b_{\beta+1},\ldots$  equal to  $0$ ) so  $c_{i+1}\in\mathbb{F}$ . Thus  $H\in\mathbb{F}[x]$  as desired.  $\square$ Let  $K$  be an algebraic extension of  $\mathbb{F}_p$  (for the problem just take  $K:=\mathbb{F}_p$ ). <details><summary>Solution</summary>Lemma 1: Let  $\omega$  be an algebraic integer such that its minimal polynomial has degree  $n$ . Then,  $\omega,\omega^p,\omega^{p^2},\ldots,\omega^{p^{n-1}}$  are the roots of its minimal polynomial.

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Let the minimal polynomial of  $\omega$  be  $P(x)=a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\ldots+a_1x+a_0$ . Then, note that  $P\left(\omega^{p^m}\right)=a_n\omega^{np^m}+a_{n-1}\omega^{(n-1)p^m}+\ldots+a_1\omega^{p^m}+a_0=(a_n\omega^n+a_{n-1}\omega^{n-1}+\ldots+a_1\omega+a_0)^{p^m}=0$  because  $(a+b)^p=a^p+b^p$  in  $\mathbb{F}_p$ .

Furthermore, the numbers  $\omega,\omega^p,\omega^{p^2},\ldots,\omega^{p^n}$  are all distinct. If we had  $\omega^{p^i}=\omega^{p^j}$  with  $m>i>j\geq0$ , then  $\omega^{p^{i-j}}=\omega$ , which implies that  $\omega$  is an element of  $\mathbb{F}_{p^{i-j}}$ , a contradiction since the splitting field of  $\omega$  is  $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ .</details>

Given an irreducible polynomial  $P$  with degree  $n$ , let its roots be  $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$ , where  $a_{i+1}=a_i^p$  and  $a_{i+n}=a_i$  for all  $i$ . Define the sequence  $\{a_i\}$  as the root sequence of  $P$ .

Lemma 2: An irreducible polynomial divides  $\Psi(F)$  if and only if its root sequence satisfies the linear recursion with characteristic polynomial  $F$ .

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Let the root sequence be  $a_1,a_2,\ldots$  and let  $F(x)=f_0+f_1x+f_2x^2+\ldots+f_kx^k$ . We have that  $a_i$  is a root of  $\Psi(F)$  if and only if  $\Psi(F)(a_i)=f_0a_i+f_1a_i^p+f_2a_i^{p^2}+\ldots+f_ka_i^{p^k}=0$ . Since  $a_{i}^{p^m}=a_{i+m}$  by Lemma 1, this is equivalent to  $f_0a_i+f_1a_{i+1}+f_2a_{i+2}+\ldots+f_ka_{i+k}=0$ . This is the linear recurrence with characteristic polynomial  $P$ , so the lemma is proven.</details>

By Lemma 2, an irreducible polynomial divides both  $\Psi(F)$  and  $\Psi(G)$  if and only if its root sequence satisfies both the linear recurrence with characteristic polynomial  $F$  and the linear recurrence with characteristic polynomial  $G$ . It is well known that a sequence satisfies both of these recurrences if and only if it satisfies the linear recurrence with characteristic polynomial  $\gcd(F,G)$ . This is equivalent to the polynomial dividing  $\Psi(\gcd(F,G))$  by Lemma 2, so we are done.</details>

<details><summary>An ounce of linear algebra</summary>Define the (well-known to be) linear map  $T:\mathbb{F}_p[x]\to \mathbb{F}_p[x]$  by  $T(P(x))=P(x)^p$ , and let  $T^0:=\text{id}$ ,  $T_{k+1}=T_k\circ T$  ( $k\ge 0$ ). 

For any polynomial  $F(x)=\sum a_kx^k$ , define the linear map  $\Phi(F)=\sum a_k T^k$ . Moreover, for any  $P\in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$  and  $S:\mathbb{F}_p[x]\to \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ , define the polynomial  $\text{Ev}_P S:=S(P)$ . Say that  $P\sim Q$  if they are constant multiples of each other.

Note that  $\Phi$  and  $\text{Ev}_P$  are both linear maps, and  $\Phi(F\cdot G)=\Phi(F)\circ \Phi(G)$  (trivial if  $F(x)=x^k$  because  $T^k$  is linear, and for  $F(x)=\sum x^k$ , it is a linear combination of these trivial statements). It follows that 
\[
\text{Ev}_P\Phi(F\cdot G)=\Phi(F)\big(\text{Ev}_P\Phi(G)\big).\eqno(1)
\]
Moreover, we will finish off by using the fact  $(2)$  that  $F$  divides  $\text{Ev}_F(\Phi(G))$  for any  $F,G\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ , which is clear from definition. $ $ I will prove that for any  $P,F,G\in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ , we have
\[
\text{Ev}_P \Phi(\gcd(F,G))\sim\gcd\Big(\text{Ev}_P\Phi(F),\text{Ev}_P\Phi(G)\Big).\eqno(3)
\]
The problem statement is a special case of this, as  $\Psi(F)=\text{Ev}_x\Phi(F)$ . Then, the two sides are equal, as the leading coefficients equate.

Putting  $\gcd(F,G)=D$ , and  $F=DA$ ,  $G=DB$ , we can use  $(1)$  to make  $(3)$  become
\[
\text{Ev}_P\Phi(D)\sim\gcd\Big(\Phi(A)\big(\text{Ev}_P\Phi(D)\big),\Phi(B)\big(\text{Ev}_P\Phi(D)\big)\Big),
\]
so if we let  $H=\text{Ev}_P\Phi(D)$ , it remains to show
\[
H\sim \gcd(\text{Ev}_H\Phi(A),\text{Ev}_H\Phi(B)),\eqno(4)
\]
where  $1=U\cdot A+V\cdot B$  by Bézout for some  $U,V\in\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ .

Here,  $(2)$  immediately shows that the LHS of  $(4)$  divides its RHS. In fact,  $(2)$  also tells us that  $\text{Ev}_H\Phi(A)$  divides
\[
\Phi(U)(\text{Ev}_H(\Phi(A)))=\text{Ev}_H(\Phi(U)\circ \Phi(A))=\text{Ev}_H(\Phi(U\cdot A)),
\]
and from this and the similar relation for  $B$ , we extract that  $\gcd(\text{Ev}_H\Phi(A),\text{Ev}_H\Phi(B))$  divides
\[
\text{Ev}_H(\Phi(U\cdot A))+\text{Ev}_H(\Phi(V\cdot B))=\text{Ev}_H(\Phi(U\cdot A+V\cdot B))=\text{Ev}_H(\Phi(1))=\text{Ev}_H(\text{id})=H,
\]
so the RHS divides the LHS as well. This establishes  $(4)$ , and so  $(3)$  is proven, and we are done.</details>

\]Now, let  $H' = \gcd(\Psi(F'), \Psi(G'))$ , and we have  $H'\mid \Psi(F')\mid \Psi(A)\circ \Psi(F')$  and  $H'\mid \Psi(B)\circ\Psi(G')$ , so  $H\mid x$  as well; thus  $H' = x$  and we are done.  $\blacksquare$

Let  $\Phi:\mathbb{F}_p[X]\to\mathbb{F}_p[Y]$  be given by
\[\Phi\left(\sum_{i=0}^n a_iX^i\right) = \sum_{i=0}^n a_iY^{1+p+p^2+\cdots+p^{i-1}}.\]
For example,  $\Phi(X^2+X+1)=Y^{p+1}+Y+1$ . Note that
\[\Psi(F)(X)=X\Phi(F)(X^{p-1}).\]
The crux of the solution is lemma 2 below, but we need lemma 1 as a prerequisite..

<u>Lemma 1:</u> Suppose  $P\in\mathbb{F}_p[Y]$ . Then  $P(Y^{p^k})=P(Y)^{p^k}$ .

<u>Proof of Lemma 1:</u> It's clear we can show the lemma for  $k=1$ , and the other  $k$  follow by repition of the  $k=1$  case. This is the lemma that utilizes the fact that we are working mod  $p$ . Suppose
\[P(Y)=\sum_{i=0}^np_iY^i.\]
Then,
\[P(Y)^p=\sum_{a_0+\cdots+a_n=r}\frac{p!}{a_0!a_1!\cdots a_n!}p_{a_0}\cdots p_{a_n}Y^p.\]
But if at least two of  $a_0,\ldots,a_n$  are nonzero, then  $\frac{p!}{a_0!a_1!\cdots a_n!}\equiv 0\pmod{p}$ , so the lemma is proved.  $\blacksquare$ <u>Lemma 2:</u> Suppose  $A,F\in\mathbb{F}_p[X]$ . There exists a polynomial  $\bar{A}\in\mathbb{F}_p[Y]$  such that
\[\Phi(A\cdot F)=\bar{A}\cdot\Phi(F).\]

<u>Proof of Lemma 2:</u> For brevity, let  $\bar{F}=\Phi(F)$ . Suppose
\[A(X)=\sum_{i=0}^na_iX^i\]
and
\[F(X)=\sum_{i=0}^mf_iX^i.\]
Let
\[\bar{A}(Y):=\sum_{i=0}^n a_iY^{1+p+\cdots+p^{i-1}}\bar{F}(Y)^{p^i-1}.\]
Then, we have that
\begin{align*}
\bar{A}(Y)\bar{F}(Y)&=\sum_{i=0}^n a_i Y^{1+p+\cdots+p^{i-1}}\bar{F}(Y)^{p^i} 
&= \sum_{i=0}^n a_i Y^{1+p+\cdots+p^{i-1}}\bar{F}(Y^{p^i}) 
&= \sum_{i=0}^n a_i Y^{1+p+\cdots+p^{i-1}}\sum_{j=0}^m f_j Y^{(1+p+\cdots+p^{i-1})p^j} 
&= \sum_{i=0}^n\sum_{j=0}^m a_if_j Y^{1+p+\cdots+p^{i+j-1}} 
&= \Phi(A\cdot F)(Y),
\end{align*}
as desired.  $\blacksquare$ Suppose  $\gcd(F,G)=H$ . We see that  $\Phi(H)\mid\Phi(F)$  by lemma 2, so  $\Psi(H)\mid\Psi(F)$ , and similarly  $\Psi(H)\mid\Psi(G)$ . Therefore,  $\Psi(H)\mid\gcd(\Psi(F),\Psi(G))$ . If we showed that there were  $A',B'\in\mathbb{F}_P[X]$  so that
\[\Psi(H)=A'\Psi(F)+B'\Psi(G),\]
then we'd be done (because this would imply  $\gcd(\Psi(F),\Psi(G))\mid\Psi(H)$ , and we already have  $\Psi(H)\mid\gcd(\Psi(F),\Psi(G))$ ).

Suppose  $H(X)=A(X)F(X)+B(X)G(X)$ . Then, construct  $\bar{A},\bar{B}\in\mathbb{F}_p[Y]$  according to lemma 2. Thus,
\[\Phi(H)=\Phi(A\cdot F)+\Phi(B\cdot G)=\bar{A}\cdot\Phi(F)+\bar{B}\cdot\Phi(G).\]
Let  $A'(X)=\bar{A}(X^{p-1})$  and  $B'(X)=\bar{B}(X^{p-1})$ . Thus,
\[\Psi(H)(X)=X\Phi(H)(X^{p-1})=A'(X)\Psi(F)(X)+B'(X)\Psi(G)(X),\]
so  $\gcd(\Psi(F),\Psi(G))=\Psi(H)$ , as desired.  $\square$

Even though I love geometry, I found this problem to be the easiest USA TST P3 that I have tried till now. Weird ;). Anyway, I'll provide my solution (which I guess is nothing new for this forum, but still :D): I don't like  $F$  and  $G$  so I'll use  $P$  and  $Q$ . First of all a trivial observation (proof's not included obviously)-**OBSERVATION**  $\Psi(P+Q)=\Psi(P)+\Psi(Q)$ . In particular,  $\Psi(aP)=a\Psi(P)$ , where  $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ .

Now, for some serious claims, which will help us conquer the problem. But before that a well-known lemma which we'll require later on-**LEMMA** Let  $a_1,a_2, \dots ,a_n$  be  $n$  integers and  $p$  be a prime. Then   $$ (a_1+a_2+ \dots +a_n)^p \equiv a_1^p+a_2^p+ \dots +a_n^p \pmod{p} $$  *<u>Proof of Lemma</u>* The proof proceeds by induction on  $n$ . For  $n=2$ , we just need to apply binomial theorem on the LHS, and use the fact that  $p \mid \binom{p}{i}$  for  $i \in \{1,2, \dots ,p-1\}$ . Then the inductive step is fairly simple to use.  $\Box$ **CLAIM 1**  $\Psi(P) \mid \Psi(Px^m)$  for all  $m \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ .

*<u>Proof of Claim 1</u>* Let  $P(x)=a_0+a_1x+ \dots +a_nx^n$ . Then   $$ \Psi(Px^m)=\Psi(a_0x^m+a_1x^{m+1}+ \dots +a_nx^{m+n})=a_0x^{p^m}+a_1x^{p^{m+1}}+ \dots +a_mx^{p^{m+n}} $$  Now, By Fermat's Little Theorem, and using the fact that  $\gcd(a_i,p)=1$  for all  $i \in \{0,1, \dots ,n\}$  as  $a_i \in \mathbb{F}_p$ , we have that   $$ a_i \equiv a_i^{p^m} \pmod{p} \quad \forall i \in \{0,1, \dots ,n\} $$  Using the above equality, and working in  $\mathbb{F}_p$ , we have   $$ \Psi(Px^m)=\sum_{i=0}^n \left(a_ix^{p^i} \right)^{p^m} \overset{\text{LEMMA}}{\Longrightarrow} \Psi(Px^m)=\left(\sum_{i=0}^n a_ix^{p^i} \right)^{p^m}=(\Psi(P))^{p^m} \Rightarrow \Psi(P) \mid \Psi(Px^m) \quad \Box $$  **CLAIM 2** (Key Claim)  $\Psi(P) \mid \Psi(PQ)$  for all  $P,Q \in \mathbb F_p[x]$ .

*<u>Proof of Claim 2</u>* Let  $Q(x)=b_0+b_1x+ \dots +b_kx^k$ . Then using our initial observation, we have   $$ \Psi(PQ)=\Psi(b_0P+b_1xP+ \dots +b_kx^kP)=b_0\Psi(P)+b_1 \Psi(Px)+ \dots b_k \Psi(Px^k) \overset{\text{CLAIM 1}}{\Longrightarrow} \Psi(P) \mid \Psi(PQ) \quad \Box $$  --------
Return to the problem at hand. Let  $\gcd(P,Q)=R$ . Then, by Claim 2,  $\Psi(R) \mid \Psi(P)$  and  $\Psi(R) \mid \Psi(Q)$ , which together gives that  $\Psi(R) \mid \gcd(\Psi(P),\Psi(Q))$ . 

Now, By Bezout's Identity, we can write  $R=AP+BQ$  for polynomials  $A,B \in \mathbb F_p[x]$ . Then, using our observation once again, we get that   $$ \Psi(R)=\Psi(AP+BQ)=\Psi(AP)+\Psi(BQ) \overset{\text{CLAIM 2}}{\Longrightarrow} \Psi(R)=C\Psi(P)+D\Psi(Q) \text{ for some polynomials } C,D \in \mathbb F_p[x] $$  But this means (again by Bezout's Identity) that  $\gcd(\Psi(P),\Psi(Q)) \mid \Psi(R)$ . Thus, we have   $$ \gcd(\Psi(P),\Psi(Q))=\Psi(R)=\Psi(\gcd(P,Q)) \quad \blacksquare $$

**Claim 1:**  $\left(\sum_{i = 1}^n a_i\right)^p = \sum_{i = 1}^n a_i^p$  for  $a_i \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ .
*Proof.*  $p \left| \binom{p}{k}\right.$  for all  $1 \le k < p$  since no number in the denominator is divisible by  $p$ .
\begin{align*}
\left(\sum_{i = i}^n a_i\right)^p = \left(a_n + \sum_{i = 1}^{n - 1} a_i\right)^p &= a_n^p + \sum_{k = 1}^{p - 1} \binom{p}{k} a_n^k \left(\sum_{i = 1} a_i\right)^{p - k} + \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{n - 1} a_i\right)^{p}
&=  a_n^p + \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{n-1} a_i\right)^{p} = \cdots = \sum_{i = 1}^n a_i^p\qquad\qquad\qquad\square
\end{align*}

Let  $\circ$  refer to composition of functions.
Let  $\mathbb{S}$  be the image of  $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$  under  $\Psi$ .**Claim 2:**  $(\mathbb{S}, +, \circ)$  is a ring.
*Proof.* Clearly  $S$  is closed under addition.
Let  $P(x) = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i x^{p^i}$  and  $Q(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i x^{p^i}$ \[(Q(x))^{p^j} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i x^{p^i}\right)^{p^j} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^{p} x^{p^{i + 1}}\right)^{p^{j - 1}} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i x^{p^{i + 1}}\right)^{p^{j - 1}} = \cdots = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i x^{p^{i + j}} \]
\[(P\circ Q)(x) = P(Q(x)) = \sum_{j = 1}^m a_j (Q(x))^{p^j} = \sum_{j = 1}^m \sum_{i=1}^n a_j b_i x^{p^{i + j}} \in \mathbb{S}\]
Thus  $\mathbb{S}$  is closed under composition.
Clearly both the identities are present in  $\mathbb{S}$  and additive inverse is present in  $\mathbb{S}$ .
Thus,  $(\mathbb{S}, +, \circ)$  is a ring.  $\square$ It's well-known that  $(\mathbb{F}_p[x], +, \times)$  is a ring.

We'll call the rings  $\mathbb{S}$  and  $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ .**Claim 3:**  $\mathbb{F}_p[x] \cong \mathbb{S}$  with  $\Psi$  as the isomorphism.
*Proof.* It's trivial to prove that  $\Psi$  distributes over  $+$  and is bijective.
Multiplicative identity of  $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$  is  $1$  and that of  $S$  is  $P(x) = x$ . So clearly  $\Psi(1) = x$ .
Now from the proof of claim 2 we know that for  $P(x) = \sum_{i = 1}^m a_i x^{i}$  and  $Q(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i x^{i}$ ,
\[(\Psi (P) \circ \Psi (Q))(x) = \sum_{i = 1}^m \sum_{j =1}^n a_i b_j x^{p^{i + j}} = \Psi\left(\sum_{i = 1}^m \sum_{j =1}^n a_i b_j x^{i + j}\right) = \Psi\left(P(x) \times Q(x)\right).\]
Thus,  $\Psi$  is an isomorphism from  $\mathbb{F}_p[x] \to \mathbb{S}$ .  $\square$ **Claim 4:** If  $P, Q \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$  such that  $Q | P$ , then  $\Psi(Q) | \Psi(P)$ .
*Proof.* Let  $P = QR$ . Since  $x | T(x)$  for all  $T \in \mathbb{S}$ , replacing  $T$  with  $\Psi(R)$  and  $x$  with  $\Psi(Q)$ .
\[\Psi(Q) | \Psi R (\Psi Q) =  (\Psi R) \circ (\Psi Q) = \Psi(RQ) = \Psi(P).\qquad \square\]**Claim 5:**  $\Psi(\gcd(P, Q)) | \gcd(\Psi(P), \Psi(Q))$  for all  $P, Q \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ .
*Proof.* \[\left.\begin{cases} \gcd(P, Q) | P \gcd(P, Q) | Q \end{cases}\hspace{-1em}\right\} \implies \left.\begin{cases} \Psi(\gcd(P, Q)) | \Psi(P) \Psi(\gcd(P, Q)) | \Psi(Q) \end{cases}\hspace{-1em}\right\} \implies \Psi(\gcd(P, Q)) | \gcd(\Psi(P), \Psi(Q)) \qquad\square\]**Claim 6:**  $\gcd(\Psi(P), \Psi(Q)) | \Psi(\gcd(P, Q))$  for all  $P, Q \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ .
*Proof.* Let  $\gcd(P, Q) = PX +  QY$  for  $X, Y \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$  by Bezout's Identity for polynomials.
Now,
\[\Psi(\gcd(P, Q))  = \Psi(PX + QY) = \Psi(PX) + \Psi(QY)\]
Since  $P|PX$  and  $Q|QY$ ,  $\Psi(P)|\Psi(PX)$  and  $\Psi(Q)|\Psi(QY)$ .
Therefore
\[\gcd(\Psi(P), \Psi(Q))| \Psi(PX) + \Psi(QY)\]
as desired.  $\square$ Combining claim 5 and 6, we get the desired result,
\[\gcd(\Psi(P), \Psi(Q)) = \Psi(\gcd(P, Q))\]
for all  $P, Q \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ .

For an  $A \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ , let  $f_A(x)$  denote the polynomial  $\Psi(A)$ . Observe that  $\Psi(kA) = k\Psi(A)$  for a constant  $k$  and  $\Psi(A+B) = \Psi(A) + \Psi(B).$ **Lemma:** $f_{AB}(x) = f_A(f_B(x))$ .
<details><summary>Proof</summary>We'll first prove it for  $A(x) = x^k$ , for which  $f_A(x) = x^{p^k}$ . Then if  $B(x) = \sum b_ix^i$  we have
\[f_{x^kB} = \Psi \left( \sum b_ix^{i+k} \right) = \sum \left(b_ix^{p^i} \right)^{p^k}= \left( \sum b_ix^{p^i} \right)^{p^k} = f_{x^k}(f_B(x)),\]as desired. Now consider the general case  $A(x) = \sum a_ix^i$  and write
\begin{align*}
f_{AB} &= \Psi \left( \left(\sum a_ix^i \right) B(x)\right)
&=\sum a_i\Psi \left( x^i  B(x)\right)
&=\sum a_i(f_B(x))^{p^i} 
&=f_A(f_B(x)),
\end{align*}
as desired.</details>**Lemma:**Let  $d(x)$  be a monic polynomial. Then for relatively prime polynomials  $A, B$  we have
\[\gcd(f_A(d), f_B(d)) = d. \]
<details><summary>Proof</summary>We strong induct on  $\deg A + \deg B$ . If  $A$  and  $B$  are both constant, then this is clear. The inductive step proceeds as follows: WLOG  $\deg A - \deg B = k \ge 0$ . As  $\gcd(A-x^kB, B) = \gcd(A, B)=1$ , by hypothesis we have
\[\gcd(f_{A-x^kB}(d), f_B(d)) =d.\]
But we also have
\begin{align*}
\gcd(f_{A-x^kB}(d), f_B(d)) &= \gcd(f_{A}(d)-f_{x^kB}(d), f_B(d))
&=\gcd(f_{A}(d)-f_B(d)^{p^k}, f_B(d))
&=\gcd(f_A(d), f_B(d))
\end{align*}
so the induction is complete.</details>

To finish, let  $d = \gcd(F, G)$  and write  $\gcd(\Psi(F), \Psi(G)) = \gcd( f_{F/d}(f_d), f_{G/d}(f_d))$  by the first lemma. Then apply the second lemma to get that this  $\gcd$  is just  $f_d=\Psi(\gcd(F, G))$ .  $\blacksquare$

Note that $\Psi(P+Q)=\Psi(P)+\Psi(Q)$ and $\Psi(kP)=k\Psi(P)$ . **Lemma:** For $P\in\mathbb F_p[x]$ and $k\in\mathbb Z$ , we have $\Psi(Px^k)=\Psi(P)^{p^k}$ . *Proof.* Let $\textstyle P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^na_ix^i$ . Write \[\Psi(Px^k)=\Psi\left(\sum_{i=0}^na_ix^{i+k}\right)=\sum_{i=0}^na_i\left(x^{p^i}\right)^{p^k}=\left(\sum_{i=0}^na_ix^{p^i}\right)^{p^k}=\Psi(P)^{p^k},\] where the third equality is by Frobenius. $\blacksquare$ **Lemma:** For $P,Q\in\mathbb F_p[x]$ , if $P\mid Q$ , then $\Psi(P)\mid\Psi(Q)$ . *Proof.* Let $Q=PR$ and $\textstyle R=\sum_{i=0}^na_ix^i$ . Then \[\Psi(Q)=\Psi\left(P\sum_{i=0}^na_ix^i\right)=\sum_{i=0}^na_i\Psi(Px^i)=\sum_{i=0}^na_i\Psi(P)^{p^i},\] which is divisible by $\Psi(P)$ . $\blacksquare$ Let $H=\gcd(F,G)$ and $I=\gcd(\Psi(F),\Psi(G))$ , so it suffices to prove $\Psi(H)=I$ . Note the following: - By the above lemma, we have $\Psi(H)\mid\Psi(F)$ and $\Psi(H)\mid\Psi(G)$ , so $\Psi(H)\mid I$ . - Let $H=AF+BG$ for $A,B\in\mathbb F_p[x]$ by B\'ezout's lemma. We have $I\mid\Psi(F)\mid\Psi(AF)$ and $I\mid\Psi(G)\mid\Psi(BG)$ , so $I\mid\Psi(AF)+\Psi(BG)=\Psi(H)$ . The conclusion follows.

Take some three polynomials  $P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_ix^i$ ,  $Q(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}b_ix^i$  and  $R(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}c_ix^i$ , where coefficients are zero if large enough for simplicity

We have  $\Psi(PQ) = \Psi(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_ib_jx^{i+j}) = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_ib_jx^{p^{i+j}}$ , now notice  $\Psi(P+Q)=\Psi(P)+\Psi(Q)$  and the main claim:  $$ gcd(\Psi(PQ), \Psi(PR)) = gcd(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_ib_jx^{p^{i+j}}, \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_ic_jx^{p^{i+j}}) = $$    $$ = gcd(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_i(b_j-c_j)x^{p^{i+j}}, \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_ic_jx^{p^{i+j}}) = gcd(\Psi(P(Q-R)), \Psi(PR)) $$  This follows from  $gcd(X,Y)=gcd(X-Y,Y)$ , the standard number theory lemma but for polynomials. Keep repeating the main result above,  $gcd(\Psi(PQ), \Psi(PR))=gcd(\Psi(P(Q-R)), \Psi(PR))$ , and by the Euclidian algorithm we arrive at  $gcd(\Psi(F),\Psi(G)) = gcd(\Psi(P), \Psi(0)) = \Psi(P) = \Psi(gcd(F,G)) \implies gcd(\Psi(F),\Psi(G)) = \Psi(gcd(F,G))$ , which we wanted to prove  $\blacksquare$ EDIT: Am I mistaken or does this method generalize from  $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$  to  $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ ?

First, we claim that  $a_1^p+a_2^p+\ldots +a_n^p$  leaves a remainder with all terms divisible by  $p$  when divided by  $a_1+\ldots +a_n$ . We prove this with induction on  $n$ . For  $n=2$ , the claim is trivial as  $a_1+a_2|a_1^p+a_2^p$ . Now, suppose the claim is true for  $n-1$ . Now,   $$ a_1^p+a_2^p+\ldots+a_n^p=(a_1^p+\ldots + a_{n-2}^p+(a_{n-1}+a_n)^p)-\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}a_{n-1}^ia_n^{p-i}\binom{p}{i} $$  For the first term, we are guaranteed a remainder divisible by  $p$  by induction. On the other hand, for the latter term,  $\binom{p}{i}$  is always divisible by  $p$ , so of course, subtracting it will preserve the fact that the remainder has all coefficients divisible by  $p$ , as desired.

Now, note that if  $P(x)=a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\ldots + a_0$ , then  $\Psi(P(x))=a_nx^{p^n}+\ldots +a_0x^{p^0}$  and  $\Psi(xP(x))=\left(a_nx^{p^n}\right)^p+\ldots +\left(a_0x^{p^0}\right)^p$  as  $a^p\equiv a\pmod p$ . Now, using our claims, the remainder when  $\Psi(xP(x))$  is divided by  $\Psi(P(x))$  has all terms divisible by  $p$ , and since we are working in  $\mathbb{F}_p$ , this means  $\Psi(P(x))|\Psi(xP(x))$ . Using induction, this gives  $\Psi(P(x))|\Psi(x^kP(x))$ , and since  $\Psi$  is additive, we get  $\Psi(P(x))|\Psi(Q(x))$  whenver  $P|Q$ .

To finish, we just use the Euclidean Algorithm. We have that  $\gcd(\Psi(P(x)),\Psi(Q(x)))=\gcd(\Psi(P(x)),\Psi(Q(x)-R(x)P(x)))$  by properties of  $\gcd$ , additivity of  $\Psi$ , and the fact that  $\Psi(P(x))|\Psi(P(x)R(x))$ , so applying normal Euclidean algorithm gives   $$ \gcd(\Psi(P(x)),\Psi(Q(x)))=\gcd(\Psi(\gcd(P(x),Q(x))),\Psi(\gcd(P(x),Q(x))))=\Psi(\gcd(P(x),Q(x))) $$   as desired.

We have the three following key properties:


- $\Psi(f+g)=\Psi(f)+\Psi(g)$ . This is obvious.
- $c\Psi(f)=\Psi(cf)$ , where  $c \in \mathbb{F}_p$ . This is clear because  $c^p=c$  in  $\mathbb{F}_p$ .
- $\Psi(f)^p=\Psi(\mathrm{id}\cdot f)$  (as a polynomial equality). This is because if  $f(x)=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0$ , then both sides are equal to  $a_nx^{p^{n+1}}+\cdots+a_0x^{p^1}$ , since for any  $a \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$  we have  $a(x^p)=a(x)^p$ .


Now we will essentially apply the Euclidean algorithm to  $\Psi(\gcd(F,G))$  and essentially show that the same thing works on  $\gcd(\Psi(F),\Psi(G))$ . Indeed, WLOG let  $\deg F>\deg G$  select  $c \in \mathbb{F}_p$  and  $k\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$  such that  $$ \deg F-cx^kG < \deg F, $$  so  $$ \Psi(\gcd(F(x),G(x)))=\Psi(\gcd(F(x)-cx^kG(x),G(x))) $$  Likewise, we have  $$ \gcd(\Psi(F(x)),\Psi(G(x)))=\gcd(\Psi(F(x))-c\Psi(G(x))^{p^k},\Psi(G(x)))=\gcd(\Psi(F(x)-cx^kG(x)),\Psi(G(x))). $$  Thus by repeatedly doing this (which is just the Euclidean algorithm on  $F$  and  $G$ ), we reduce  $\Psi(\gcd(F,G))$  to  $\Psi(\gcd(H,H))=\Psi(H)$  where  $H=\gcd(F,G)$ . The same sequence of operations reduce  $\gcd(\Psi(F),\Psi(G))$  to  $\gcd(\Psi(H),\Psi(H))$ , which clearly equals  $\Psi(H)$  as well. Thus we are done.  $\blacksquare$ **Remark:** My initial solution to this was a bit different. Similarly to the third key property we may prove the more general statement that  $\Psi(fg)=\Psi(f)(\Psi(g))$  (if  $f \equiv \mathrm{id}$  we obtain the third key property). Then if  $F \equiv ab$  and  $G \equiv ac$  where  $b \perp c$ , we want to prove that  $\Psi(a)=\gcd(\Psi(ab),\Psi(ac))=\gcd(\Psi(b)(\Psi(a)),\Psi(c)(\Psi(a)))$ . From here the solution basically remains the same. The "necessity" of the third property or its generalization come from a need to find some property of  $\Psi$  which will connect it with  $\gcd$ .
It's a bit unclear how the third property actually relates to  $\gcd$ , but in its general form it seems much clearer, since  $\gcd$  is certainly related to products of polynomials. Indeed, from the general form it is essentially immediate that at the very least we have  $\Psi(a) \mid \gcd(\Psi(b)(\Psi(a)),\Psi(c)(\Psi(a)))$ , which indicates that this route should be pushed further.

Neat problem, the key idea is to inductively show that all pairs $(F(x), G(x))$ in $\mathbb{F}_p[x]^2$ work. For $(F, G) \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]^2$ , let \[ \alpha(F, G) = \begin{cases} 1 & (F, G) \ \text{works} 0 & (F, G) \ \text{does not work}. \end{cases} \] We say that $(F, G) \sim (H, K)$ if $\alpha(F, G)=1$ implies $\alpha(H, K)=1$ . **Lemma:** [Symmetry] We have $(F, G) \sim (G, F)$ . *Proof.* Note that $\gcd(F, G)$ is symmetric with respect to $F, G$ , so we are done. :yoda: The above lemma completes the proof of the fact that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation. **Lemma:** [Euclidean algorithm] We have $(F, G) \sim (F-G, G)$ , $(F, G) \sim (F+G, G)$ . *Proof.* This holds due to the linearity property of $\Psi$ . :yoda: **Lemma:** [Factoring monomials] We have $(F, G) \sim (xF, xG)$ . *Proof.* By definition, it can be easily seen that \begin{align*} \Psi(xF(x)) &= F(x^p) &= F(x)^p , \end{align*} from which the lemma follows (this is by the use of $\gcd$ on $p$ th powers of polynomials). :yoda: Now onto the hardest one. **Lemma:** [Factoring monomials from one term] If $x \nmid G$ , then $(F, G) \sim (xF, G)$ . *Proof.* As in the proof of the prior lemma, $\Psi(xF(x)) = \Psi(F)^p$ . Note that $\Psi(G)'(x)=G(0)$ for all $x$ must be nonzero, so $\Psi(G)$ must have no double root. Thus, $\gcd(\Psi(F)^p, \Psi(G)) = \gcd(\Psi(F), \Psi(G))$ , and we are done from our first observation. :yoda: Using the above lemmas, we can inductively show that $\alpha(F, G)=1$ for all $F, G$ by following an algorithm similar to that of the Euclidean Algorithm. We are done. :starwars:

The key is to offer the following characterization of $\Psi$ multiplicatively.**Claim.** We have $\Psi(fg) = \Psi(f) \circ \Psi(g)$ . *Proof.* It suffices to prove the monomial case $$ \Psi(x^n f(x)) = \Psi(f(x))^{p^n} $$ because $\Psi$ is additive. To see this, set $f(x) = pg(x) + h(x)$ in $\mathbb Z$ and apply the binomial theorem. $\blacksquare$ Now we obviously have $\Psi(\gcd(f, g)) \mid \gcd(\Psi(f), \Psi(g))$ because if $f \mid g$ , then $\Psi(f)\mid \Psi(g)$ . (This is because in the above expression, $\Psi$ has no constant term.) To show the other direction, use Bezout's lemma: there exists polynomials $a, b$ such that $$ af+bg = \gcd(f, g). $$ Taking $\Psi$ of both sides, $$ \Psi(f) \circ \Psi(a) + \Psi(g) \circ \Psi(b) = \Psi(\gcd(f, g)). $$ On the other hand, $\gcd(\Psi(f), \Psi(g))$ divides both terms on the LHS, so it divides the RHS too. Thus $\Psi(\gcd(f, g)) =\gcd(\Psi(f), \Psi(g))$ , as needed.

(USA Team Selection Test 2016) Let $\mathbb{F}_p$ denote the integers modulo a fixed prime $p$ . Define $\Psi \colon \mathbb{F}_p[x] \mapsto \mathbb{F}_p[x]$ by, \begin{align*} \Psi\left(\sum_{i = 0}^n a_ix^i\right) = \sum_{i = 0}^n a_ix^{p^i} \end{align*} Denote by $S$ the image of $\Psi$ . Show that, - $S$ is a ring with addition given by polynomial addition, and multiplication given by \textit{function composition}. - Prove that $\Psi \colon \mathbb{F}_p[x] \mapsto S$ is then a ring isomorphism. [/list]
We begin by characterizing $S$ ; Take two arbitrary elements in $S$ : \begin{align*} A = \sum_{i= 0}^{n} a_ix^{p^i} B = \sum_{i = 0}^n b_ix^{p_i} \end{align*} with some $a_i$ and $b_i$ possibly $0$ .**Claim:** $S$ is closed under addition. *Proof*. Simply note that, \begin{align*} A + B = \sum_{i = 0}^n (a_i + b_i)x^{p^i} = \sum_{i = 0}^n (a_i + b_i \bmod{p})x^{p^i} \in S \end{align*} Also, there is an additive identity, namely the $0$ polynomial. $\square$ **Claim:** $S$ obeys multiplication given by function composition. *Proof*. We first demonstrate $S$ obeys exponentiation by powers of $p$ . Then we wish to show that, \begin{align*} \left( \sum_{i = 0}^n a_ix^{p^i} \right)^p &\in S \end{align*} We are working with something of the form $(y_1 + y_2 + \dots + y_n)^p \equiv 0 \bmod{p}$ . Note that lower order terms not of the form $y_i^{p}$ die modulo $p$ ; to see this say that some term in our expansion is of the form, \begin{align*} \prod_{i = 0}^k y_i^{e_i} \end{align*} where we without loss of generality assume that the $k$ variables are $y_1$ , $y_2$ , and so on. The coefficient of this term is then, \begin{align*} \binom{p}{e_1} \cdot \binom{p - e_1}{e_2} \dots \end{align*} Clearly $p$ divides this coefficient, given that $e_1 < p$ , thus proving that these terms vanish. This in turn proves that $S$ behaves well under exponentiation by $p$ and in fact that, \begin{align*} \left( \sum_{i = 0}^n a_ix^{p^i} \right)^{p^t} &\in S \end{align*} lies in $S$ for any $t$ , by induction. Now to see that $S$ obeys function composition, simply take $A, B \in S$ and note, \begin{align*} A \circ B = \sum_{i = 0}^n a_iB^{p^i} \in S \end{align*} which is clearly in $S$ as $S$ is closed under exponentiation by powers of $p$ and addition. Moreover it clearly has identity element $x$ , is associative, and distributes over addition. $\square$ Therefore $S = (S, + , \circ)$ is a ring, finishing the first bullet. For the second bullet we wish to show that $\Psi \colon \mathbb{F}_p[x] \mapsto S$ is a ring isomorphism. Thus we wish to show $\Psi$ is a bijective map satisfying, [list] - $\Psi(x + y) = \Psi(x) + \Psi(y)$ - $\Psi(x \times y) = \Psi(x) \circ \Psi(y)$ - $\Psi(1) = x$ The first and last bullets follow easily from the definition of $\Psi$ , and so does the bijectivity of the map. It remains to verify the second bullet; namely we wish to show, \begin{align*} \Psi(AB) = \Psi(A) \circ \Psi(B) \end{align*} The right hand side clearly is just, \begin{align*} \sum_{i = 0}^n a_iB^{p^i} &= \sum_{i = 0}^n \left( a_i\left(\sum_{j = 0}^n b_jx^{p^{j + 1}} \right) \right) &= \sum_{i = 0}^n \left(\sum_{j = 0}^n a_ib_jx^{p^{i + j}} \right) \end{align*} whereas we may observe the left hand side is, \begin{align*} \Psi\left(\sum_{i = 0}^n a_ix^i \cdot B \right) &= \sum_{i = 0}^n \Psi(a_ix^i \cdot B) &= \sum_{i = 0}^n a_i \Psi\left(\sum_{j = 0}^n b_jx^{i + j}\right) &= \sum_{i = 0}^n \left(\sum_{j = 0}^n a_ib_jx^{p^{i + j}} \right) \end{align*} which are clearly equal. This finishes the problem.**Remarks:** Oops I got braindead and needed help on the last part (which was supposed to be easy :wacko: ).

All statements made in this solution are in $\mathbb F_p$ . Run two Euclidean algorithms in parallel! Ritwin writes two polynomials in $\mathbb F_p$ , $B$ and $C$ , on a whiteboard. Ivy writes $\Psi(B)$ and $\Psi(C)$ on the whiteboard. In each step, they select a nonnegative integer $k$ , and say Ritwin has $(R_1,R_2)$ and Ivy has $(I_1,I_2)$ written respectively. Then, Ritwin replaces $R_2$ with $R_2-x^kR_1$ (either that or replace $R_1$ with $R_1-x^kR_2$ ), and Ivy replaces $I_2$ with $I_2-I_1^{p^k}$ , (or other way, but using the same index as Ritwin). Claim: During every step of this process, we always have $I_1=\Psi(R_1)$ and $I_2=\Psi(R_2)$ . Use induction. This is clearly true at the start. Note that $$ \Psi(R_2-x^kR_1)=\Psi(R_2)-\Psi(x^kR_1)=I_2-\Psi(x^kR_1). $$ Now, we wish to show that $\Psi(x^kR_1)=\Psi(R_1)^{p^k}$ , to show that Ivy's new polynomial is still the $\Psi$ of Ritwin's new polynomial. However, if we shift all the exponents of $x$ up by $k$ before applying $\Psi$ , it multiplies every exponent later by $p^k$ due to the definition of $\Psi$ . However, on the RHS, raising the result of $\Phi(R_1)$ to the power of $p^k$ is also equivalent to multiplying every exponent by $p^k$ as we are working in $\mathbb F_p$ (Freshman's dream!), so we have shown the claim. Have Ritwin perform the Euclidean algorithm on $B$ and $C$ until one of his polynomials is $0$ . Then, suppose he ends with $(0,G)$ . By the above claim, Ivy ends with $(0,\Phi(G))$ . However, note that because $$ I_1\mid I_1^{p^k}, $$ Ivy is also performing a Euclidean algorithm, which means from Ivy's process that $$ \gcd(\Phi(B),\Phi(C))=\Phi(G) $$ and we are done! **Remark:** The way found this solution was like this. First, I realized that we can freely subtract constant multiples of $B$ from $C$ because $\Psi$ is an additive function so the Euclidean algorithm is automatically being handled there. However, this alone isn't enough, as eventually in the algorithm, once the degrees are different, we must start subtracting multiples of $x^k$ . So first, I just experimented with trying to replace $C$ with $C-xB$ . When this is done, on the other side, $\gcd(\Psi(B),\Psi(C))$ becomes $\gcd(\Psi(B),\Psi(C-xB))=\gcd(\Psi(B),\Psi(C)-\Psi(xB)).$ In order for this to be a legal Euclidean algorithm move, we must have $\Psi(B)\mid \Psi(xB)$ . After a bit of playing around however, I realized that $\Psi(xB)$ is just $\Psi(B)^p$ , and then I realized this generalized to higher powers of $x$ as well and solved the problem. Finally, I phrased the solution this way to hopefully be easier to understand, and also of course as a tribute to some friends from MOP :D

stem_md: Let  $n \ge 4$  be an integer. Find all functions  $W : \{1, \dots, n\}^2 \to \mathbb R$  such that for every partition  $[n] = A \cup B \cup C$  into disjoint sets, \[ \sum_{a \in A} \sum_{b \in B} \sum_{c \in C} W(a,b) W(b,c) = |A| |B| |C|. \]
solution_md:
oops sniped by v_Enhance

<details><summary>Solution during TST</summary>All solutions are of the following form:  $W(a,a)$  can be anything, and for all distinct  $a,b\in[n]$ ,  $W(a,b)$  equals a constant  $k$ , where either  $k=1$  or  $k=-1$ . It is easy to see that they all work.

Let  $P(A,B,C)$  be the condition. Denote  $f=W$  because laziness. By  $P(\{1\},\{2\},\{3,4,5,\ldots\})$  and  $P(\{1\},\{3\},\{2,4,5,\ldots\})$ , we get that
\[f(1,2)f(2,4)+f(1,2)f(2,5)+\cdots+f(1,2)f(2,n)=(n-2)-f(1,2)f(2,3),\]
\[f(1,3)f(3,4)+f(1,3)f(3,5)+\cdots+f(1,3)f(3,n)=(n-2)-f(1,3)f(3,2).\]
Now, consider  $P(\{1\},\{2,3\},\{4,5,\ldots\})$ . We see that
\[f(1,2)f(2,4)+f(1,2)f(2,5)+\cdots+f(1,2)f(2,n)+f(1,3)f(3,4)+f(1,3)f(3,5)+\cdots+f(1,3)f(3,n)=2(n-3),\]
which becomes
\[(n-2)-f(1,2)f(2,3)+(n-2)-f(1,3)f(3,2)=2(n-3)\implies f(1,2)f(2,3)+f(1,3)f(3,2)=2.\]
Similarly,  $f(a,b)f(b,c)+f(a,c)f(c,b)=2$  for any distinct  $a,b,c$ . By instead considering  $P(\{3,4,5,\ldots\},\{2\},\{1\})$ ,  $P(\{2,4,5,\ldots\},\{3\},\{1\})$ , and  $P(\{4,5,\ldots\},\{2,3\},\{1\})$ , we see that  $f(3,2)f(2,1)+f(2,3)f(3,1)=2$ , which generalizes to give  $f(a,b)f(b,c)+f(b,a)f(a,c)=2$ . Thus, we see that
\[f(a,c)f(c,b)=f(b,a)f(a,c)\implies f(a,c)=0\quad\text{or}\quad f(c,b)=f(b,a)\]
for each triple of distinct  $a,b,c\in[n]$ . Suppose that  $f(a,c)=0$  for some  $a\neq c$ . Then, considering  $P(\{a\},\{c\},[n]-\{a,c\})$ , we see that  $0=n-2$ , a contradiction. Thus, we have  $f(c,b)=f(b,a)$  for all distinct  $a,b,c$ . Letting  $c\in[n]$  be different from  $b,a_1,a_2$ , we see that  $(b,a_1)=f(c,b)=f(b,a_2)$ . Similarly, if  $a\in[n]$  is distinct from  $c_1,c_2,b$ , we see that  $f(c_1,b)=f(b,a)=f(c_2,b)$ . This implies that  $f(x,b)$  and  $f(b,x)$  are constant for each  $b$  for all  $x\neq b$ . This implies that  $f(x,y)$  is itself a constant  $k$  if  $x\neq y$ . From above, we see that  $2k^2=2$ , so  $k=1$  or  $k=-1$ . This gives us the characterization detailed above.</details>
